summary: A flowering shrub native to East China and Japan, it has thin, flexible stems and almost linear leaves. Abundant white flowers appear in spring and early summer.

A deciduous tree native to southwestern Europe and northwestern North Africa, it is rarely found in the Pyrenees despite its common name. It has deeply, irregularly lobed leaves, frequently sends up shoots from its roots and may retain dead leaves when young.

A deciduous oak tree native to southern Europe and southwest Asia. Open-grown trees develop broad, irregular crowns and often several trunks. Minute hairs cover the leaves, especially when young, and the foliage can remain green until early winter.

A clump-forming evergreen perennial native to South Africa, it has long, pale green, sword-like leaves that grow in fans and tend to arch. In spring and summer, it bears pale yellow flowers marked with three dark purple spots and orange outlines.

A tuber-forming flowering plant native to South Africa’s Cape Province. Its highly branched growth bears dull yellow or brown, often speckled flowers with a rotten smell; coastal populations flower annually, while mountain populations flower actively only after fires.

summary: A perennial grass found throughout most of Europe and eastward across much of Asia, and introduced to North America. It forms dense tufts of short, bristle-like grey-green leaves and has slightly feathery, one-sided flower clusters.

Tree fern endemic to New Zealand. Its slender black trunk is usually surrounded by dead brown fronds, while the living fronds spread almost horizontally like a small umbrella. Spreading underground stems can create dense groves.

A feather moss native to western North America from southern Alaska to northern California. Its dark red stems and green leaves form rusty-yellow mats whose colour varies with moisture, and each leaf has one main rib and two fainter side ribs. It forms large clumps on branches, stumps and trunks.

Flowering arum native to rainforests of Maritime Southeast Asia, New Guinea and Australia’s Murray Islands. Its giant heart-shaped leaves can serve as makeshift umbrellas; its starchy rhizome, above-ground stem, leaves and leaf stalks are used as food but must be thoroughly cooked because its irritating sap contains needle-like calcium oxalate crystals.
edibilityNote: Rhizome, above-ground stem, leaves and leaf stalks are food but require thorough cooking because the sap is irritating.

summary: Annual flowering plant native to Texas. Its lightly scented, flat, star-shaped flowers may be single or double and range from white and cream through pink, purple and red to nearly black.
A bulb-forming perennial native to Eurasia. It has green-tinged yellow flowers and favours moist, shady, base-rich places; in East Anglia it has been used as an indicator of ancient woodland.

A perennial onion native to China. Unlike the common onion, it does not form bulbs; its leaves and flowering stems are hollow. It grows in evergreen clumps, with larger varieties resembling leeks and smaller ones resembling chives.
edibilityNote: Used as a scallion or salad onion and as an ingredient, spice, herb or garnish, especially in East and Southeast Asian cuisines.

summary: A small tree described in the source as native to the Andes of Ecuador, Bolivia and Peru, and widely grown for its fruit. Its fruit is made up of fused smaller fruits, and its juice is served in South American bars and restaurants.
edibilityNote: The fruit is cultivated for consumption, including juice served in South America.

summary: An annual vine native to Southern Africa, the horned melon bears spiny fruit with orange skin and soft, lime-green flesh when ripe. A traditional African food, the fruit may be eaten at any ripeness and is mainly served as a snack or salad in northern Zimbabwe.
edibilityNote: Fruit is eaten at any ripeness, mainly as a snack or salad in northern Zimbabwe; some people also eat the peel.

summary: A perennial climbing vine native from Mexico to Venezuela, it produces grape-sized edible fruits with a cucumber-like, slightly sour taste. The fruits are eaten raw or pickled, and each plant can produce hundreds of them.
edibilityNote: Fruit is eaten raw or pickled; it may have been eaten by Indigenous peoples before European colonization.

summary: Large perennial herb native to Mexico, Central America, the West Indies and much of northern South America. Its fleshy rhizomes are edible and processed into an easily digested starch used in foods; archaeological evidence from Colombia shows arrowroot food use by 8200 BC.
edibilityNote: The edible rhizomes yield food starch; evidence of arrowroot food use in Colombia dates to 8200 BC.

summary: A climbing evergreen vine native to China, Japan except Hokkaido, and the Korean peninsula, five-leaf akebia has leaves divided into five notched leaflets. Its clustered flowers have a chocolate-like scent, while its sausage-shaped fruits split open when ripe.
edibilityNote: The sweet fruit pulp is eaten fresh or processed, especially in Japan; the slightly bitter rind is fried and stuffed, while bitter seeds are discarded or swallowed whole.

summary: An upright shrub native from Mexico through Central America and northern South America to Trinidad and Peru. It bears irritating hairs and purple, blue or whitish-lilac flowers, and contact can cause severe dermatitis.

Deciduous blueberry shrub native to the southeastern and south-central United States. Its pale pink, bell-shaped flowers open before the new leaves; edible berries occur in a tart, shiny blue-black form and a sweeter form with a whitish bloom.
edibilityNote: The berries are edible; one variant is tart and shiny blue-black, while another is sweeter with a whitish waxy bloom.

summary: An upright annual native to south and east Asia. Its purple-and-white flowers have yellow throat spots and appear throughout the growing season; it often occupies wet grasslands, streambanks and disturbed ground.

A conifer tree native to central and southern Chile and western Argentina, it has thick, sharply pointed leaves and develops a distinctive umbrella-shaped crown when mature. Its nut-like seeds are edible and traditionally harvested by Indigenous peoples in Argentina and Chile.
edibilityNote: The nut-like seeds are edible and traditionally harvested by Indigenous peoples in Argentina and Chile.

summary: Flowering shrub native to the eastern United States. Its solitary spring flowers are dark red to reddish purple and aromatic, while the leaves also release fragrance when bruised.
edibilityNote: The bark is reportedly edible and used as a cinnamon substitute; caution is advised because an alkaloid may cause heart convulsions.

summary: A large banyan-type fig tree native to eastern South and Southeast Asia, it develops aerial and buttressing roots and broad, shiny oval leaves. In parts of India, its roots are guided across gaps to form living bridges. Young leaf tips can be eaten as salad greens, while its milky latex is toxic if swallowed.
edibilityNote: Young leaf tips are used as salad greens; the milky latex is toxic if ingested, and the small figs are barely edible.

summary: A tree native to Mozambique, Madagascar, Mauritius and nearby Indian Ocean islands, it has richly colored evergreen leaves and thick, irregular stems. Its small, usually white flowers are extremely fragrant and appear in midwinter.

A slow-growing shrub native to tropical Africa from Sudan to Mozambique and west to Côte d’Ivoire and Angola, it often develops several slender stems. Its glossy leaves form rosettes, while its strongly fragrant flowers open white after beginning pink.

A biennial or once-flowering perennial herb native to western, central and southern Europe, extending north to England and southern Wales. Its stems and leaves are densely covered in pale woolly hairs, and its yellow flowers have five orange stamens with densely white-haired stems.

Evergreen shrub or small tree native to southern Japan and the Ryukyu Islands. Its autumn-to-spring flowers are white in wild plants, while cultivated varieties may be pink, red or two-coloured. The leaves can substitute for tea, and refined seed oil is suitable for cooking.
edibilityNote: Leaves are used as a tea substitute; oil pressed from the seeds is suitable for cooking after refining.

summary: Evergreen perennial flowering plant native to Greece and Turkey. Its cup-shaped, hanging flowers appear from late winter into spring, and all parts are poisonous.
edibilityNote: All parts are poisonous; ingesting large quantities can cause mouth and throat burning, vomiting, abdominal cramps and diarrhoea.

summary: A sunflower native to the United States along the Atlantic and Gulf Coasts, cucumberleaf sunflower may be annual or perennial and is usually perennial, but may last only one season where freezes occur. It can spread along the ground into dense cover, with showy flower heads usually yellow in the wild.
A tree native to tropical Africa, it bears showy bell-shaped flowers that are usually red-orange or crimson, but rarely yellow. Its water-filled flower buds can squirt liquid when squeezed.

A perennial herb or shrub native to the Americas from Mexico through Central and South America to Argentina, as well as many Caribbean islands. Its rough, sharply toothed leaves accompany very narrow flower spikes bearing occasional purple-blue to lavender flowers, each lasting only one day.
Perennial herb native to central Europe. It spreads through underground stems and bears globe-shaped heads of purple to reddish flowers bordered by black or dark-brown bracts.

Herbaceous perennial native to Asia from the Caucasus through the Himalayas to China, Japan and Korea. Its orange-red flowers open successively and each lasts only one day. Flowers, young leaves, shoots and tubers are edible, though leaves and shoots should be eaten very young before becoming fibrous.
edibilityNote: Flowers and young tubers may be eaten raw or cooked; leaves and shoots are eaten raw or cooked only while very young.

summary: A woody shrub native to tropical and subtropical Central and South America, including parts of the Caribbean; whether it is native to North America is unknown. It grows upright or scrambles as a climber, with feathery leaves that curl when touched and ridged stems lined with sharp, backward-curving thorns. It is invasive across the tropics and can form impenetrable thickets.
A deciduous shrub native to East Asia, with an upright, vase-shaped habit. Its large trumpet-shaped flowers last only a day each, but abundant buds sustain flowering through much of summer.
edibilityNote: In Korea, the flowers were eaten and the leaves brewed as a herbal infusion.

summary: An evergreen perennial native to Mexico, the Caribbean and South America, it forms colonies of stems with lance-shaped leaves. Its trumpet-shaped flowers are metallic blue to purple, and outside its native range it can form dense invasive stands that threaten native plants.

Evergreen or partly deciduous climber native to southern Brazil, Bolivia, northeastern Argentina and Paraguay. Dense clusters of orange flowers appear from winter to spring, while forked tendrils cling to rough surfaces such as brick walls.

A bulbous flowering plant native to western Asia, from southern Turkey through Syria and Lebanon to northern Israel. It produces strongly fragrant flowers exceptionally early in the season, with cultivated varieties in many bright colours. All parts are reportedly toxic if eaten.
edibilityNote: All parts are reportedly toxic to humans if eaten.

summary: A deciduous tree native to eastern North America, shining sumac has compound leaves with winged central stalks. Its glossy foliage turns brilliant orange-red in autumn, while showy red fruit clusters persist into winter; the sour fruits are edible and can make a lemonade-like drink.
edibilityNote: The sour fruits are edible and can be made into a lemonade-like drink; Native Americans also added them to drinking water for lemony flavour.

summary: Deciduous shrub or small tree native to Japan. Its slightly fragrant, star-shaped white-to-pink flowers appear on bare branches in late winter or early spring, each with at least 12 narrow, petal-like segments.

An evergreen flowering shrub native to southern Japan and southern Korea. It has large, leathery, deeply lobed leaves and dense clusters of small white flowers in late autumn or early winter, followed by black fruit in spring.

A deciduous tree native to southwestern Asia, black mulberry has been cultivated so long that its precise natural range is unknown. Its leaves are rough above and uniformly hairy beneath, and its edible ripe fruit is dark purple to almost black with a rich flavour.
edibilityNote: The ripe fruit is edible; the tree has long been cultivated for it, and the fruit is often made into jams and sherbets.

summary: Poisonous woodland perennial found across much of Europe and in Algeria, Iran, Turkey and the Caucasus. It spreads by underground stems to form dense carpets in shady woodland and beneath hedges, and bears inconspicuous green flowers from late winter into spring.
edibilityNote: All parts are highly poisonous; eating it has caused severe illness and a recorded death, even after boiling and frying.

summary: A deciduous tree or large shrub native to central and southern Europe, northwest Africa, southwest Asia and parts of central Asia, the St Lucie cherry has fragrant white flowers and small fruits that ripen from green through red to dark purple or black and taste very bitter. Its fragrant seed kernels are ground or powdered, or their oil is extracted, for a bitter-almond-flavoured spice used sparingly in sweet foods.
edibilityNote: Seed kernels are ground or powdered, or their oil extracted, and used in small quantities as a spice in sweet foods.

summary: A shrub native to wet soils in the Allegheny Mountains and elsewhere in eastern North America. It has glossy, toothed leaves that turn golden yellow, while fragrant white or sometimes pink flowers form spike-like clusters from early summer through September.

Tropical perennial native to northwestern South America, quito-orange has large heart- or oval-shaped leaves covered in short purple hairs. Its citrus-flavoured fruit has a distinctive ring of green flesh when ripe, and is eaten fresh or used in juice, desserts and native dishes.
edibilityNote: The fruit is eaten fresh and in desserts and native dishes; its freshly squeezed juice is commonly mixed with sugar and water.

summary: A large evergreen banyan tree native to eastern Australia. It is remembered for imposing buttress roots and seedlings that begin in a host tree's canopy, send roots to the ground and may eventually strangle the host.
edibilityNote: The fruits are edible and taste like other fig varieties.

summary: A twining herbaceous vine native from northern South America to Mexico, cypress vine is naturalised elsewhere in the tropics. It has deeply divided leaves and pointed trumpet-shaped flowers that may be red, pink or white.

An evergreen succulent considered native to the southeastern Arabian Peninsula, aloe vera has thick, fleshy, serrated leaves and spreads through offsets. Some varieties have white-flecked leaves, and yellow tubular flowers appear on a tall summer spike.
edibilityNote: The gel is used in yogurts, beverages and desserts; high or prolonged doses of latex or whole-leaf extract can be toxic.

summary: Evergreen flowering shrub native to western North America, from southeastern Alaska to northern California and central New Mexico. It has glossy, holly-like spiny leaflets and dense clusters of yellow spring flowers followed by tart, dusty-blue berries.
edibilityNote: Tart, large-seeded fruits are eaten raw after the first frosts; traditionally used sparingly with sweeter fruit, and now sometimes made into jelly or wine.

summary: An evergreen shrub or small tree native to the Andes of southern Colombia, Ecuador, Peru, western Bolivia and northern Chile. It has strongly fragrant, nodding white or cream trumpet flowers and fine velvety white down on its young shoots, leaves, flower stalks and fruit.

Evergreen shrub native to China, winter daphne is remembered for its intensely fragrant, fleshy pale-pink flowers and glossy foliage. It rarely produces fruit, but when it does, red berries follow the flowers.
edibilityNote: All parts are poisonous to humans.

summary: A rainforest herb native to eastern Australia, cunjevoi has very large, glossy, spade-shaped leaves and heavily scented greenish-cream flowers. The plant is poisonous: eating any part causes immediate pain, burning and swelling of the lips, tongue and mouth, and its sap can irritate skin and eyes.
edibilityNote: All parts are poisonous when eaten, causing immediate oral pain, burning and swelling; a small number of children have died.

summary: A herbaceous plant with no stated native origin, wild leadwort has a pantropical distribution. Its smooth stems may climb, trail or stand upright, and it bears white flowers on sticky, glandular flower stalks.

An evergreen upright shrub native to eastern Asia from the Himalayas to Japan. Its compound leaves are often tinged red when very young or old, and its ripe berries range from bright red to dark violet.
edibilityNote: The source calls all parts poisonous and potentially fatal if ingested, but also cites a category generally considered non-toxic to humans.

summary: Boreal quillwort native to both sides of the northern Atlantic Ocean, lake quillwort occurs widely across northern Europe, with isolated populations in glacial lakes in Bulgaria’s Pirin mountains.

A deciduous shrub native to nearly all of Europe, northern and central Asia, Japan, Greenland, western Canada and the western United States. It spreads by rhizomes into broad patches, and its light-green leaves redden before falling. Its edible blue-black berries contain pigment in both skin and flesh and are widely used in cooking.
edibilityNote: The berries are edible and commonly used in pies, cakes, jams, sauces, syrups, juices and sweets; the leaves may be unsafe to consume.

summary: A salt-tolerant flowering plant of unspecified native origin, it is normally coastal but now flourishes beside European roads and motorways. It has small mauve flowers and is rich in vitamin C.
A small moss native to most of Europe and North America. Its oval leaves are usually broadest above the middle, while stout rootlike threads grow from the leaf joints.
A moss with an almost cosmopolitan distribution. In one study, it showed intermediate sensitivity to exposure to the herbicide Asulam.

Annual flowering plant native to eastern Asia, specifically China and Japan, and now found as a weed nearly worldwide. It has yellow flowers, large divided leaves at its base and wind-dispersed fruits; it can bloom year-round in tropical areas but flowers in late spring and early summer in temperate regions.

Herbaceous perennial native to a very localized area of Peru. Its wiry white stems climb without tendrils, and its leaves, stems and flower buds smell strongly of blackcurrant. Deep purple flowers sit in green cups on long, sticky flower stalks that frequently trap insects.

An evergreen fern native to western Europe and North Africa, common polypody produces isolated fronds along a horizontal rhizome. Its spore clusters appear beneath the fronds, changing from bright yellow or orange to dark grey at maturity.
edibilityNote: The bittersweet rhizome was traditionally used for its aroma in some confectionery, including nougat.

summary: A perennial flowering herb native to the southeastern United States and northern Bahamas, fourleaf vetch grows in moist habitats. It has compound leaves and pea-like flowers, and differs from similar Vicia floridana by larger flowers and longer seed pods.

Evergreen shrub or tree native to eastern China, Taiwan and Japan. Its conspicuous bronze or red young leaves turn green, and fragrant white or pink urn-shaped flowers hang in clusters from branch tips.
edibilityNote: The flowers and leaves are poisonous when eaten and may cause vomiting, heart failure and death in humans.

summary: A low-growing legume vine native to Africa, Asia and Europe. Its pink-and-white flower clusters rise above thick, fern-like foliage, while its aggressive spread can crowd out neighbouring plants and has made it invasive in many US states.

A perennial sedge native to North America, North Asia and Europe, common cottongrass grows in bogs and other open wetlands, often on peat or acidic soil. Its small brown-green flowers develop conspicuous white, cotton-like seed heads in early summer.
edibilityNote: Seeds and stems are used in traditional Alaska Native, Inuit and Inupiat cooking; leaves and roots are also described as edible.

summary: A flowering plant native to Siberia, Altay and Mongolia, elephant's-ears has a thick, creeping, highly branched rhizome and rounded leaves that redden by autumn. It is used locally as a tea substitute.
edibilityNote: Used as a tea substitute in its native Siberia, Altay and Mongolia; the plant part is unspecified.

summary: An aquatic perennial native to wetlands of the south-central and southeastern United States, from Texas to South Carolina. Its narrow blue-green leaves accompany large, lightly scented canary-yellow flowers that open in the evening and wither in the following day's heat.

A clumping perennial sedge native to eastern North America, from eastern Canada and the northeastern and midwestern United States south through the Appalachian Mountains. It typically grows in acidic soil in upland forests, rocky outcrops and Appalachian balds.

A perennial, short-rhizomed sedge found across Europe and the Mediterranean–Caspian region. It forms a tufted base, with a single terminal reddish male flower spike and one to several dense female spikes whose brown fruit cases are hairy.

An aromatic, many-branched subshrub native to parts of South Africa, Zimbabwe and Mozambique, rose-scented geranium has soft, velvety, deeply cut leaves. The natural form smells minty, while cultivars may smell of rose, citrus, cinnamon, fruit, or little at all.
edibilityNote: The flowers and leaves are used to flavour cakes, preserves, frozen desserts, salads, sugars and teas.

summary: A deciduous flowering vine native to several provinces of China. Its counterclockwise-twining stems support masses of fragrant white, violet or blue flowers, which open together before the spring foliage expands.
edibilityNote: All parts contain wisterine and are toxic if eaten; reported effects include nausea, vomiting, stomach pain and diarrhoea.

summary: A perennial climbing flowering plant native across almost all of Britain, Ireland and their associated islands. Branched tendrils curl around nearby plants, while its mostly hairless stems bear reddish-lilac or lilac-blue flowers followed by black pods.

Tuberous perennial native to Mediterranean woodlands, shrublands and rocky areas from southern France to western Turkey and on Mediterranean islands. It flowers before its ivy-like, naturally patterned leaves appear in autumn, grows through winter and lies dormant in summer.

A moss widespread across cool, moist parts of the Northern Hemisphere, flat-top bogmoss grows as upright carpets on land or submerged in water. It ranges from green to yellow-brown and has a star-shaped, domed head when viewed from above.

A grass-like perennial native to northern North America, from Newfoundland to easternmost Alaska and south into Pennsylvania and New Mexico. It forms clumps of slender, sharp-edged leaves and bears small groups of purple flowers with yellow bases and stamens.

An evergreen tropical shrub native from Malesia through Papuasia to Queensland and several Pacific islands. Its thick, shiny leaves vary dramatically in shape and may show vivid patterns of green, yellow, purple and other colours, depending on the variety and light.
edibilityNote: The entire plant is poisonous; its fruit is inedible and toxic, and eating the seeds can be fatal to children or adults.

summary: A woodland shrub native to much of western and southern Europe, Algeria, Morocco and the Azores. Its glossy evergreen leaves cluster near the shoot tips, while honey-scented yellow-green flowers appear in late winter and early spring. All parts, including its black berries, are poisonous to humans.
edibilityNote: All parts, including the fruit, are poisonous to humans.

summary: A deciduous shrub native to the Himalayas and southwestern China. Its hanging clusters pair small pale flowers with purple-pink bracts, followed by berries that become soft, sweet and deep purple-brown when ripe; unripe berries are unpleasantly bitter.
edibilityNote: Only soft, ripe, deep purple-brown berries are described as sweet and edible; unripe berries are unpleasantly bitter.

summary: A perennial flowering plant native to Armenia, Iran and Turkey. Its thick, curved leaves have a soft, silver-grey, felt-like covering resembling lamb’s ears. In Brazil, it is sometimes eaten after being breaded and fried, with a reportedly fish-like taste.
edibilityNote: In Brazil, it is sometimes breaded and fried, with a reportedly fish-like taste.

summary: Large dry-season deciduous or semi-evergreen tree native to the Indian subcontinent and Indochina. Its heart-shaped leaves have notably extended tips, and the tree is sacred in Hinduism, Buddhism, Sikhism and Jainism.

An evergreen shrub or small tree native to the Iberian Peninsula, Morocco, the Macaronesian archipelagos and the French Basque Country. It has glossy dark-green leaves, white flowers and cherry-like fruit that ripens dark purple or black. Fully ripe fruit is somewhat edible, but bitter fruit should not be eaten.
edibilityNote: Fully ripe fruit is somewhat edible, but bitter fruit may contain too much hydrogen cyanide and should not be eaten.

summary: A rhizomatous perennial endemic to the southern and central United States, Copper Iris grows in freshwater wetlands. Its slightly fragrant flowers range from copper-red to deep red, with all six petals drooping outward.
edibilityNote: The foliage and rhizomes are described as deadly toxic.

summary: Red seaweed of unstated native origin, purple laver forms smooth, delicate sheets only one cell thick and often clings to rocks. Usually brownish, it becomes a dark green pulp when boiled and is eaten as laverbread.
edibilityNote: The seaweed is edible and is boiled into a dark green pulp used to make laverbread.

summary: Variable evergreen perennial native to southern Africa, from Mozambique to South Africa. Its compact 'Meyersii' form has dense foliage plumes valued for flower arranging, and the species is widely cultivated.

A flowering liana native to Central America, the Caribbean, northern South America and Africa, it produces the largest seedpods in the pea family. Its buoyant seeds can remain viable while drifting on ocean currents for at least two years.

A shrub or small tree native to the Central American tropics and northern South America, although its exact origin is unknown. Its soft-spined red-brown pods expose seeds covered by waxy blood-red arils. The ground seeds provide annatto, an orange-red condiment and food coloring used widely in traditional dishes.
edibilityNote: Ground seeds are used as a spice or paste; heating them in oil or fat extracts color and subtle flavor for foods.

summary: A flowering perennial native to parts of southeastern and south-central Canada and the eastern and north-central United States. Its small white flowers appear in spring and early summer, with purple veins on the lower petals and often backward-bent upper petals. Reddish stalks support heart-shaped, sparsely hairy leaves.

A herbaceous perennial native to central and eastern Asia, from eastern Tibet through northern China to eastern Siberia. Its late-spring buds open into fragrant cup- or bowl-shaped flowers in white, pink or crimson, and many cultivated forms have extra petals.
Conifer tree native to south-central and southeast China. It has a pyramidal crown and spirally arranged, narrow green leaves; its fragrant, durable wood resists termites, rot and many fungi.

Small deciduous tree native to China and considered vulnerable in the wild. Tearing a leaf exposes latex strands that solidify like rubber and hold the pieces together; its fruit is a single-seeded winged structure resembling an elm fruit.
A conifer tree endemic to Norfolk Island, it is not a true pine and has a straight trunk with regularly layered, symmetrical branches. Its mature cones break apart to release nut-like edible seeds.
edibilityNote: The nut-like seeds released when mature cones break apart are edible.

summary: An epiphytic fern native to tropical and subtropical parts of the Americas. Its creeping rhizome is densely covered with golden-brown scales, and its large, deeply lobed fronds range from bright to bluish green. The fronds remain evergreen with year-round rain but may be briefly shed where there is a marked dry season.

An evergreen woody vine or scrambling shrub native from Florida and southern Texas through Bermuda, Mexico, Central America and the Caribbean to the Galápagos and tropical South America. It bears yellow bell-shaped flowers throughout the year and white fruits usually containing two dark-brown seeds.

Flowering mallow native to the Great Plains of the United States and neighbouring northern Mexico. It spreads across the ground with cut leaves and masses of wine-crimson, cup-shaped flowers, while its above-ground growth largely dies back in winter.

A flowering perennial herb native to Brazil and Argentina, though it is often grown as an annual in temperate climates because it is not fully hardy. It has spreading stems, toothed leaves and scented clusters of bright purple or magenta summer flowers.
A branching aromatic plant native across a wide region of Eurasia and North America. It grows in open places with dry sandy soil, including steppes, rocky slopes and waste ground.

A low-growing perennial herb native to eastern North America, from Newfoundland west to Ontario and Minnesota and south to Georgia. Its basal leaves accompany five-petalled flowers that are violet or dark blue, and occasionally white.

Orchid native to mainland Europe, western Asia and the Mediterranean area. Its leaves are reduced to scales, and the adult plant is believed to depend entirely on fungi for nutrition. Seedlings develop underground for eight to ten years before flowering.
Herbaceous perennial flowering plant native mainly to mountainous areas of Southern Europe. It has leaves divided into nine leaflets and bowl-shaped deep pink or deep red flowers in late spring.

A tropical annual native to Central America, including Panama and Guatemala, globe amaranth has rounded flowerheads with tiny, inconspicuous true flowers. Cultivars come in vivid colours, and the flowerheads retain their shape and colour after drying.
edibilityNote: Documented as an edible plant, but the edible parts and preparation are not specified.

summary: A large perennial grass originating in New Guinea. Its stout, jointed stalks contain fibrous white pith in sugary sap; stem pieces have been chewed since ancient times for the sweet juice, which was later extracted and boiled into a concentrate.
edibilityNote: Stem pieces have long been chewed for sweet juice; the extracted juice was later boiled to concentrate it.

summary: Deciduous tree native to south-central and southeastern China. Its hanging flower heads are surrounded by two large white bracts that flutter like doves or handkerchiefs, while its hard nuts contain seeds that may take three years to germinate.

A small deciduous tree native to East Asia, including Korea, China and Japan, kousa dogwood has showy whitish bracts that may fade red and sweet pink-to-red berries. The berry pulp is eaten raw, while the tough, bitter rind is usually discarded; the fruit is sometimes made into wine, and young leaves can be cooked and eaten.
edibilityNote: Berry pulp is eaten raw; the edible but tough, bitter rind is usually discarded. Fruit is sometimes made into wine, and young leaves are cooked.

summary: A herbaceous perennial whose chromosome count points to Mexico as its origin; it is widespread from the southeastern United States to northern South America. It has hairy, scallop-edged leaves and variable flowers, with the naturalized variety typically bearing tubular bright-red blooms.

Herbaceous perennial native to the southeastern United States, extending north along the eastern coast to New Jersey. Its purple or pinkish flowers bloom from spring through summer, with each flower lasting about one day. Mature capsules burst open and propel the seeds away from the parent plant.

An evergreen vine native to South America, it occurs naturally from southeastern Brazil to Argentina, Uruguay and Paraguay. It climbs by winding its leaf stalks around supports and bears abundant white or pale blue flowers, followed by dark blue or black berries.
edibilityNote: The plant is poisonous and may cause abdominal pain if ingested.

summary: Orchid native from Mexico to Nicaragua, and possibly Costa Rica. Its small, single flowers are red with yellow or brown speckles and smell strongly of coconuts.

A small flowering plant native to southeastern Asia. It has hairless, kidney-shaped to round leaves with scalloped, shallowly lobed edges, and small faint-yellow flowers tinged with purple. It grows in habitats ranging from dry ground to occasionally submerged sites and can appear in pavement cracks.

An evergreen shrub or small tree native to Asia. Its deeply veined, crinkled leaves are dark blue-green above and pale and downy beneath; fragrant creamy-white spring flowers are followed by blue berries that ripen glossy black.
An annual flowering herb native to South America, including Brazil. It has purplish flowers packed into short, compact spikes and has become an invasive weed in many regions outside its native range.

A flowering shrub or small tree native to the southeastern United States and northeastern Mexico, Eastern Coral Bean has curved spines. Its bright red tubular flowers grow in long spikes and are followed by pods of vivid red seeds.
edibilityNote: In some Central American countries, the flowers are traditionally added to bean soup or meat patties; this report is marked citation needed.

summary: A deciduous flowering shrub native to China, Taiwan and Vietnam, Chinese privet has densely hairy shoots and white flowers. Its rounded fruit is considered poisonous.
edibilityNote: Its fruit is considered poisonous.

summary: A branching shrub native to eastern North America from Canada into the central United States, it has glossy leaves that turn red in autumn and white or pink late-spring flowers followed by black fruit in September. The raw fruit is astringent, but tastes better in recipes with added sugar.
edibilityNote: The fruit is eaten in recipes with added sugar; raw fruit is astringent.

summary: Willow shrub or small tree native to much of temperate Canada and the United States. It has dark, scaly bark and thick leaves that are hairy underneath; silky catkins emerge before the leaves in early spring.
Perennial herb native to North America, occurring in eastern Canada and much of the United States, especially the south-central states. It bears yellow flowers and attracts bees and butterflies.
Shrub native to the eastern and central United States, Ontario and northeastern Mexico. It spreads by underground stems and bears purple-red fruits that persist through winter.

A shrub or vine native to central and eastern North America, it has trailing or climbing stems that can root where they touch the ground. Fragrant pink, occasionally white, flowers bloom from May to July, followed by bright-red rose hips later in summer.

Flowering plant native to North America and occurring mainly in the eastern United States, with additional inland reports from Tennessee, Arkansas and Oklahoma. It inhabits hardwood forests, longleaf pinelands and wooded floodplains, as well as disturbed roadsides and firebreaks.

An evergreen flowering shrub native to Japan, Taiwan, China, Vietnam, the Philippines and the Russian Far East, Japanese skimmia has glossy leaves and fragrant spring flowers. Fruit develops on female plants in autumn, although one variety has bisexual flowers.

A small herbaceous perennial native to Bermuda and the southeastern United States. It spreads along the ground and occurs in habitats including pine-oak savannas and woods, with a preference for strong light and dry loamy soil.

A flowering plant with a disjunct distribution across parts of Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria, Cyprus, Turkey and Morocco. Its flower structure rises above the leaves and has a white inner sheath with purple accents around a small dark-purple central spike. It is threatened by agricultural development and urbanization.
An evergreen coniferous shrub or small tree native to Australia. It has green or bluish-green leaves and rounded female cones borne in clusters.

An annual grass native to most of the United States and southwestern Canada. It grows through winter and produces mature grain by April; its small edible grains were dried, processed and cooked by Native Americans before maize-based agriculture became dominant.
edibilityNote: Small grains were dried, processed and cooked; Native Americans cultivated and ate them during the Pre-Columbian era.

summary: A herbaceous perennial native to Europe and western Asia, it forms ground-covering mats with short upright shoots bearing soft violet flowers. It is sometimes grown as an edible herb, and its slightly bitter, astringent foliage was used as a tea substitute in 19th-century France.
edibilityNote: Sometimes grown as an edible herb; used as a tea substitute in 19th-century France because of its tea-like smell.

summary: An evergreen vine native to Southeast Asia, particularly Indochina, it bears large pale blue, violet or mauve trumpet-shaped flowers in hanging clusters. Its extensive tuberous roots readily resprout, helping it form dense, difficult-to-remove growth.
edibilityNote: In Assam, India, the leaves are eaten as a leaf vegetable.

summary: A herbaceous perennial climbing plant native to East Africa. Its bright, entirely orange flowers lack the dark centre of the related black-eyed Susan vine, and flowering may continue year-round in warmer climates but is limited to summer and autumn in cooler ones.

An herbaceous perennial native to China, Japan, Korea and Sakhalin, it bears male and female flowers on separate plants, although sterile flowers with both forms occasionally occur. Its shoots are traditionally treated to reduce harshness before being fried, steamed or boiled.
edibilityNote: Shoots are eaten after treatments such as soaking, boiling or frying; the plant contains liver-toxic and carcinogenic pyrrolizidine alkaloids.

summary: Deciduous shrub native to eastern North America. Its arching stems form a mound, while thin strips of outer bark peel away to reveal brown inner bark; white to pinkish flowers are followed by drooping clusters of papery seed pods.

A bulbous ornamental herb of uncertain native origin, the garden tulip is widely cultivated in many countries. It is tall and late-blooming, usually bearing one large, showy flower above broad, spear-shaped leaves, while its bulb produces side bulbs.
edibilityNote: Bulbs may be eaten with little ill effect or dried, powdered and added to cereals or flour; flowers and bulbs can cause dermatitis.

summary: Deciduous tree native to Japan, Korea, eastern China and Taiwan. Its short trunk divides into a broad, vase-shaped crown, while its leaves turn yellow, orange and red in autumn. Gray bark may peel in patches to reveal orange beneath.

A slow-growing evergreen conifer endemic to Japan, koyamaki has reddish-brown bark that peels in vertical strips. Its glossy dark green, needle-like modified stems form distinctive umbrella-shaped clusters at the branch ends, while its seed cones take about two years to mature.

Annual flowering herb native to western Europe and western North Africa. It flowers in spring, bearing pink flowers with dark red or purple tips, while its weak branched stems become sprawling or climbing.

A compact biennial herb native to central and northern Europe, common lousewort grows on moist acidic ground such as moorland, heath and marsh edges. Its pinkish-purple, white-marked flowers have a hooded upper lip with two small teeth, and it partly feeds by tapping nearby plants’ roots for water and nutrients.

An annual sunflower-family herb widespread across tropical and subtropical regions worldwide. It usually has one central stem and flower heads packed with pink, purple or red florets but no ray florets, followed by hairy seeds.
Evergreen fern native to the Northern Hemisphere. Its most striking feature is its simple, strap-shaped, undivided fronds.
edibilityNote: An 18th-century manuscript contains a recipe for hart’s-tongue ale.

summary: A deciduous shrub native to the southeastern United States. Its stems are often covered in glandular bristles, while its pink or purple pea-like flowers hang in small clusters above flat pods.
A herbaceous perennial of unstated native origin. It has flat heads of many small flowers, downward-angled stiff hairs on the stem, and a basal rosette of spear-shaped leaves.

A finely hairy annual flowering plant native to southern and western Europe and North Africa. It sprawls across dry, sandy ground, often near the sea, and bears clusters of lemon-yellow pea-like flowers, some of which may be inverted.
A flowering plant native to mainland Portugal. It grows mainly on coastal rocks and cliffs, only rarely in stony, salty inland places.

A shrub native to Mediterranean parts of Spain, Italy, Greece and Turkey, including several islands. It is pale yellow overall, with orange flowers and coiled, hairy-centred pods, and primarily grows among shrubs on rocky shores.

A herbaceous plant native to eastern North America, excluding Mexico. Its nettle-like serrated leaves and most other surfaces bear stiff bristles, while spikes of unusually white flowers open in summer.

Deciduous shrub or small tree native from the northern Mediterranean through Southwest and Central Asia, from Spain and southern France east to Afghanistan and Tajikistan. Its shoots zigzag, with one straight and one curved spine at each bend, and its dry nut sits in the centre of a distinctive circular wing.
A creeping or climbing perennial vine native to the Americas, corkystem passionflower develops corky lower stems as it ages. Leaves on the same plant can vary greatly in shape and size.
edibilityNote: The fruit is described as inedible, but the source also notes unverified claims that people eat it.

summary: A grass-like flowering plant native to central and southwestern Texas and northeastern Mexico, Texas sotol has a small crown and long foliage. Indigenous peoples pit-bake its crowns, then dry and pound them into bread flour; its fermented inner cores are also used to make sotol.
edibilityNote: Indigenous peoples pit-bake crowns for bread flour; fermented inner cores have historically been used to make the alcoholic drink sotol.

summary: A shrub or small tree native to central and northwestern Mexico and the southwestern United States. It has curved prickles, crowded bright-scarlet flowers and scarlet seeds; the seed walls are potentially lethal if eaten.
edibilityNote: The seed walls are potentially lethal if consumed because they contain alkaloids.

summary: A flowering shrub with a Mediterranean distribution. It can dominate limestone shrublands and is used as a purgative; a 2020 mainland Portugal assessment reported only one known population of 40 plants and classified it as Critically Endangered.

summary: A flowering plant of unspecified native origin, balm-leaved figwort occurs in Portugal along waterways, in wet meadows and beneath alder, chestnut or cork-oak woods. It favours cool, shady places and sometimes grows in disturbed sites.
An evergreen perennial native to central and southern Africa, from South Africa north to Cameroon and Tanzania. It grows in clumps with upright, grass-like leaves and small blue flowers.
A small evergreen succulent native to South Africa, it bears violet flowers and grows in upland areas.
A flowering plant native to Southern Africa. It forms fan-shaped basal tufts and bears short-lived white, lily-like flowers marked with yellow and violet.

Evergreen fern native to Atlantic coasts of western Europe and northwest Africa and western Mediterranean coasts. Its dark green, slightly leathery fronds grow mainly in sea-cliff crevices, often within reach of salt spray, while inland plants rarely persist.

A succulent coastal perennial of unspecified native origin, sea sandwort ranges around temperate and Arctic coasts of northern Europe, northern Asia and North America. It forms patches above the high-water mark, with branching stems buried in sand and paired fleshy leaves. Shoots and leaves are eaten raw, cooked or fermented; seeds are ground and added to flour or used as garnish.
edibilityNote: Shoots and leaves are eaten raw, cooked or fermented; seeds are ground and added to flour or used as garnish.

summary: A fleshy flowering perennial native to mainland Portugal, the Azores and Madeira. Its rounded leaves have a navel-like central depression and form rosettes, while pale pink-green, bell-shaped flowers appear from May.
A bulb-growing flowering plant native to Western Europe and Morocco. It produces dense clusters of scentless, star-like violet-blue flowers in April and May.
Perennial flowering herb native to eastern North America. Its pea-shaped pink-to-purple flowers bloom from July to September, and it is a larval host for several butterflies.

A flowering climber native to southern China, including Hainan, as well as Taiwan, Laos and Japan, including the Ryukyu Islands. It has fleshy, glossy leaves and clusters of star-shaped, heavily scented flowers that look waxy or porcelain-like. The same flowering stems can produce new blooms each year.

A conifer native to mainland Australia and New Guinea. Young trees bear awl-shaped leaves, while mature trees have curved, scale-like leaves; mature cones disintegrate to release edible, nut-like seeds.
edibilityNote: Mature cones disintegrate and release edible, nut-like seeds.

summary: A massive evergreen tree native to South America's Pampas, it has separate male and female plants and a broad, umbrella-like canopy. Its trunk is soft and spongy rather than true wood, and its sap is poisonous.
edibilityNote: The sap is described as poisonous, but ingestion-specific human toxicity and food use are not documented.

summary: An African fig tree of tropical and subtropical forests and woodlands, the knobbly fig often begins on another plant and later develops a strangling habit. Its bitter figs grow on wart-like, leafless branchlets along the trunk and main branches, and are eaten raw.
edibilityNote: The bitter figs are eaten raw.

summary: Prostrate succulent shrub native to Australia and South Africa’s Cape Provinces, growing as an annual or short-lived perennial. Its trailing stems carry fleshy leaves that are rounded to three-sided in cross-section and purple, daisy-like flowers; it grows in salty habitats such as coastal dunes and samphire flats.

A tall, many-branched herb native to Western Europe, including the British Isles, and the northern Mediterranean. It grows as a weed on farmland and disturbed ground and has been introduced to regions including southwestern Australia and North America.

A subtropical, succulent-leaved plant endemic to the Canary Islands except Lanzarote, it also occurs as a subspontaneous plant in Portugal’s Serra de Sintra. It has woolly growth and soft leaves whose margins are widest near the base.

A succulent perennial naturally endemic to South Africa’s Western Cape, it forms sprawling groundcover with bright pink-purple flowers. Its stout, sword-shaped, dull blue-green leaves sometimes have reddish edges, and its edible fruits are traditionally made into jam in southern Africa.
edibilityNote: The fruits are edible and traditionally used to make jam in southern Africa.

summary: A perennial herb of unspecified native origin, it occurs in South Africa on moist sandy slopes and flats in northwestern and southwestern Cape Province. Its cream flowers are often reddish outside and in the throat, and it has the longest flower tube in its genus.

A gymnosperm native to southern Japan, including the Ryukyu Islands, it has a thick, fibrous trunk crowned with glossy dark-green leaves. Its pith supplies edible starch for sago only after careful repeated washing and cooking to remove toxins; seeds should not be eaten, and all parts are toxic.
edibilityNote: Pith starch is made into sago after careful repeated washing and cooking; seeds should not be eaten, and all plant parts contain toxins.

summary: Orchid found across Europe, North Africa and southwestern Asia. Its flowers are usually pink to red, but rarely white, and it may pass many years without flowering.

summary: A perennial herb native to Europe and central and western Asia, hedge woundwort grows in woodland edges, hedgerows and rough ground. It has spikes of purple, white-marked flowers and leaves that release an unpleasant smell when crushed or bruised.

A hardy herbaceous perennial native to most of temperate and subarctic Europe and western Asia. Its hairy, branching stems bear deeply divided leaves and solitary bright-crimson flowers from May to October. It commonly grows in grassland, especially coastal dunes, as well as open woodland and rocky slopes on lime-rich soils.

A deciduous shrub or small tree native to eastern North America, it has a short crooked trunk, spreading branches and leaves that turn red in autumn. Its dark blue-black fruit hangs until winter and becomes edible after frost; the Meskwaki eat it raw or cooked as jam.
edibilityNote: Fruit becomes edible after frost; the Meskwaki eat it raw and cook it into jam.

summary: A perennial flowering herb native to warmer parts of the central and eastern United States. It bears lavender to bluish tubular flowers near the middle of its stems. Unlike many herbs, it keeps growing as its fruit matures and may become twice as tall after flowering.

A reed-stemmed orchid found in Neotropical montane forests, including southeastern Peru and Brazil, though it also occurs near sea level in disturbed Brazilian roadsides. It is a poorly understood complex with many varieties, bearing lilac, red, orange or yellow flowers around the central stem and unusually long orchid seeds.

A red alga of rocky North Atlantic coasts in Europe and North America, with soft, branching fronds ranging from greenish-yellow to dark purple. It forms a jelly when boiled and is traditionally used fresh to thicken milk-based carrageen pudding in Scotland and Ireland.
edibilityNote: Traditionally used fresh as a thickener in carrageen pudding, a milk-based dish eaten in Scotland and Ireland.

summary: Coastal flowering plant with no stated native origin, found on sandy shores of every continent except Antarctica. Its seeds float in seawater, and it has white flowers and narrower leaves than the similar, usually purple-flowered Ipomoea pes-caprae.
A green alga with a generally worldwide distribution across Atlantic and Pacific waters. Its branched fronds are completely tubular with rounded tips, and it may reproduce throughout the year.

A red seaweed recorded on rocky North Atlantic intertidal coasts. Its reddish-brown, channelled fronds distinguish it from Irish moss; in Ireland and Scotland it is collected with Irish moss, dried and sold for cooking.
edibilityNote: Collected in Ireland and Scotland, dried, and sold for cooking, often alongside Irish moss.

summary: Spiny evergreen shrub native to tropical and southern Africa. It has glossy leaves, fragrant white flowers whose scent strengthens at night, and crimson fruit that may appear year-round in moderate coastal areas. The fruit is eaten raw or made into pies, preserves and sauces.
edibilityNote: The fruit is eaten raw and made into pies, jams, jellies and sauces; it is also described as a traditional African food.

summary: A perennial moss native to southern South America, southern Africa, southern and eastern Australia, New Zealand and other Southern Hemisphere islands, heath star-moss forms dense yellowish-to-olive carpets. Broken stem tips and even whole cushions can spread by wind, animals or people, allowing extensive colonies to develop.
A perennial native to Europe, heath milkwort grows in heaths and grassy places. Its lower leaves occur in opposite pairs, and it flowers from May to August.
A perennial mat-forming herb native across much of northern and central Europe. It has hairless, four-sided stems and whorls of leaves, and mainly grows on light, non-calcareous soils.

Perennial flowering herb native to eastern and central North America. It bears yellow, daisy-like flowerheads from midsummer to early autumn; unlike true sunflowers, its outer ray flowers are fertile.

A deciduous, multi-stemmed shrub native to the eastern United States, wild hydrangea can spread rapidly into colonies. Its bark peels away in successive thin layers of different colours, inspiring the name sevenbark.

A small leafy annual of unspecified native origin, this plant occurs across warm, dry regions from Macaronesia and North Africa to Arabia, Pakistan and southern Africa. Its ground seeds were made into gruel by Egyptian Bedouins, while the leaves are locally eaten during famines.
edibilityNote: Egyptian Bedouins made gruel from ground seeds; leaves are locally eaten during famines.

summary: A loosely growing moss of unspecified native origin. It commonly covers boreal forest floors in Canada, Scandinavia and northern Russia.

Flowering plant native to European mountains from east-central Spain and southern Italy through the Alps and Balkans to the eastern Carpathians. In mainland Portugal, 2016–2019 assessments classified it as Critically Endangered; one recently rediscovered known site may hold fewer than 50 mature plants, following historical records from at least three additional Gerês sites.

summary: A large shrub or small tree endemic to an area near Albany in Western Australia. It forms a dense crown, often reaching the ground, and produces lavender to rose-pink pom-pom flower heads from spring to midsummer.

An evergreen fern native to the Americas, the southern sword fern has long, highly divided fronds and a slim, tuberous underground stem. Wild plants have erect fronds, while the Boston fern and some other cultivars arch gracefully.
An herb with jointed, slightly grooved stems, Juba's bush has smooth-edged opposite leaves and minute greenish-white flowers. It is used in Peru to treat ovary inflammation.

A sprawling shrub or small tree native to tropical and subtropical South America, specifically Argentina, Brazil and Paraguay. Its branches may be upright, reclining or nearly vine-like, and it bears dense clusters of small fruit.
edibilityNote: Dried drupes are sold as pink peppercorns and the seeds season food, though fruit compounds may cause throat irritation and digestive illness.

summary: An evergreen shrub native to East and Southeast Asia, Fortune's spindle can creep or climb like a vine using small rootlets on its stems. Its juvenile climbing phase does not flower, but elevated growth can develop into a flowering adult form without climbing rootlets.

A woody climbing vine native to eastern North America, occurring in thickets, moist woods and along streams. Its purple-black berries contain a distinctive crescent-shaped seed, but the fruit is poisonous and may be mistaken for wild grapes.
edibilityNote: All parts are poisonous; the fruit can be fatal and may be confused with wild grapes.

summary: Virginia spiderwort is a clump-forming herbaceous perennial native to the eastern and central United States, Ontario and Cuba. It spreads through underground stems into large colonies, bearing short-lived pink, white, blue or purple flowers daily for several weeks.
edibilityNote: Cherokee people historically mixed young leaves with other greens and ate them raw or boiled; leaves and sap may cause mild mouth and stomach irritation.

summary: An underwater seagrass found in the Mediterranean, along parts of the North African Atlantic coast, and around the Canary Islands and Madeira. It forms seabed meadows and has very narrow light-green or grey-green leaves; inconspicuous grass-like flowers sometimes appear in spring.

sources.attribution: Andre Carapeto % Ana Francisco, Paulo Pereira, Miguel Porto, felipe (2020). Lista Vermelha da Flora Vascular de Portugal Continental. Plazi.org taxonomic treatments database. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/ge693f accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-12.

summary: A perennial flowering herb common across northern Europe and western Asia, especially in nutrient-poor heathland and damp grassland. Its root develops a woody, blunt-ended stump, while its tightly packed flower heads are usually bluish to violet.

A trailing herbaceous vine found on pantropical and subtropical upper beaches, cliffs and dunes. It forms leafy mats, tolerates salt and produces buoyant seeds carried by ocean currents. Young seeds and pods are edible, especially after boiling, and the flowers can be made into a spice.
edibilityNote: Young seeds and pods are edible, especially after boiling; the flowers can be made into a spice.

summary: Terrestrial orchid native to Japan, Korea, Myanmar and China. It has pleated, spear-shaped leaves and produces clusters of magenta-pink flowers after emerging from dormancy in early spring.

A flowering plant native to dry, barren coastal sands of the southeastern United States. It often grows with sand pine or oaks and regenerates from seed after periodic wildfires; despite resembling culinary rosemary, it is inedible.
edibilityNote: The plant is explicitly described as inedible.

summary: A seaweed of unspecified native origin, it occurs in warmer waters around the Canary Islands, Caribbean, Hawaii, Singapore and Western Australia. Its olive-to-bright-green growth forms dense clumps, with fine branched bristles arranged like a stiff bottlebrush.
An annual herb originating in the tropical Americas, asthma plant is notably hairy and produces abundant white latex, with dense clusters of flowers and fruit held close to the stem.

A toxic autumn-blooming herbaceous perennial native to Great Britain and Ireland, autumn crocus produces flowers well before its leaves appear. It is lethally toxic because of colchicine, and its leaves have been mistaken by foragers for wild garlic.
edibilityNote: All parts are regarded as poisonous; corms have the highest toxin levels, and leaves have been mistaken by foragers for wild garlic.

summary: An evergreen shrub or tree native to central and southern Florida, the Caribbean, Bermuda, eastern Mexico and Central America. It typically grows in partly shaded coastal hammocks and other sandy areas.
A herbaceous orchid native to northern Europe. Its dense flower spikes have a light clove-like scent and white, pink or pink-purple flowers, which bloom in summer and are pollinated mainly by moths.

summary: A perennial herb native to Switzerland, with a wider European–West Asian distribution. It grows in varied habitats but prefers cool, damp places, and has opposite stalked leaves and large two-lipped flowers with a hood-shaped upper lip.

sources.title: Prunella grandiflora (L.) Scholler
sources.attribution: GBIF Secretariat (2023). GBIF Backbone Taxonomy. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/39omei accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-15.

summary: A flowering comfrey found throughout Europe, with softly hairy, deeply veined leaves and pale creamy-yellow flowers. In spring, fresh young leaves may be cooked but are mildly toxic and not eaten raw; the roasted root is used as a coffee substitute.
edibilityNote: Fresh young leaves may be cooked in spring but are mildly toxic and not eaten raw; roasted root is used as a coffee substitute.

summary: A woody shrub native to Australia, heath-leaved banksia occurs naturally in separate parts of central and northern coastal New South Wales. Its orange or red autumn flower spikes stand out against fine, heath-like green foliage. Fire kills the parent plant, but opens its seed-bearing structures, allowing regeneration from seed.
Medium-sized fern endemic to New Zealand, the silver fern is widely associated with the country and appears on the symbol of its national rugby team, the All Blacks.

Rhizomatous herbaceous perennial found across most of Europe, Central Asia and Russia. It has grass-like leaves and branched flower spikes bearing scentless pure-white flowers with bright-yellow anthers from June through August.
Flowering plant with no native origin given in the supplied information. It bears long spikes of blue, pink, purple or white flowers; cultivated varieties also include red and white forms.

A fern with no explicitly stated native origin, found across Central and South America. It usually grows on trees, where its fine, scaly roots form baskets that collect leaf litter and dust; it has simple leaves with a wax-like coating when dry.

A flowering plant native to Iceland, the Faroes, Europe, Macaronesia and northwest Africa. It can produce nuisance growth in lakes and streams and has been introduced to Australia, New Zealand and parts of northern North America.

A flowering plant native to Mexico and Central America, Mexican sunflower may be annual or perennial depending on the area. It grows upright, sometimes as a woody shrub, and bears showy, honey-scented yellow-to-orange flowers, mostly from April to June.

A herbaceous perennial climber native to East Africa. It has twining stems, heart- or arrow-shaped leaves and usually warm-orange flowers with a characteristic dark centre; cultivated forms vary widely in flower colour and may lack the dark centre.

A tree whose native origin is not stated, it is distributed from northeastern South Africa to Uganda and Kenya. Its bark can be harvested repeatedly to make barkcloth, while the tree remains unharmed, and it is also valued for fast-growing, hardy bonsai.

A deciduous tree native to much of Europe, little-leaf linden has heart-shaped leaves with small brown hair tufts at the vein joints and richly scented yellow-green flowers visited heavily by bees. Its young leaves can be eaten as a salad vegetable.
edibilityNote: Young leaves can be eaten as a salad vegetable.

summary: A herbaceous orchid native across parts of southern Europe, Mediterranean islands, Turkey and the Caucasus. Its basal leaves bear purplish-brown spots, while its flowers range from creamy white or pale yellow to pink and purple in some varieties.

sources.title: Lista Vermelha da Flora Vascular de Portugal Continental — Orchis provincialis
sources.attribution: Andre Carapeto % Ana Francisco, Paulo Pereira, Miguel Porto, felipe (2020). Lista Vermelha da Flora Vascular de Portugal Continental. Plazi.org taxonomic treatments database. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/ge693f accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-12.

summary: A perennial orchid widespread across Europe, northwest Africa and parts of the Middle East. Its pinkish-purple to purple flowers bloom from April to June, while some plants have brownish-purple leaf spots. The nectarless flowers resemble other species and attract pollinating insects.
edibilityNote: Ground tubers of this or some other orchid species are used to make the flour salep or sachlav.

summary: A low, clump-forming perennial herb found wild predominantly in Europe and western Asia. Its yellow flowers almost always have four notched petals, an unusual number in the rose family. The bitter root has little food value but is used in regional liqueurs, while the dry fruits are inedible.
edibilityNote: The bitter, low-calorie root is used in Bavarian, Black Forest and Ukrainian alcoholic drinks; the dry fruits are inedible.

summary: Sprawling perennial flowering plant with no native origin explicitly stated, found across most of Europe and east to the western Himalayas. Its honey-scented yellow flowers include short-lived inner male flowers and outer bisexual flowers, while each group of four leaflike structures contains only two true leaves.
A moss with a cosmopolitan distribution. In northeastern hardwood forests, it usually grows on old sugar maples and can indicate late-successional or old-growth stands.

An annual herb of unspecified native origin, it occurs in the western Mediterranean along roads, in cultivated fields and in scrub. Its pinkish-white to pink-purple flowers have dark purple-black tips, and it flowers from winter into early summer.

Herbaceous perennial native to southern Canada and the eastern and south-central United States. Its upright tubular stem carries purple markings, and its branching heads bear small pink or purple flowers. It blooms from midsummer until the first frosts and attracts butterflies, bees and other nectar-feeding insects.

A perennial herb native to the southwestern and south-central United States and northern Mexico. Its branching underground base can produce numerous stems, each bearing either a single flower head or a tight cluster.

A shrubby begonia native to the Caribbean, especially Martinique and nearby islands, it favours mountainous areas of humid forest but is also common beside roads. Its asymmetrical dark-green leaves are paler or purplish beneath, while branched stalks carry many fragrant pinkish to reddish male or female flowers.

Small palm native to southern Europe and distributed across North Africa and southwestern Europe. It branches from the base, with stiff, fan-shaped greyish or blue-green leaves and yellow-spined stalks. Male and female flowers occur on separate plants, and the fleshy fruit darkens from green to reddish or blackish as it ripens.

A moss native to Europe, Japan and America, delicate peatmoss is the smallest British Sphagnum. It usually forms small yellow-orange or yellow-brown patches or cushions on acidic, bare peat in bogs, wet heaths and rainy slopes, becoming duller green when submerged.

A peat moss native across the Northern Hemisphere, with isolated populations in South America. Its strongly spreading branch leaves create a distinctive spiky, bottle-brush appearance, and it forms loose pale-green to yellow-green carpets in nutrient-rich wetlands.
A moss with an almost worldwide distribution that forms dense cushions or hummocks. It grows in wet places, including bogs, marshes, ditches and damp woodland.
A moss found widely across Europe and elsewhere in the world, with no native origin specified. In one study it was the third most sensitive of 18 moss species exposed to the herbicide Asulam.

A peat moss native to places such as China’s Changbai Mountains, narrowleaf peatmoss is small and green to yellowish, forming carpets in wet, moderately nutrient-rich mires. Its branch clusters contain exactly four branches, while the leaves on hanging branches have distinctive large pores near their tips.

Peat moss found across temperate regions worldwide, from the Arctic to New Zealand and along the Andes. It forms loose carpets or soft mounds in wetlands and is best recognized by the fringed upper margins of its stem leaves.

A bulbous perennial native to South Africa's Northern and Western Cape Provinces. In late summer and early autumn, it produces clusters of scarlet, lily-like flowers with conspicuous stamens and purple anthers. Its cut flowers are notably long-lasting.

A woody flowering shrub native to South Africa’s fynbos, the king protea has the largest flower head in its genus, surrounded by colourful bracts. After wildfires, it can regrow from dormant buds in its thick underground stem.
Evergreen shrub native to South Africa. Its aromatic leaves accompany hairy orange flowers arranged in tiers around square stems; flowering season varies by area.

A perennial herb native to northern Europe and the Caucasus, pyramidal bugle has a square, hairy stem rising from a rosette of large leaves. Its bluish-violet flowers form a pyramid-shaped spike beneath leaf-like bracts that become smaller toward the tip.

A perennial plant native to Europe and Asia, with slender underground runners and opposite, toothed leaves. Its dense flower whorls are white or pale pink, and it grows mainly beside water and in marshes.

A perennial herb whose stated origin is western Alpine–Pyrenean, or more broadly southern European. It forms a basal rosette of narrow, nearly parallel-sided leaves and bears cylindrical spikes of small whitish flowers, typically in long-snow-covered alpine pastures.

summary: A short-lived flowering perennial native primarily to the south-central United States and northeastern Mexico, it favours limestone clearings and rocky prairies. It produces yellow flower heads in summer, usually arranged in flat-topped groups.
Flowering plant native to Morocco, Algeria, southern, central and eastern Europe, the Caucasus, Kazakhstan, the Altai and western Siberia. Smooth crosswort is often found in beech forests.

An evergreen shrub native to parts of the Mediterranean Basin. It has reddish bark that peels in strips, large dark-green leaves with whitish undersides, and late-spring white flowers marked yellow at each petal's base.
A perennial herb native to central Portugal and Spain and endemic to the Iberian Peninsula. It spreads by rhizomes and has solitary yellow flowers, growing on rocky mountain ground.

A perennial herb endemic to the northwestern Iberian Peninsula. Its blue-green leaves grow in whorls, while its conspicuous deep pink to purple flowers appear in clusters of three to five and have a narrow yellow-edged opening and curved spur.

A flowering shrub native to Mexico, parts of Central and South America, and the West Indies. It has deeply lobed leaves and bitter yellow or orange latex, and has become an aggressive invasive weed in Hawaii.
Vine native to Andean valleys from Venezuela to Bolivia. Cultivated since pre-Columbian times, it produces ripe yellow-orange fruit containing sweet, edible orange pulp and black seeds.
edibilityNote: The ripe yellow-orange fruit contains sweet, edible orange pulp with black seeds.

summary: An evergreen tree found only in Colombia and Panama. Its reddish-grey or grey bark becomes fissured, square-scaled and flaky, and its leaves cluster at branch tips. Each scaly cup holds one light-brown acorn whose shell is woolly inside.
Fig tree native to the Afrotropics. Its ripe, rosy-speckled figs hang in clusters from surface roots, the trunk or lower branches and are eaten fresh or dried by people in many regions.
edibilityNote: Figs are eaten fresh or dried by native people in many regions; preserves can be made if other suitable fruit are added.

summary: An evergreen perennial moss native to Sphagnum bogs and other moist temperate habitats, it has a circumboreal range and also occurs in South America and Antarctica. It forms dense hummocks and has narrow leaves that hug the stem when dry but spread when moist, with distinctive woolly white rhizoids extending up its stems.

A biennial or short-lived perennial flowering plant native to Asia and Europe. Despite its common name, its flowers may be white or yellow. Its stem leaves differ in colour and hairiness between their upper and lower surfaces, with the underside much hairier.
An evergreen shrub native to East and Southeast Asia, Japanese holly has small, glossy dark-green leaves and black stone fruits. Its alternate leaves distinguish it from similar-looking boxwood.

A short herb native to Europe, it spreads through underground stems and bears pale flowers marked with purple veins, usually with yellow centres. It may be poisonous, and its resemblance to related plants can make identification difficult.
edibilityNote: The plant may be poisonous, but the evidence is qualified and gives no edible-use or ingestion details.

summary: Shrub or small tree native to South America, including northern Argentina, southern Brazil, Paraguay and Uruguay. It has a strong odour and large grey-green leaves densely covered with yellowish, star-shaped hairs.
A low, spreading perennial flowering plant native to beaches in Bermuda and the eastern United States from Louisiana to New Jersey.

An evergreen, vine-like herb of unspecified native origin, it is found from the southern United States and Caribbean through Central America to tropical South America. It bears glossy bright-red berries and tolerates full shade as well as saline soils and salt spray.
edibilityNote: Berry juice was reported safe in tests on male rats, but no human food use is documented.

summary: A shrub native to southeastern China, Indochina and the Philippines. It grows mainly in wet tropical areas, and its flowers have recorded medicinal use for tuberculosis and haemorrhage.

sources.title: Ixora chinensis Lam.
