summary: Dense evergreen flowering shrub native to southern India, Bangladesh and Sri Lanka. It has glossy, leathery leaves and dense rounded clusters of small tubular scarlet flowers produced almost year-round.
A flowering plant native to the Neotropical realm, where it is widespread in well-drained areas. It flowers and fruits throughout the year.

A shrub or small tree native to coastal areas of the Indo-Pacific region, the simpleleaf chastetree has leaves usually divided into three or five leaflets, green above and greyish green beneath. Its clustered flowers are mauve or purple, followed by small fleshy fruits containing four seeds.

Tree native to the Atlantic and Gulf coasts of the United States, Mexico's Yucatán coast, Bermuda and parts of the Caribbean. Its trunk bears sharp, strap-like leaves and eventually topples before its tip turns upward and continues growing. Humans eat the fruit and the showy white flowers, which may be eaten raw or cooked.
edibilityNote: The fruit is eaten by humans, and the flowers can be eaten raw or cooked.

summary: A bulb-forming coastal perennial found in Florida, Mexico and the West Indies, it grows on beaches, dunes, mangrove swamps and other wetlands. It bears showy white flowers and large green seeds.

An aquatic flowering plant native to seacoasts of some warmer oceans, shoalgrass grows in intertidal salt marshes and may be submerged at high tide. Its flat, dark reddish-brown leaves have a few marginal teeth, and flowering is rare.
An annual flowering plant native to India and Myanmar. It has a thick, soft stem, brightly coloured flowers, and ripe seed capsules that burst open.
A deciduous flowering tree native to China, the Hupeh crabapple has pink buds that open into fragrant white blossoms in spring. In autumn, it bears bright red crab apples about the size of cherries.

A small tree or large shrub native to eastern North America and especially common in the lower Appalachian Mountains. It has white bell-shaped flowers and notably bright autumn colour, while juice from its flowers is used to make jelly.
edibilityNote: Juice from the flowers is used to make jelly.

summary: Deciduous tree native to China and Japan. Its rounded, heart-based leaves turn pink and yellow in autumn and can release a distinctive caramel-like scent as they fall.

A deciduous shrub native from southern Europe through central Asia and the Himalayas to northern China, it can display peach, yellow or scarlet autumn foliage. Its feathery pinkish flower plumes create a distinctive smoky appearance.

A conifer native to central Japan, hinoki cypress has blunt, scale-like leaves and dark reddish-brown bark. Its lemon-scented, straight-grained wood is highly resistant to rot and traditionally used for major Japanese buildings.

A low-growing evergreen conifer shrub native to Japan, Japanese garden juniper spreads through long branches that intertwine into a dense mat. Its needle-like leaves grow in threes, and female plants bear dark, berry-like cones with a pale blue-white coating.

A deciduous tree native to southern Japan and Korea, Japanese stewartia develops smooth, mottled bark that peels as it ages. Its foliage turns yellow, red or purple in autumn, while short-lived white summer flowers open successively over many weeks.

Deciduous shrub or small tree native to eastern North America, especially wet sites along the Atlantic coastal plain. It bears white flowers in early spring and sweet, edible fruit that ripens dark purple in June and July within its native range.
edibilityNote: The ripe, dark-purple fruit is edible and sweet, ripening in June and July within its native range.

summary: An evergreen tree or large shrub native to Japan, Korea, northeastern China and extreme southeastern Russia, Japanese yew has flat, dark green leaves. Its single seed sits partly inside bright red, berry-like flesh. Every part except that flesh is toxic, with seeds containing the highest toxin concentrations.
edibilityNote: All parts except the red aril are toxic; ingested leaves or seeds require urgent medical advice, and seeds contain the most toxin.

summary: A deciduous shrub or small tree native to southern and eastern China, Korea, Japan and Sakhalin, Russia. In late summer it bears large cone-shaped flower clusters combining creamy-white fertile flowers with pinkish-white sterile ones; some florets open pale green and turn white.
A free-standing shrub native to eastern, southern and central Europe, this clematis is unusual because it does not climb. It usually grows along woodland margins.

A strongly aromatic evergreen shrub native to the Mediterranean basin. It bears purple flower spikes on slender leafless stems, and its flowers are used as a culinary herb, especially in the North American version of herbes de Provence.
edibilityNote: The flowers are used as a culinary herb, especially in the North American version of herbes de Provence.

summary: An evergreen shrub or small tree native to western and southern Europe, northwest Africa and southwest Asia, it has small oval leaves and strongly scented, petal-free flowers. Its exceptionally hard, heavy wood has long been used for engraving, instruments and tools.

sources.title: Lista Vermelha da Flora Vascular de Portugal Continental — Buxus sempervirens
sources.attribution: Andre Carapeto % Ana Francisco, Paulo Pereira, Miguel Porto, felipe (2020). Lista Vermelha da Flora Vascular de Portugal Continental. Plazi.org taxonomic treatments database. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/ge693f accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-12.

summary: A perennial herb native to the south-central and southern United States, from Texas east to Florida and north to the Carolinas, Arkansas and Kansas. Its flower heads vary greatly: the ray florets may be purple, yellow or white and are sometimes entirely absent. The rare variety winkleri is restricted to the Pineywoods of Texas.

A herbaceous perennial native to Europe and northern and western Asia, it has a thick, twisted rootstock and upright stems topped by club-like spikes of rose-pink flowers. It loses its foliage during dry conditions until moisture returns.
edibilityNote: Roots, leaves and young shoots have been cooked; leaves made Northern English Lent pudding, while roots are eaten in Russia and northern Asia.

summary: An evergreen shrub or tree found in coastal moist forests of the Ryukyu Islands, Taiwan, the Philippines and Java. It has thick, leathery leaves and smooth yellow fruits containing one to four seeds.

A deciduous tree native to tropical South Asia, Southeast Asia and Melanesia, giant crepe-myrtle bears abundant bright pink to light purple flowers. Its smooth, flaky pale bark and woody fruits that darken from green through brown to black are also distinctive.
edibilityNote: In Vietnam, young leaves are eaten as vegetables; leaves and other parts are also prepared as tea in the Philippines, Taiwan and Japan.

summary: A shrub native to Southwest China, specifically Guizhou, Hubei and Sichuan, the China rose grows in hedges or thickets. Its wild form has five pink-to-red petals and red hips, while its purplish-brown branches may bear many curved spines or none.
edibilityNote: Young plant parts, flower buds and flowers are brewed or eaten; rosehip flesh is eaten raw or cooked, and ground seeds are added to foods.

summary: An epiphytic fern native to eastern Australia, the elkhorn fern usually grows on tree trunks and branches. It has overlapping shield-like nest fronds and very different fertile fronds that fork repeatedly, while colonies expand as new plantlets form along nest-frond margins.

A bromeliad endemic to the Atlantic Forest of southeastern Brazil. The cultivated petropolitana variety forms a stiff rosette of heavily spined dark-green leaves and bears white-lavender flowers with orange sepals; the smaller extensa variety has yellow-green leaves, coral-red flower clusters and berries that darken to purple.

Flowering plant native to mainland Portugal and endemic to the Iberian Peninsula. In Portugal it occurs only in wet high-altitude grasslands of upper Serra da Estrela and was assessed as Vulnerable from work conducted in 2016–2019.

sources.title: Lista Vermelha da Flora Vascular de Portugal Continental — Campanula herminii
sources.attribution: Andre Carapeto % Ana Francisco, Paulo Pereira, Miguel Porto, felipe (2020). Lista Vermelha da Flora Vascular de Portugal Continental. Plazi.org taxonomic treatments database. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/ge693f accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-12.

summary: A moss with a mainly circumboreal range, typically growing around cold, lime-poor and nutrient-poor springs. It forms yellow-green to bluish-green cushions and has a fine waxy coating that makes it difficult to wet.

A herbaceous flowering plant native from western Europe to central Asia and northern Japan, and in Mediterranean northern Africa, upright hedge-parsley may be annual or biennial depending on location. Its bristly fruits disperse readily, and it is an aggressive invasive plant in North America.

A flowering perennial native to northwestern North America from Alaska to Oregon, wandering fleabane grows beside streams, in bogs and in moist mountain meadows. It spreads through underground stems and usually bears one flower head per stem, with blue, purple, pink or white rays.

A juniper shrub or small tree native across the Mediterranean region, it grows on rocky sites from sea level. Its needle-like leaves occur in threes and have two white bands, while its berry-like cones ripen orange-red, sometimes with a pink waxy coating.

A semi-evergreen shrub native from Panama south to Venezuela and Colombia, and also to the West Indies. It bears masses of yellow flowers from autumn into winter. Its edible leaves can be cooked as a vegetable with other leaves, beans or peas.
edibilityNote: Leaves are edible and may be cooked as a vegetable with other leaves, beans or peas.

summary: Tree native to Mexico and Central America, with male and female flowers borne on separate trees. It is widely planted but has become invasive in Hawaii.

Flowering plant native across much of Asia, from the Indian Subcontinent to Japan and the Philippines, but not Bangladesh, Xinjiang or Qinghai. It commonly grows along roads, on slopes, at forest edges and in scrub below 2,000 metres.

An annual flowering plant native to the southern United States and northern Mexico, smallflower desert-chicory grows in prairies, clay soils and disturbed places. Its flowers open in the morning, broken stems release milky sap, and its dried seeds resemble dandelion puffs. The roots are brewed as tea or coffee, while the bitter edible leaves are often boiled.
edibilityNote: Roots are brewed as tea or coffee; bitter leaves are often boiled, and the plant can also be made into jelly.

summary: A flowering plant native to Europe and Asia, extending from Russia and East Asia to Afghanistan and northern Pakistan. Its refined seed oil has EU novel-food status and other human food approvals, while the purpose of seeds found at Ukrainian archaeological sites remains unknown.
edibilityNote: Refined seed oil has EU novel-food status and human food-use approvals in Brazil, with limited approvals in Korea and Japan.

summary: A banana-like plant native to eastern South Africa through southern Mozambique, and also considered native to Botswana and Zimbabwe, it forms tall woody clumps. Fan-shaped grey-green leaves rise above flowers with a dark blue bract, white sepals and a bluish-purple tongue. It is among the few plants verified to contain bilirubin.

Small evergreen shrub native to Albania, Croatia, Cyprus, Greece, Italy, Montenegro and Turkey. Its aromatic, sage-like leaves are wrinkled and grey-green with white, finely hairy undersides; deep-yellow tubular flowers form dense rings in summer.

An evergreen conifer native to southern Japan and southern and eastern China. Its mature cone scales become reddish-purple, fleshy and berry-like; the ripe arils are edible, but the seed should not be eaten.
edibilityNote: Ripe cone arils are edible, but the seed should not be eaten.

summary: A small tree originating in Central Asia, though its native range is uncertain because of prehistoric cultivation, the apricot bears white to pink flowers before its leaves in early spring. Its yellow-to-orange, peach-like fruit may be smooth or velvety, with succulent flesh ranging from sweet to tart.
edibilityNote: Oil pressed from cultivar kernels has been used for cooking; kernels require proper processing to reduce harmful effects from hydrogen cyanide.

summary: Medium-sized tree native to the Himalayas, Tibet, southern China, Indochinese rainforests and mountainous Sumatra and Java. It has a spreading, weeping canopy and ripe fruit that may be white, pink or red and is described as honey-sweet.

A deciduous succulent tree endemic to Queensland, Australia, distinguished by its swollen bottle-shaped trunk and narrow or divided leaves. Aboriginal people ate the roots of young plants and secretions induced from wounded trunks.
edibilityNote: Aboriginal people ate young plants' roots and secretions induced by wounding the trunk.

summary: A spreading shrub endemic to south-eastern continental Australia. It has narrow leaves with shaggy undersides and small clusters of pink to red and cream flowers; its fruit is also shaggy-haired.
Herbaceous plant native to South Africa’s Cape Provinces and KwaZulu-Natal.

An evergreen coniferous tree native to New Guinea and Queensland, Australia, Queensland kauri has a straight trunk and smooth orange-brown to grey-brown bark that sheds in large flakes. Its green, rounded seed cones break apart when mature to release the seeds.

Evergreen tree native to northeastern New South Wales and coastal Queensland, Australia. It has a dome-like crown of dense, dark green, leathery leaves, while coastal plants can become stunted and wind-sheared.

An Australian tree often found beside streams near the eastern coast, where trunks and branches can be shaped by floodwater. Its bright yellow flowers attract bees, and it is widely planted as a shade and street tree.

Tall tree native to coastal and sub-coastal eastern Australia, from New South Wales into Queensland. It has a remarkably straight trunk, mostly smooth pale bark with a rough brownish base, and white flowers from mid-autumn to late winter.

Palm native to eastern Australia, it grows in moist forests and swampy or coastal sites from Queensland through New South Wales to eastern Victoria. Its tall, slender trunk bears a crown of dark, glossy green leaves folded like fans, with cream-white flowers appearing in summer.
edibilityNote: New growth was eaten raw or cooked.

summary: Flowering tree endemic to southwestern Western Australia. It has rough bark, white to pink flowers, and unusually large oval or urn-shaped fruit known locally as honky nuts.
edibilityNote: The blossoms provide sugary syrup that may be sucked directly or steeped in water to make the sweet drink numbit.

summary: Subtropical evergreen tree native to Macaronesia and northwestern mainland Africa, although its origin in the Azores is uncertain. Its repeatedly branching crown develops an umbrella-like shape as it matures. Cuts to its bark or leaves release a reddish resin known as dragon’s blood.

A usually multi-stemmed deciduous tree native to East, South and Southeast Asia. Its thin, mottled pinkish-grey bark sheds annually, while its crimped flowers may be white, pink, mauve, purple or carmine.

A slow-growing palm native only to Australia's Lord Howe Island, with long fronds. Widely cultivated as a houseplant, it became popular in Victorian interiors because it tolerates low light and other indoor conditions.

A tree native to Brazil’s cerrado, particularly Bahia and Rio Grande do Sul. In traditional Brazilian medicine, its stems, leaves and bark are used for different purposes, and its wood is made into whips.

A large deciduous oak native to southern and south-eastern Europe, Asia Minor and the Levant. Its deeply furrowed dark-grey bark may show orange streaks near the trunk base, while its acorns sit in cups densely covered with soft, moss-like bristles.

Tree native to eastern Australia, with peeling, spongy bark, sharply pointed leaves and creamy-white flower spikes. It occurs mainly in moist coastal places but tolerates conditions ranging from swampy to hot and dry.
A large deciduous tree native to East and Southeast Asia. Its three-lobed leaves turn red in autumn, while its branches often bear corky projections and its fruit is burr-like.
An evergreen shrub or vine native to Bhutan and India. Its strongly scented white flowers bloom throughout the year, opening at night and closing in the morning.
edibilityNote: The flowers flavor jasmine tea; although edible, they are rarely used in cuisine, with ice cream given as an unusual example.

summary: Deciduous flowering tree native to northern Vietnam and southern China. It has light-gray bark and large papery leaves, and its chemicals inspired the chemotherapy drugs topotecan and irinotecan, although these are now produced in laboratories.

An evergreen, short-lived shrub native to Bolivia, Colombia and Peru. It bears dense clusters of intensely vanilla-scented, bright-purple flowers, but ingesting any part can cause stomach upset and liver damage in humans.
edibilityNote: Ingesting any part can cause stomach upset and liver damage; the seeds are specifically described as poisonous.

summary: A palm native to Baja California, Mexico. Its broad grey-blue fans crown a stout trunk, while persistent dead leaves form a shag around wild plants and long flower clusters extend beyond the crown.
edibilityNote: The Cocopah people ate the roasted seeds.

summary: A cycad native to southern Mozambique and South Africa’s eastern Cape Province and KwaZulu-Natal. It has fernlike but leathery leaves, an underground tuber-shaped stem and pine-like cones.

A coniferous tree native to the Japanese islands of Honshū, Kyūshū and Shikoku, northern Japanese hemlock has a narrow, dense, conical crown. Its young shoots are bright orange to red-brown, while its glossy dark-green needles have two chalk-white bands beneath.

Cycad endemic to southeastern Veracruz in eastern Mexico. Its stiff, fuzzy leaflets form a circular, palm-like crown, although it is not a palm. All parts are poisonous to humans and other animals, with the seeds especially dangerous.
edibilityNote: All parts are poisonous; seeds can cause liver and kidney failure and eventual paralysis in humans.

summary: An Ephedra species from the western Mediterranean, North Africa, Madeira and the Canary Islands. It grows on rocky hills and stone walls.
Evergreen conifer endemic to eastern coastal Australia. Its dark blue-purple, berry-like seed cones have an edible fleshy base used in condiments and as an alternative to sloes in Australian gin.
edibilityNote: The fleshy seed-cone base is used in condiments and as a sloe substitute in Australian gin.

summary: Evergreen conifer native only to Chile, the willow podocarp has arching branches with long, narrow, willow-like leaves. When male and female plants grow together, it bears red, fleshy oval fruits.

Large pine tree native to the Himalayas, from Afghanistan and Tibet through northern India, Nepal and Bhutan to Myanmar. It has thick, deeply fissured red-brown bark and slender yellowish-green needles grouped in threes; its cones open slowly with age or after heating by forest fire.

A pine tree native to coastal Japan and South Korea, Japanese black pine develops thick, dark, plated bark as it ages. Its needles grow in pairs, and its seed cones open in late winter after maturing for slightly less than two years.
An evergreen conifer native to China and Japan. It has pale-green, narrow, pointed scale-like leaves in four rows, upright egg-shaped cones, and notably durable wood.

Evergreen coniferous tree native to the Himalaya, Karakoram and Hindu Kush mountains, ranging from eastern Afghanistan to southwest China. Its flexible needles grow in bundles of five and often droop gracefully, while its mature cones are long, slender and yellow-buff.

A conifer ranging from Nepal and eastern India through Indochina and Malesia, it grows mainly in tropical and subtropical wet forests across varied rocky, swampy, limestone and sandstone sites. In Cambodia it can take a dwarf form, and its yellowish wood is used for construction there.
A conifer endemic to Mexico. It has a straight trunk and dense crown, and its resin is used to produce turpentine.
A conifer endemic to New Zealand. On the South Island it occurs in lowland and mountain forest and scrub, from northern Marlborough westward and south to southern Westland.

An evergreen coniferous tree native to south-central Chile and a few adjacent areas of westernmost Argentina. Its modified cones bear dark-purple, berry-like scales with soft edible pulp; Indigenous people in Chile eat the fruit and make it into marmalade.
edibilityNote: The blue-purple fruit is eaten by Indigenous people in Chile and made into marmalade.

summary: A conifer native to high-elevation habitats from southwestern through central and southeastern Europe, it has dark green needles in pairs and nut-brown cones. Its young cones and buds are gathered wild in spring and made into syrup by drying them through summer into autumn, then boiling the dripped liquid with sugar; they may instead be macerated in sugar and fermented.
edibilityNote: Young cones and buds are wild-harvested in spring, then dried and boiled with sugar for syrup, or macerated in sugar, fermented and strained.

summary: A large pine tree native to the mountains of southern Mexico and western Central America. Its needles grow in bundles of five, and its notably long, slender cones have thin, flexible scales. Despite its tropical origin, cultivated trees have survived severe cold in Scotland and Pennsylvania.

An evergreen coniferous tree endemic to the Drina River valley in western Serbia and eastern Bosnia and Herzegovina. Its crown is very narrow at high elevations but broader lower down; flattened dark-green needles have two blue-white bands underneath, and young cones are deep purple.

A large conifer endemic to Taiwan. Its often-crooked trunk, needles bundled in fives and large mature cones are distinctive; it is now scarce at lower elevations and occurs mostly higher up in less accessible places.
edibilityNote: The leaves can be juiced and consumed as a drink.

summary: A large evergreen conifer from southern Europe, Turkey, Mediterranean islands, Crimea and the high mountains of northwestern Africa. Its bark develops deeply fissured, scaly plates, while its rounded conical shape becomes irregular with age.

Evergreen coniferous tree native to Japan. It forms a broad, dense, conical crown, with needles in bundles of five and cones bearing broad, rounded scales. It is popular for bonsai and is also grown in parks and gardens.
An evergreen spruce native to western China. It has orange-brown shoots, greyish- to bluish-green needles with conspicuous pale lines, and pale-brown cones with stiff scales.

Large evergreen conifer native to the Caucasus and adjacent northeastern Turkey. It has the shortest needles of any spruce, with glossy dark-green foliage; its slender young cones are green or red-purple and mature to dark brown five to seven months after pollination.

An evergreen spruce native to the western Himalaya and adjacent mountains from northeastern Afghanistan to central Nepal, it has a conical crown and usually drooping branchlets. Its needles are described as the longest of any spruce, and its young green cones mature to buff-brown.

A slow-growing pine tree native to northeastern and central China. Its smooth grey-green bark flakes away in rounded scales, revealing pale yellow patches that darken to olive-brown, red and purple in light.
edibilityNote: Its seeds are edible and are used in traditional Chinese medicine for respiratory ailments.

summary: A pine native to the New World, Caribbean pine grows rapidly in tropical Brazil and produces resinous timber. Its wood is used industrially for veneers, boards, resin, pulp, charcoal and paper.
A cycad native to Queensland, Australia, Moore's zamia palm is the tallest-growing Macrozamia species. Its long leaves have short, heavily spined stalks and numerous narrow leaflets.

Cycad endemic to southern Western Australia, often growing trunkless in jarrah forests and bearing long, glossy, palm-like fronds. Its large cones contain seeds used as food by Indigenous Australians only after proper processing; unprepared seeds have caused severe poisoning.
edibilityNote: Properly processed seeds were an important Noongar food; unprepared seeds caused vomiting and poisoning. Processed trunk pith starch was also used as flour.

summary: A usually trunkless cycad endemic to New South Wales in eastern Australia, it grows in low-nutrient forest soils. Its leaf axis is often strongly twisted, and mature plants can regrow from the ground after bushfire.

An evergreen shrub or small tree native to northern China, Mongolia, Korea, Japan and far southeastern Russia. It has bright green to yellowish needle-like leaves in threes and berry-like cones that ripen dark purple or brown.

Evergreen coniferous shrub, rarely a small tree, native to the Himalayas and China. It has flaky brown bark, often blue-green needle-like leaves, and glossy black berry-like cones that mature in about 18 months.

A large shrub or tree native to mountains of the western Mediterranean, from southern France through Spain to Morocco and locally northern Algeria, it has strongly aromatic, spicy-resinous foliage. Male and female plants are separate, and its cones are berry-like, blue-black and waxy, maturing in about 18 months.

A palm-like cycad endemic to eastern Australia, pineapple zamia produces some of the largest cycad cones and has crowns of long, glossy, dark-green leaves. All parts are toxic to humans, especially the seeds, which can cause severe illness if eaten.
edibilityNote: All parts are toxic to humans, especially the seeds; ingestion can cause severe digestive symptoms, liver damage and muscular paralysis.

summary: Cycad native to eastern New South Wales, Australia. Its cones form after fire, with separate male and female plants and large female seeds ripening red or yellow. The starchy seeds are poisonous unless treated; Cadigal people pounded and soaked them for a week with daily water changes, then roasted cakes made from the pulp.
edibilityNote: Seeds are poisonous untreated; Cadigal people soaked pounded seeds for a week with daily water changes, then made and roasted pulp cakes.

summary: A conifer native to China, Japan and Taiwan, Asian bayberry has male and female cones on separate trees. Its glossy leaves lack a mid-vein, and older branches become reddish-brown and peel in small layers. The seed oil is edible, while young leaves are sometimes cooked and eaten.
edibilityNote: The seeds yield edible oil, and young leaves are sometimes cooked and eaten.

summary: A highly variable evergreen tree or shrub native to China, Myanmar, Japan, Korea and the Russian Far East. It bears both needle-like young leaves and scale-like adult leaves, often retaining some young foliage when mature, and produces blue-black, wax-coated berry-like cones.

A cycad endemic to South Africa’s oNgoye Forest, Wood’s cycad is extinct in the wild and all surviving plants are clones of the only known male. It resembles a palm, with a crown of glossy dark-green leaves and vivid yellow-orange male cones.

A large evergreen shrub or tree native to the western Canary Islands and, as subsp. maderensis, Madeira. Its needle-like leaves grow in threes, while berry-like cones ripen orange-red and may have a pink waxy coating. It is endangered in its native range, where large trees are now rare.

A very rare, tree-like cycad native to South Africa’s Eastern Cape province. It bears a crown of bright green, feather-like leaves, while separate male and female plants produce olive-green cones; it no longer naturally reproduces in the wild.

A cycad native to Gauteng and Mpumalanga in South Africa, it grows in open grasslands and sheltered valleys. Its trunk often produces secondary stems from basal suckers, while leathery leaves form a crown at the top. Only an estimated 184–200 mature wild plants remain.

A tree-like cycad from KwaZulu-Natal, it has stiff, light-green leaves with robust spine-tipped leaflets. Its pale-yellow male cones contrast with female cones that may have fine brown hairs, while the seeds have a red outer covering.

A perennial cycad recorded in Africa, though its native origin is not explicitly stated. It is tree-like, often sprouts extra stems from its base, and bears crowns of leathery, spine-edged leaves. Male and female plants produce separate green cones, while the seeds have bright red coverings.

A cycad native to Mount Mruwere and adjacent mountains in Mozambique’s Manica province. It has an upright, sometimes suckering stem crowned with dark-green divided leaves; ripe seeds have an orange-red fleshy covering.

A cycad native to the Lebombo Mountains of South Africa, Mozambique and Eswatini. It has stiff, glossy green leaves with prickles near their bases; male and female plants bear yellowish cones of different shapes, and the seed coats are glossy red.

A cycad occurring in Ngoye Forest in KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa. Its dark green leaves have leaflets tapering to thorns near the base, and separate plants bear yellow male or female cones; the seeds have a red outer covering.

A cycad endemic to mountains near Barberton in South Africa’s Mpumalanga Province and near Piggs Peak in northwestern Eswatini. It has a tall upright trunk crowned with bright green to yellowish-green leaves made up of numerous toothed leaflets; male and female cones grow on separate plants.
Tall, tree-like cycad native to South Africa's Eastern Cape Province. It has a crown of silvery- to bluish-green leaves, and male and female cones grow on separate plants.

A cycad native to the Lebombo Mountains of Mozambique, Eswatini and South Africa’s KwaZulu-Natal province. It commonly forms clumps from basal shoots and has stiff leaves with glossy dark-green leaflets. Male and female cones grow on separate plants, and its seeds have bright red outer coats.
Cycad native to South Africa's Eastern Cape Province. It has an upright stem that often produces basal shoots and a crown of grey-green to blue leaves with leathery, sharply tipped, spiny leaflets.

A cycad from Africa. Its short stem remains underground, supporting a few slightly curved leaves with tough, spiny-edged leaflets; separate male and female plants produce olive-green to yellowish cones.

Low-growing, palm-like cycad endemic to South Africa, where it occurs mainly on dry sandstone slopes and ridges in Eastern Cape. Its strongly keeled leaves are blue or silver, while its seeds are red.

A low-growing, palm-like cycad endemic to South Africa. With age it develops a very thick trunk crowned by arching dark or metallic-green leaves, and it produces the largest pollen cones in its genus.
edibilityNote: A historical account says its seeds poisoned General Jan Smuts and members of a Boer commando.

summary: Large cycad endemic to South Africa, particularly KwaZulu-Natal and parts of the Eastern Cape. It often has a leaning trunk crowned by huge evergreen leaves, while ripe female cones split open to reveal bright red, poisonous seeds.
edibilityNote: The seeds are poisonous; fruit-eating monkeys, baboons, bats and hornbills discard them.

summary: A palm-like cycad native to a small part of Limpopo, South Africa, the Modjadji cycad has shiny, spiny leaves and large cones containing bright orange-red seeds. It forms pure forests on two hills near Modjadjiskloof, described as Southern Africa’s only cycad forests.

A cycad found in South Sudan, northern Uganda, northern Democratic Republic of the Congo and the Central African Republic, the Nile cycad has a rounded, partly underground stem crowned by grey-green, feather-like leaves. Male and female plants are separate; females bear solitary hanging cones and reddish-coated seeds.

A cycad native to South Africa, it has a mostly underground trunk and appears dwarf-like. Its crown bears tightly packed bracts covered in dense grey woolly hair, while its leaf and cone shapes vary notably across its broad range.

An evergreen shrub or small tree native to the Azores, the Azores juniper has blue-green, needle-like leaves arranged in groups of three, each with a divided white band. Its berry-like cones ripen from green to orange-red, sometimes with a pink waxy coating.

An evergreen cycad tree found across northeastern India and parts of southern and Southeast Asia into southern China. It has a crown of dark green leaves, unusually large yellowish or orange male cones, and orange to red-yellow seeds when mature.
edibilityNote: Young fronds are eaten as vegetables in Manipur and Sikkim; indigenous communities in Assam and nearby Meghalaya eat the starchy seeds raw or roasted.

summary: A cycad native to Indonesia, New Guinea and Christmas Island, queen sago looks like a palm but is not one. It has glossy, palm-like fronds and grey bark divided by distinctive rectangular or diamond-shaped cracks.
edibilityNote: Sago is prepared from dried, ground and washed trunk pith; toxic seeds become edible only after pounding, repeated washing and cooking.

summary: Cycad native to northern Vietnam and southern China. It is widespread in southern and central Guangxi and occurs in Vietnam’s Cao Bang and Thanh Hoa provinces.

A small cycad native to the southeastern African coast, including southern Mozambique and northern Natal. It has a mostly underground trunk, hard leaves with spine-tipped lobes and unusual dark salmon-coloured cones. Local people have obtained and eaten starch from its stem.
edibilityNote: Local people have obtained and consumed starch from the stem.

summary: Evergreen tree-like cycad of unspecified native origin, found around Madagascar, nearby western Indian Ocean islands and parts of coastal East Africa. Its young leaves have a distinctive bluish tint, and its seeds contain a spongy layer that lets them float. Although toxic, the seeds are eaten on Ngazidja after repeated washing, fermentation and drying remove their cyanotoxins.
edibilityNote: On Ngazidja, toxic seeds are made edible by repeated washing, fermentation and drying to remove cyanotoxins.

summary: Cycad native to Oaxaca and Puebla in Mexico. A beetle lives and breeds in its male cones, eating pollen and cone tissue while carrying pollen to female cones.
Cycad endemic to limestone cliffs and rocky rainforest hillsides in Veracruz and Oaxaca, Mexico. It is among the tallest cycads, and its seed cones are also among the group's largest.
Cycad native to Mexico and endemic to its eastern coast. Mature leaves lack the leaflet-edge spines seen on juvenile growth, and females usually produce cones at much longer intervals than males.

A cycad endemic to KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa, the Ngotshe cycad is known from a single population among sandstone cliffs in shortgrass savannah. It has an unbranched stem, leaves with pointed, spiny-edged leaflets, yellow to yellow-green cones, and red-coated seeds.

A small, stemless cycad of unstated native origin, it is found in Limpopo Province, South Africa. A crown of spiny-edged leaflets tops the plant, while apple-green male cones and apricot-coated seeds add distinctive colour.

A cycad endemic to South Africa’s Eastern Cape, it has a partly buried, egg-shaped stem and leathery leaves. Male and female cones grow on separate plants, and its nearly spherical seeds have a red outer covering. It is endangered, with an estimated global population of no more than about 1,500 mature plants.
A cycad endemic to the Chimanimani Mountains of eastern Zimbabwe. It bears oblong seeds with a red fleshy covering and is threatened, having been locally eliminated by cycad collectors.

A palm-like cycad endemic to South Africa, it may be branched or unbranched, with straight or backward-curving leaves whose rigid, broad leaflets often have toothed edges. It bears greenish-yellow cones and scarlet seeds; the cones are poisonous to humans.
edibilityNote: The cones are poisonous to humans.

summary: A short cycad recorded in Eswatini, Encephalartos aplanatus bears a few long, dark-green leaves that stand upright when young and lie flatter as they mature. Male and female plants produce separate yellow cones, while the seeds have a red outer covering.

Cycad occurring in Kenya and Tanzania. It develops a crown of tough leaves with leaflets that become spiny near the base, and produces greenish male or female cones and seeds with a red-orange outer coat.

A tree-like cycad native to Limpopo Province, South Africa, recorded on southeast-facing quartzite cliffs. As of 2020, up to ten wild individuals were assumed to remain, and over-collecting for ornamental use had effectively eliminated it from the wild.

A tree-like cycad found in parts of South Africa and at Piggs Peak in Eswatini, it is critically endangered in the wild but widely cultivated. It may produce extra stems from its base, while its seeds have a yellow-orange fleshy covering.
Small, low-growing cycad native to Eastern Cape Province, South Africa. Its stiff, spiny leaves are notably blue-grey to varying degrees; young leaves are silvery blue but become green with age.

An evergreen cycad endemic to South Africa and strongly associated with the Natal Drakensberg. Its form varies with habitat, from robust high-elevation plants with fire-scarred bases to dwarf, sometimes multi-trunked plants at lower elevations. Its lemon-coloured cones are densely woolly, and its seeds and their fleshy covering are poisonous.
edibilityNote: The seeds and fleshy covering are poisonous; toxins also occur at lower concentrations in the roots, stems and leaves.

summary: A cycad native to South Africa’s Eastern Cape and KwaZulu-Natal provinces, it has a tree-like trunk and an open, woolly brown crown. Its stiff leaves spread horizontally; young leaves are silvery and turn yellowish with age, and their tips bear sharp thorns.

A cycad native to the Winterberg mountains north of Bedford in South Africa’s Eastern Cape. It has an underground trunk, often sends up secondary stems from its base, and carries a crown of olive-green leaves. Male and female cones occur on separate plants.
Cycad endemic to the Mexican states of Tamaulipas and Nuevo León. It occurs mainly in the Sierra Madre Oriental and nearby mountain and low-hill areas.
A cycad endemic to Thailand, Cycas petraea is known only from a single line of limestone mountains east of the Phu Kra Dueng massif in Phu Kradueng National Park, Loei Province.
Coniferous shrub or small tree native to northern Burma and China. It has long, soft, often sickle-shaped leaves, while its fruit covering changes from yellow or green to purple when ripe.

A large conifer native to the mountains of the Eastern Mediterranean basin, the Lebanon cedar has a conical crown when young that broadens and flattens with age, although trees in dense forests stay more conical. Its dark, deeply fissured bark and wide-spreading, level branches give old trees a striking form.

An evergreen conifer native to the eastern Himalaya in Bhutan and adjacent northeastern India, Bhutan cypress has strongly drooping sprays of slender blue-green foliage. Its natural populations are fragmented, with few occurrences and few large trees.

A cycad native to southern India and Sri Lanka, it is reported in the wild only from southern India and is the only gymnosperm among Sri Lanka’s native flora. An unreferenced account says its poisonous seeds can be made into flour for tortillas, tamales, soup and porridge after at least five water soakings.
edibilityNote: An unreferenced account says poisonous seeds are soaked at least five times, then dried and ground into flour used in several foods.

summary: A plant endemic to Hidalgo, Puebla, Querétaro, San Luis Potosí and Veracruz in Mexico. It inhabits moist lowland and mountain forests and is threatened by habitat loss.
An endangered tree native to southeastern China, Taiwan, Laos and Vietnam, Taiwan-fir belongs to the cypress family.

A cycad native to islands northeast of Papua New Guinea, including New Britain, the Bismarck Archipelago and the Solomon Islands, it grows near coasts on coral sand dunes and in nearby forests. Its young leaves have dense white to orange hairs, later becoming glossy bright green.

A palm-like, cone-bearing plant from seasonally dry tropical woodlands in northern Australia, Cycas media has thick, dark-green leaves that emerge in annual flushes. It often grows new foliage immediately after dry-season fires. All parts are considered highly toxic, but Aboriginal Australians ate the seeds after extensive toxin-removing preparation.
edibilityNote: Aboriginal Australians ate seeds only after extensive preparation, including pounding, drying, prolonged soaking, grinding and baking, to remove toxins.

summary: Large coniferous tree endemic to Australia, naturally concentrated in southeast Queensland with two very small isolated populations in the northeast. It has a distinctive egg-shaped crown, very large cones and rigid, sharp-tipped leaves. Its edible nuts are eaten raw, cooked, ground into paste or bread, or traditionally creek-fermented by Indigenous Australians; shoots are also eaten.
edibilityNote: Indigenous Australians eat nuts raw, cooked, immature, as paste or bread, and traditionally creek-fermented; shoots are also eaten.

summary: A large coniferous tree native to the Rif and Atlas Mountains of Morocco and the Tell Atlas of Algeria, the Atlas cedar forms mountain forests, sometimes in nearly pure stands. Cultivated forms often have bluish foliage.

Conifer tree endemic to New Caledonia. Its long, slender branches curve upward and branch at their ends, creating a chandelier-like outline. It is endangered, with fragmented populations largely confined to dry, nickel-rich soils affected by mining.

A large evergreen conifer native to central and southern Japan, it has a broad conical crown and flattened needles. Young trees have double-pointed needle tips, while mature trees have single-pointed tips; its cones disintegrate when mature in October.
Evergreen coniferous tree native to the mountains of Europe. Its flattened dark-green needles have two pale bands beneath, while its upright cones break apart at maturity to release winged seeds.
edibilityNote: Branches, including leaves, bark and wood, were used to make spruce beer; aphid honeydew yields honey sold as fir honey.

summary: Evergreen coniferous tree native to montane forests of southern Africa. Its grey-brown to reddish trunk becomes increasingly flaky with age, and some specimens in the Knysna-Amatole forests are over 1,000 years old. Its seed is edible but resinous, enclosed by a fleshy covering that ripens yellow and jelly-soft on female trees only every few years.
edibilityNote: The seed is edible but resinous.

summary: An annual plant with no explicitly stated native origin, marsh cudweed is widespread across much of Europe, Asia and North America, especially on damp, disturbed ground. It is notably woolly, with narrow leaves woolly on both sides and clusters of brownish-yellow flower heads surrounded by long leaves.
A flowering plant native to eastern North America. The Royal Horticultural Society considers it a good plant for attracting pollinators.

Small conifer tree native to the mountain forests of São Tomé Island in the Gulf of Guinea. It is the only gymnosperm found on São Tomé and Príncipe. Vigorous young trees have larger lance-shaped leaves, and each highly modified seed cone carries one seed with a thin fleshy coating.

An evergreen conifer tree native to the higher mountains of South Korea, including Jeju Island, Korean fir grows in cool, wet forests with snowy winters. Its needles are glossy dark green above with vivid white bands beneath, and its young cones are dark purple-blue.

Large evergreen conifer native to mountains south and east of the Black Sea in Turkey, Georgia and the Russian Caucasus. Its flattened, glossy dark-green needles have blue-white bands beneath, and its mature cones break apart to release winged seeds.
An evergreen fir tree endemic to Jebel Babor in Algeria. It has glossy dark-green needles and green cones tinged pink or violet that turn brown and break apart when mature, releasing winged seeds.

Evergreen conifer tree native to southern Spain and northern Morocco. Its pale blue-green leaves radiate around the shoots and have whitish wax on both sides, while its green to pinkish-purple cones disintegrate when mature to release winged seeds.

An evergreen fir native to the mountains of central and southern Mexico and western Guatemala, it grows in high-elevation cloud forests. Its dark blue-purple cones disintegrate at maturity to release winged seeds, while monarch butterflies gather in protected forests of these firs from December to March.

A fern ranging across most of Europe, far-western Russia, Turkey and Iran. Its fronds have a medium-sized, ladder-like oval outline with lower leaflets that tend to fold inward, while the young fertile spots beneath them become bright yellow before opening.

Small winter-annual fern native to regions around the eastern North Atlantic, the Mediterranean and the Caucasus, with some records in India and Vietnam. It has a simple sterile blade beside a spike-like fertile blade and rarely grows taller than two centimetres.
An aquatic fern with no native origin stated, it is widespread in Australian flood plains and swamps. Its fronds are broad and clover-like.

An aquatic spore-bearing plant native to the Mediterranean region, northwestern Africa and western European coasts as far north as Cornwall. It mainly occupies temporarily wet pools and loses its leaves in summer; large black scales between the leaves may be present.
Fern native to Japan and south-central and southeast China. It is grown as an ornamental and has received the Royal Horticultural Society’s Award of Garden Merit.

A fern native to south-central and southeastern China, Japan, Korea, the Nansei Islands and Taiwan, it produces coppery-red young fronds that mature to dark green. In cooler climates it is semi-evergreen.

A fern native to the British Isles, western Europe and western Asia. It grows among mountain scree; in Portugal it is currently known only from Serra da Estrela, while a survey of its historical Serra do Gerês site found none.

summary: Fern native to Macaronesia, Northwest Africa and mainland Portugal. It grows in humid woods and other shady places, sometimes on exposed slopes with high ocean humidity.

summary: A perennial vetch not native to north-western Europe, it is widespread across Europe and parts of Asia and northern Africa. It has rough upright or spreading stems, numerous narrow leaflets ending in split tendrils, and red, pink or bluish-purple flowers.
edibilityNote: In a few countries, this vetch is used as human food.

summary: A flowering legume native to Madeira and from Mediterranean countries through Central Asia to the western Himalayas. It has palatability issues but potential as green manure, forage and a bean crop.
A flowering plant native to mainland Portugal. It grows in damp meadows on temporarily waterlogged, compact clay or limestone ground, often near watercourses.

An annual flowering plant native to mainland Portugal and Madeira, but introduced in the Azores. It has low, rough-haired stems, three-part leaves and whitish flowers; as fruit develops, its hairy floral cup forms stiff, outward-curving teeth.

summary: A fast-growing shrub native to South America, with spreading, scrambling or upright growth and arching branches. Its bright yellow flowers appear prominently around Easter or early autumn in the Southern Hemisphere, with a smaller flowering period around Christmas. Long cylindrical pods hang from the branches.
A shrub or deciduous tree native to South and Central America. Its bright yellow flowers appear in summer, and its many leaflets close at night and reopen at dawn.

Small evergreen flowering tree occurring in southern Africa, including dry waterways in parts of South Africa. It has a gnarled trunk and numerous bright red-to-pink flowers in February and March. Its pods turn brown when ripe and burst open, catapulting the seeds away from the parent tree.
Annual herb whose native origin is not stated in the supplied information. It supports itself and has broad, compound leaves.

A shrub or tree native from Bolivia to Brazil and northeastern Argentina, chiefly in seasonally dry tropical areas. Its lower branches bear curved thorns, while fragrant white flowers form round clusters followed by straight, brown segmented pods.

summary: A perennial herb native to mainland Portugal, it grows in sandy soil in places including open woodlands, pine woods and meadows. In a 2016–2019 mainland assessment, all known groups were small and highly restricted, and the species was assessed as Vulnerable.

summary: A plant species native to the Madeira archipelago. It has a zigzagging taproot with whitish, soft, brittle and juicy roots.

A legume-family plant found across much of the Iberian Peninsula, southwestern France and northern Morocco, although its native origin is not explicitly stated. It grows characteristically in low scrub on acidic ground, and its March-to-June flowers are used in cooking, including carqueja rice.
edibilityNote: The flowers are used in cooking, including carqueja rice, and are also prepared as medicinal infusions.

summary: A perennial shrub endemic to Madeira, it has a silky, silvery covering and yellow flowers in clusters at the ends of its branches.

A tree native to West Africa from Mauritania to Chad and Cameroon, where it grows in wooded grassland or savanna. It has thorny leaf stalks and clusters of bright red flowers. Its seeds are poisonous.
edibilityNote: The seeds are poisonous.

summary: A thorny deciduous tree native to tropical and subtropical eastern Africa, the Indian subcontinent, northern Australia, and Indian and western Pacific islands east to Fiji, the Indian coral tree bears dense scarlet or crimson flower clusters and black seeds. Its raw seeds are poisonous but can be cooked and eaten.
edibilityNote: The seeds are poisonous raw but can be cooked and eaten.

summary: A shrub, or sometimes a tree, endemic to China, where it grows in southern and north-central regions and Manchuria. It has pink or milky-white flowers and almost circular leaves that taper to a point.
A flowering plant native to Brazil, it is planted as a street tree in several Brazilian cities.
A broadleaf evergreen flowering tree native to South America, Brazilian orchid tree has a dense, symmetrical crown that may be vase-shaped, rounded or spreading.

A flowering shrub probably native to Malaysia, parts of Indonesia and the Philippines, although extensive cultivation obscures its exact native range. Its hoof-shaped, two-lobed leaves and fragrant white flowers are distinctive. It is used in culinary dishes in Odisha, though the plant part and preparation are unspecified.
edibilityNote: Used in culinary dishes in Odisha; the plant part and preparation are not specified.

summary: A leguminous plant native to Australia, it has fluffy yellow, tube-shaped flowers in winter. Its evergreen foliage may fall during very cold weather.
An orchid native to Bangladesh, southern China, the eastern Himalayas and Indochina.

An evergreen perennial herb native to southern Asia, including the Indian subcontinent and Southeast Asia. Its false trunk consists of tightly packed leaf sheaths, and many modern edible dessert bananas derive from it, although some are hybrids with Musa balbisiana.
edibilityNote: The fruit's starchy pulp is eaten; many modern dessert bananas derive from this species, while others are hybrids with Musa balbisiana.

summary: A large non-woody evergreen perennial whose wild form is native from South Africa north to Ethiopia and west to the Congo. It has huge banana-like leaves and flowers only once, at the end of its life. In Ethiopia, its cooked heart and corm are eaten, while pulverised trunk and flower stalk are fermented into kocho or processed into bulla; the fruits are inedible.
edibilityNote: Cooked hearts and corms are eaten; trunk and flower stalk become kocho or bulla. Fruits are inedible.

summary: Perennial geophyte native to South Africa’s Eastern and Western Cape, it occurs from the Great Swartberg through the Langkloof to Butterworth and forms part of the fynbos and Albany thickets biomes.

A climbing perennial flowering plant native to most of Africa except North Africa, tropical South and Southeast Asia, and south-central China, it uses curled leaf-tip tendrils for support. Its bright yellow-to-red flowers have wavy segments that bend backwards; most parts, especially the seeds and tubers, are poisonous, and ingestion can be fatal.
edibilityNote: Most parts are poisonous, especially the seeds and tubers; ingestion can be fatal.

summary: A sedge native to Europe, the Atlas Mountains and western Asia, specializing in riverside forests. It forms bright-green, grass-like clumps with pale-green flower spikes arranged in a corkscrew pattern along the stem.
A perennial sedge native to parts of Spain and Portugal. It grows in compact clumps.
A flowering plant native to mainland Portugal.
A flowering plant native to mainland Portugal.

A geophyte of the western Mediterranean, found mainly in Portugal and Spain, it has a short upright underground stem and basal leaves. Its pinkish-white flowers have six segments, and in the Algarve they may appear as early as late April, after the leaves have withered.
A small air plant native to Central America and Mexico, Tillandsia ionantha is usually stemless, with densely covered, narrow triangular leaves. It produces one to three purple flowers.

A solitary palm native to Sri Lanka, India, Myanmar and Malaysia, and perhaps elsewhere in the Indo-Malayan region. Its flower clusters emerge successively down the trunk, and the tree dies after completing flowering and fruiting. Flower-shoot sap is boiled into syrup, while the cabbage is eaten raw or cooked.
edibilityNote: Flower-shoot sap is boiled into syrup; cabbage is eaten raw or cooked; mature pulp is dried and powdered; fruit is eaten after stiff hairs are removed.

summary: A thyme-moss originating in North America and now also found in Middle America, Europe, Africa and much of Asia. Its sharply toothed, gradually tapering leaves form green cushions; when dry, the leaves darken and curl.

Perennial plant native to northeastern Asia, including China, eastern Siberia, Korea and Japan. Its buds swell like balloons before opening into large blue flowers; cultivated varieties may have white or pink flowers.
edibilityNote: In Korea, the fresh or dried roots are popular salad ingredients.

summary: A shrub or small tree native across tropical and southern Africa and islands of the western Indian Ocean. Its bumpy fruit ripens from green through yellow to orange; the mild, pineapple-like pulp, flowers and leaves are eaten.
edibilityNote: Fruit pulp, flowers and leaves are eaten; flowers garnish or spice meals, and leaves serve as vegetables.

summary: Mint-family plant native to tropical Africa and the Indian Subcontinent. It bears striking rings of lipped flowers, usually orange but sometimes red, white or purple, above very soft, serrated dark-green leaves.

Herb native to northwestern Spain and central and northern Portugal. It usually grows in rocky places and bears purplish-pink flowers in which incomplete separation of male and female stages makes self-pollination possible.

Flowering plant almost endemic to the mountains of central and northern mainland Portugal. It grows above 1,000 metres in stony meadows and granite rock crevices and is assessed as Vulnerable, with only five known locations.

summary: A bulbous daffodil endemic to Portugal. It grows mainly in limestone crevices, less often in rocky clearings, beside holm oak groves or under forest cover.

A bulb-forming flowering plant endemic to mainland Portugal. It has grey-green, rush-like leaves, often prostrate or spiralling, and one to three small flowers with a crown-shaped cup; it frequently grows on poor, rocky granite soils.
A daffodil native to the central Iberian Peninsula, Narcissus rupicola grows on rocky ledges and in crevices with very little soil.

Perennial flowering herb native to central and eastern North America. It blooms from late summer to late fall with white-rayed, yellow-centred flower heads; its widespread variety is hairy, while Pringle's aster is hairless or nearly so.
A flowering shrub native to Venezuela, Brazilian red-cloak is especially recognizable by its large, showy reddish-purple bracts. These surround hairy white flowers with two distinct lips.
A herbaceous perennial native to the mountains of central and southern Europe. It bears whorls of yellow flowers and has intensely bitter roots and herbage; root extracts are used in bitter liqueurs.
edibilityNote: Root extracts are used in bitter liqueurs, and gentian was occasionally used in brewing.

summary: Herbaceous perennial native to eastern North America, orange coneflower has bright yellow, daisy-like flower heads. It spreads by creeping stems and seed and grows in habitats including bogs, woodlands, bottomlands and limestone-rich slopes.
A flowering plant native to eastern Russia, Japan and northwestern North America, including Alaska, Washington and parts of western and northern Canada.
A fern native from Mexico through Central America and the Caribbean to tropical South America.

summary: A deciduous fern native to eastern Asia, forming tufts of divided fronds from a creeping underground stem. The commonly cultivated pictum form has grey-green fronds with reddish midribs and thrives in shady gardens.

A fern found in southern and tropical Africa, tropical America, Asia and Australia, African spleenwort grows on rocks or sometimes on other plants. It is critically endangered in Victoria, Australia, and considered exotic in New Zealand.

A fern native from Florida through southern Brazil and northern Argentina, and from DR Congo to Madagascar and the Mascarene Islands. It is also recorded in the Azores, where it may possibly be native.

A fern native to parts of Africa, Atlantic islands, the Americas and Hawaii. Its upright leaves have shiny, hairless, reddish dark-brown to blackish central stalks, and each fertile leaflet usually bears a single spore patch near its toothless lower edge.

A tree fern occurring widely across Asia in shaded forests with humus-rich soil. Its persistent, spiny leaf stalks are purplish near the base and scaly, while dead fronds form a skirt around the crown. Its starch-rich stems are edible.
edibilityNote: The starch-rich stems are edible.

summary: Slow-growing evergreen perennial native to Japan, Korea and China. Glossy leaves on creeping stems spread into dense mats and may yellow in direct sun or winter. White flowers rise above the foliage in late March and April at temperate Northern Hemisphere sites; in the United States and Canada, the plant is described as highly invasive and spreads aggressively underground.

A tender herbaceous perennial native to Brazil, scarlet sage bears upright spikes of scarlet tubular or bell-shaped flowers through much of summer and autumn. Its many ornamental cultivars range from white to dark purple, and it is grown as an annual where winters freeze.

Climbing aroid native from Mexico through Bolivia in Latin America. Its usually arrow-shaped leaves develop varied pale, pink or yellow markings in cultivated forms. All parts are poisonous if eaten and can cause severe mouth pain.
edibilityNote: All parts are poisonous when eaten and cause severe mouth pain.

summary: A low perennial native to Western Europe and the northwestern Maghreb, Roman chamomile has daisy-like white flowers and a sweet, crisp, fruity-herbal scent. Its dried flowers flavor tea, though chamomile is likely unsafe during pregnancy and its tea may adversely affect anticoagulant drugs.
edibilityNote: Dried flowers flavor herbal teas and foods; chamomile is likely unsafe during pregnancy, and tea may adversely affect anticoagulant drugs.

summary: Herb native to tropical America, especially Brazil. It has white to mauve flowers and becomes an invasive weed in many regions outside its natural range. Ingestion can cause liver lesions and tumours, and contaminated grain caused a mass poisoning in Ethiopia.
edibilityNote: Ingestion can cause liver lesions and tumours; contaminated grain caused a mass poisoning in Ethiopia.

summary: A peat moss distributed throughout the Northern Hemisphere, papillose peatmoss forms dense carpets or hummocks in nutrient-poor fens and acidic peatlands. Its robust golden-brown top and short, blunt branches are useful field marks, while tiny wall projections make its cells look rough.

A biennial or perennial herb native across much of Europe, northern to southeastern Asia, Canada and colder parts of the United States. It produces many small flower heads with pink, lilac or occasionally white outer florets around yellow centres.

A deciduous shrub or small tree native across central and southeastern Europe and temperate Asia; some classifications also include a separated eastern Asian population. It has matt, coarsely toothed leaves and paired reddish winged fruits.

A rare deciduous shrub native to scattered locations in Oklahoma, Texas, Arkansas, Missouri, Alabama and Tennessee. It bears pink-grey summer flowers, followed by hair-covered spent flower stalks that create a smoky effect. Its autumn foliage turns brilliant scarlet and is considered by many to have exceptionally intense colour.

A deciduous tree native to Japan and Korea, ranging from small to tall and growing slowly. Its pleasantly fragrant white flowers, sometimes tinged pale pink, open in early spring before the leaves, although young trees do not flower.

A small to medium-sized tree native to central and western China. It is valued as a street tree for its autumn foliage and fruit, which changes from red to blue as it ripens, and it tolerates drought and harsh urban conditions.

A deciduous small tree or large shrub native to Europe and northern and northeastern Asia, bird cherry bears drooping clusters of flowers and black, strongly astringent fruit. In Russia, dried berries are milled into flour for cakes, while fresh fruit may be minced and cooked as jam; some parts, including the fruit, contain potentially poisonous glycosides.
edibilityNote: In Russia, dried berries are milled into flour for cake; fresh fruit may be minced and cooked as jam. Fruit can contain potentially poisonous glycosides.

summary: A deciduous tree native to southeastern Europe and southwestern Asia. Its leaves are green above and densely covered with white hairs beneath, while strongly scented pale-yellow flowers appear in mid to late summer.

Annual herb native to Asia and introduced to North America and Europe. Its branching stems may root where lower joints touch the ground, while bristly leaf sheaths and elongated clusters of pink flowers make it distinctive.

Tree fern native to eastern Australia from southeastern Queensland to Tasmania. Its trunk is densely covered with fibrous roots and old frond bases, while numerous large fronds form a funnel-shaped crown. The trunk resists fire, and the crown can regrow after burning.
edibilityNote: The pith and young curled fronds are edible; Indigenous Australians ate the starchy upper-trunk pulp raw or roasted.

summary: A perennial flowering plant native to the forest understorey of Asia, it has long, pointed leaves and strongly scented white flowers with yellow bases. Its flower buds and young flowers are edible.
edibilityNote: The flower buds and young flowers are edible.

summary: Dwarf perennial plant native to South Africa. Its trailing stems and fleshy leaves form dense mats that may be covered by abundant vermilion, magenta or pink flowers, and the leaves turn red in cold winter temperatures.
edibilityNote: In South Africa, roots and especially leaves help prepare khadi wine; the plant is also used as beer yeast. Fermentation reportedly produces toxic oxalic acid.

summary: A deciduous oak tree native to the north-central United States and south-central Canada, primarily the Great Lakes region and Upper Mississippi Valley, northern pin oak has glossy, deeply lobed leaves. Its variable acorns mature from green to pale brown about 18 months after pollination, and its foliage turns bright red in autumn.
Bulbous perennial flowering plant native to the Pyrenees in Spain and France. Its spring flowers hang like bells, with recurved purple, brown and yellow parts and a strong chequered pattern.
A flowering plant whose subspecies Silene foetida subsp. foetida is endemic to mainland Portugal.
A tree or shrub endemic to southwestern Western Australia. It has drooping, very narrow leaves, often twisted or zigzagging branchlets, and clusters of white flowers followed by cup-shaped capsules.

A perennial monocot from Southwest Australia, it resembles a tree crowned with bunches of long, grass-like leaves. Its often fire-blackened trunk develops bands from old leaves and annual growth that record age and previous fires.

Herbaceous perennial native to parts of central and southern Europe, including European Turkey and several Mediterranean islands. Its upright, spreading stems are thick, hollow and densely hairy. From May to August, it bears yellow to orange flowers with darker centres and hairy sepals.
A flowering plant native to southeast and south-central China, it typically grows beneath mountain forests. It and its derived cultivars and hybrids are the only fragrant hostas.

A summer-flowering bulbous perennial widespread across much of Colombia, El Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras and Mexico, and naturalized in Ecuador and Peru. Its three-petalled flowers have strongly contrasting centres, opening early in the morning and closing before dusk. The roasted bulbs are edible and are used in Indigenous recipes, including as a potato substitute in Colombia’s Sibundoy Valley.
edibilityNote: Roasted bulbs are edible and used by Indigenous peoples; Sibundoy Valley communities cook them in recipes or substitute them for potatoes.

summary: Flowering plant native to Mexico. Its showy flowers are usually red but can be orange or occasionally yellow. Aztecs used its nutritious tubers as food, but this use largely died out after the Spanish conquest.
edibilityNote: Its tubers were eaten by the Aztecs, though this use largely disappeared after the Spanish conquest.

summary: Herbaceous perennial native to Mexico and grown worldwide as an ornamental. It has purple-splotched flower bracts, equally sized bright-blue petals and tuberous roots, and occurs wild in moist fields and open or pine-oak forests.

A perennial native to the Americas, Indian shot has edible, starch-rich rhizomes and exceptionally hard black seeds resembling shotgun pellets. In part of Peru, the rhizomes were traditionally wrapped in leaves and slowly baked underground for the Festival of Corpus Christi.
edibilityNote: The starch-rich rhizomes are edible; in part of Peru they were traditionally slow-baked underground for the Festival of Corpus Christi.

summary: Epiphytic orchid endemic to Colombia, the Christmas orchid has succulent leaves and a flower lip coloured yellow, blue and red. It grows in cloud forests and is endangered because of habitat destruction.

A climbing or trailing herb native to the Afrotropics and Asia, hyacinth bean has three-part leaves and flattened pods containing several seeds. Its edible seeds are cultivated for food, while the pods contain high levels of cyanogenic glycosides and must be cooked carefully for human consumption.
edibilityNote: Seeds are edible; pods contain high levels of cyanogenic glycosides and require careful cooking. In Piura, the beans commonly accompany ceviche.

summary: Perennial flowering plant native to Europe, northern Africa and western Asia. It grows on sandy seashores, with many branching stems and crowded, overlapping fleshy leaves.

Herbaceous perennial native to southwestern, central and eastern Europe and southwestern Asia. Its leaves become deeply divided higher up the stems, and bright pink, scentless flowers appear from summer to early fall.
A small flowering herb found widely in Mexico's mountains from Chihuahua to Chiapas, it often grows in protected, shaded places.
A usually perennial evergreen plant found along South Africa’s southern coast. Its regularly branched growth bears stiff, sandpapery opposite leaves and bright blue flower heads with yellow centres.

A small evergreen tree or shrub native to tropical Southeast Asia, starfruit has crisp, juicy yellow fruit that forms a star when sliced. Its leaflets fold together at night and close when shaken, while fruit flavour ranges from very sour to mildly sweet.
edibilityNote: The fruit is edible; sweet forms are eaten raw, while sour forms are pickled or made into jelly, jam and juice.

summary: Small tree native to Mexico and Central America south to Costa Rica. It bears hard, cannonball-like fruit that can be hollowed and dried as food or drink containers and used for handicrafts. Its protein-rich seeds have a sweet, licorice-like taste and are used in Honduras, El Salvador and Nicaragua to make semilla de jícaro horchata.
edibilityNote: Protein-rich, sweet seeds are used in Honduras, El Salvador and Nicaragua to make semilla de jícaro horchata.

summary: A rhizomatous herbaceous perennial found from central Europe to parts of Asia around the Himalayas, it also occurs in North Africa. Its dull-purple flowers are memorable for their separated, star-like petals and deep violet-blue spurs.

Woody perennial shrub native to the Mediterranean, rue has blue-green leaves that release a strong aroma when bruised and small, dull-yellow flowers. It is used sparingly as a bitter culinary herb because it contains toxins; pregnant people and those with liver problems should avoid it.
edibilityNote: Used sparingly as a culinary herb; excessive amounts are toxic, and pregnant people or those with liver problems should avoid it.

summary: A towering forest tree endemic to southwestern Western Australia. It is the tallest tree growing in that state and among the tallest trees worldwide. Its smooth, mottled bark sheds yearly, exposing contrasting white and orange-yellow surfaces.
edibilityNote: Karri honey is sought for its clarity, light colour and delicate flavour; major honey flows occur every four to five years.

summary: Usually perennial, but occasionally annual, flowering herb native to Australia. Its golden-yellow or sometimes white flower heads have stiff, papery bracts resembling petals, and dried flowers can last for years in arrangements.
A flowering plant introduced to both the Azores and Madeira.

A herbaceous perennial native to Nuevo León in Mexico and parts of the United States, including Texas and Oklahoma. Its compact growth carries violet-blue flower spikes and narrow, unusually shiny leaves, unlike the dull, velvety leaves of many other sages.

Woody flowering shrub native to North America, from Nevada and South Dakota south to Arizona, Chihuahua and Texas. Its gray-green, threadlike leaves and hanging flower heads distinguish it, and it often dominates deep sandy soils.

Perennial wheatgrass native to Europe, including the UK. Usually self-pollinating, it grows in clumps with green, loose leaves and varies considerably between populations in features such as flower number, bristle length and leaf hairiness.

Tropical evergreen subshrub native to Mexico and the West Indies. Its small, bright red to orange tubular flowers have a thin white rim and two purple-black petals, resembling lit cigars and attracting hummingbirds and butterflies.

Herbaceous biennial endemic to Tenerife, mainly the Macizo de Anaga. It forms a dense rosette in its first year, followed by a tall spike of white flowers in its second. In Tenerife, it blooms from February to April.

A bulbous plant native to much of southern and eastern Africa, paintbrush lily grows in cool, shady ravines and forests, often in moist leaf litter. It bears bright red round fruits, each with one opalescent seed. Its bulb is considered poisonous in significant amounts, despite reported traditional medicinal and pregnancy-related herbal use.
edibilityNote: The bulb is poisonous in significant amounts; traditional consumption during pregnancy is described as part of an herbal regime, not as food.

summary: An annual or perennial herb native from tropical and subtropical America to the Falkland Islands. It has white-woolly stems, a basal leaf rosette and leaves that are green above but white and felted beneath. Small flower heads cluster along the leaf axils.
