sources.attribution: Plants of the World Online, Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew

summary: A perennial shrub native to Mexico, where it inhabits pine–oak forests. Its leaves smell like pineapple, and it bears tubular red flowers from August onward in Mexico, generally flowering later farther north.
edibilityNote: The leaves and flowers are edible.

summary: A small deciduous tree native to southern Europe and western Asia. Deep pink flowers grow prolifically in spring on older branches and even the trunk, followed by heart-shaped leaves and long, hanging flat pods. The flowers are edible and reportedly taste sweet and tart.
edibilityNote: The flowers are edible and reportedly have a sweet and tart taste.

summary: Fern native across broad areas of Africa, Asia, Pacific islands and eastern Australia. It can grow on other plants or on moist, well-drained ground, and its frond juice is used in Assamese traditional medicine.

A herbaceous, shrubby perennial native to a wide area of central Mexico. Its leaves vary from smooth mid-green to hairy grey-green, while abundant whorls of deep purple to purple-blue flowers bloom for several months from late summer.

Non-flowering spikemoss widespread across the Mediterranean Basin. It is a small, moss-like plant with ground-hugging, forked stems and four rows of leaves; its male spore cases are red and female ones green.

A flowering plant occurring in Mexico and Guatemala, this large Echeveria forms leaf rosettes and bears red, tubular flowers from September to January. In Mexican folk medicine, it has been used as a contraceptive vaginal rinse after intercourse.
A semi-woody succulent shrub native to Mexico, dwarf tree stonecrop has a compact, tree-like growth form.

Large deciduous shrub or tree endemic to Mexico, where it grows beside watercourses and along forest edges; it has naturalized in parts of Ethiopia. Its furrowed dark bark contrasts with paired leaves and branching clusters of small fragrant white, cream or yellow flowers with orange-flushed throats.

A moss found across much of the world, including Europe, Asia, Africa and the Americas. It forms low, loose yellow-green to golden-brown carpets, with strongly ribbed, toothed leaves that are often curved. It grows on soil, rock and rotting wood in wet, lime-rich places such as springs, riverbanks and marshes.
A moss common in Britain. It forms creeping mats on decaying tree stumps, hedgebanks and other shaded places, and can also live underwater.

Moss widespread in the temperate Northern Hemisphere, with no native origin specified. It forms loose, deep-green mats; sterile shoots lie flat while fertile shoots stand upright and bear capsules with long-beaked lids. It favours damp, shaded, lime-rich places, often beside streams or in woods.

A moss with a cosmopolitan distribution across all seven continents. It withstands cold, drought, salt, acid, heavy metals and intense ultraviolet radiation, and fungal infections can produce fairy rings.

A moss found throughout the Northern Hemisphere and at some sites in South America, New Zealand and Australia, it grows in bogs, marshes, wet meadows and beside water. It usually forms small yellow-green mats, with mostly sickle-shaped leaves; spore-producing structures are extremely rare.

Moss with a nearly cosmopolitan distribution across parts of the Americas, Eurasia and New Zealand. It forms clumps or lawns whose bright yellow-green leaves can glow against reddish-brown stems, and its cylindrical spore capsules are strongly ribbed.

A bryophyte native to every continent except South America and Antarctica. It usually grows in wet soil at disturbed sites, and its capsules mature from late autumn through spring. Its size, leaves and capsule shape vary both across its range and within individual populations.

Perennial flowering plant native to Great Britain, Ireland and eastern mainland Europe from the Pyrenees to eastern Norway. It is an evergreen, creeping woodland plant with bright green pointed leaves and solitary yellow flowers on long stalks.

Palm endemic to western and northern Madagascar, where it grows in open grasslands and low-grass savannas, usually on lateritic soils. It has a grey, ringed trunk and enormous, nearly round leaves divided into many stiff segments.

Deciduous tree native to tropical and subtropical forests of South America. Its bottle-shaped trunk bears large conical prickles, while its flowers have creamy-white centres and pink petal tips; its seeds are surrounded by cotton-like fibres.
edibilityNote: Its seeds can yield vegetable oil described as edible and also useful industrially.

summary: A herb native to North America, with upright, square-edged stems and leaves bearing five to seven main veins. Those leaf veins help distinguish it from other small-flowered St John's worts.

A rhizomatous ginger native to Maluku and the southwestern Pacific islands. Its showy magenta-to-red structures are modified leaves surrounding the much smaller true flowers, and its underground stems spread horizontally before sending up leafy shoots.

A lily native to Siberia, the Russian Far East, Mongolia, northeast China, Korea and Hokkaidō. It requires winter frost and produces upright, dish-shaped flowers whose six segments curve backward from the centre.

A shrub or tree native to the Americas from Mexico to Argentina, including parts of the Caribbean, it has fragrant white flowers and firm yellow fruit. Fruit flavour varies from bitter or tart and strawberry-like to sweet enough for some varieties to be eaten raw; it is also used for preserves.
edibilityNote: Some varieties bear sweet fruit eaten raw; the fruit is also made into preserves, though other varieties taste tart or bitter.

summary: A succulent perennial herb native to Central America and southern Mexico. Its knobby, swollen stem resembles a bottle, while orange-red flower clusters rise above the leaves and its ripe capsules burst to scatter seeds. All parts are considered toxic, particularly the seeds.
edibilityNote: All parts are considered toxic, especially the seeds, which contain purgative oil and the toxin curcin.

summary: A unicellular green alga found especially in extremely salty waters, Dunaliella salina lacks a rigid cell wall and can accumulate enough beta-carotene to appear orange-red. It is commercially cultivated for beta-carotene and used as a pro-vitamin A food supplement.
edibilityNote: Used as a pro-vitamin A food supplement because it contains abundant beta-carotene; it may also provide vitamin B12.

summary: A tender shrub or small tree native to southeastern Brazil and thought extinct in the wild, it bears large, hanging trumpet-shaped flowers that are sweetly scented at night and in the early morning. Every part is poisonous, especially the seeds and leaves, and ingestion can cause severe effects including hallucinations, paralysis and death.
edibilityNote: Every part is poisonous when ingested; seeds and leaves are especially dangerous.

summary: A perennial ginger native to East Asia, it grows in upright evergreen clumps from underground stems. Its funnel-shaped flowers are white or pink with yellow centres marked by red spots and stripes; the leaves are used to wrap and flavour foods and make herbal tea.
edibilityNote: Leaves are used to wrap zongzi and muchi, flavour Okinawan noodles, and make herbal tea.

summary: A tropical flowering plant native to tropical America, although its exact native range is uncertain, tannia is an important starchy crop. Its secondary corms and leaves are eaten; corms should be boiled to reduce irritation, while primary corms are generally reserved for animal feed because they contain more oxalates.
edibilityNote: Corms and leaves are eaten; corms should be boiled to reduce irritation, while primary corms are generally animal feed because they contain more oxalates.

summary: A plant native to Central America, Mexico, the West Indies and northern South America, piñuela has prickly leaves and is commonly planted as a pasture fence in Jamaica. Its pulp can be processed into thread-making fibre, and in Nicaragua and El Salvador the plant is used to make gruel.
edibilityNote: In Nicaragua and El Salvador, the plant is used to make gruel.

summary: A trailing annual native to much of Europe, from the western Iberian Peninsula to Poland. Its paired leaves have clusters of tiny white flowers in their axils. In Portugal, submerged plants develop long stems ending in floating leaf rosettes, while terrestrial plants have short gaps between leaves.

Perennial culinary herb native to tropical parts of the Americas. It has velvety, heart-shaped leaves and white flower spikes that rise like candles. Its fragrant leaves are used in Mexican cooking as wrappers and to flavour mole, eggs and soups.
edibilityNote: Fresh or dried leaves flavour Mexican foods and drinks, though drying reduces flavour and makes them too brittle for wrappers.

summary: A tropical wetland tree native to Central and South American swamps, it has shiny, hand-shaped leaves and a slightly thickened root that stores water. Its very large flowers have narrow petals opening around brush-like stamens, and its leaves and flowers are often eaten.
edibilityNote: Leaves and flowers are often eaten.

summary: Tropical evergreen shrub native to Peru. Its short-lived white flowers emerge one after another from overlapping bright yellow bracts throughout the warm months.

A palm tree found wild in tropical South American wetlands. Its chestnut-coloured fruit has shiny scales and yellow flesh around a hard nut. The fruit is eaten or made into drinks and foods; flower-cluster buds are eaten as a vegetable, and sap is drunk fresh or fermented.
edibilityNote: Fruit is eaten or processed into drinks and foods; flower-cluster buds are vegetables, and sap is drunk fresh or fermented.

summary: Medium to large deciduous shrub native to most of Europe and western Asia. Its creamy-white flowers are followed by black, single-seeded berries. Some garden varieties reveal striking red stems after their orange-yellow autumn leaves fall.

A palm tree native to northeastern Brazil, the carnaúba has a rounded crown of fan-shaped leaves and small black fruits. It may live for up to 200 years. Its leaves carry a natural coating harvested as carnauba wax.
edibilityNote: The fruit and pith are eaten; fruit makes jelly, dried pulp makes flour, seeds yield oil, and roasted fruit is brewed as a coffee substitute.

summary: A herbaceous perennial originating in the Neotropical Americas. It is now found across tropical and subtropical regions worldwide.
A plant native to Mexico and southern Florida, Mexican alvaradoa is common in Mexico but endangered in Florida.

A liverwort possibly originating in Southeast Asia, it is now widely distributed across temperate Northern Hemisphere regions. Its highly divided leaves give its loose, pale-green to yellowish-white mats a feathery or fuzzy appearance, especially in moist, shaded places near springs and streams.

An annual herb native to Europe and Western Asia, Mediterranean hartwort has softly hairy, divided leaves and white flowers with enlarged, deeply two-lobed petals. Its round, flattened fruit is elaborately textured. The leaves are eaten in Greece as a cooked green and salad vegetable, while in Italy the plant is used as a condiment.
edibilityNote: Leaves are eaten in Greece as a potherb and salad vegetable; in Italy, the plant is used as a condiment.

summary: A perennial grass with no native origin stated, tall wheatgrass has broad leaves and yellow flowers. Its self-supporting stems can reach about five feet.

A flowering plant endemic to the Iberian Peninsula. It occupies open patches in heaths and other low scrub on acidic mountain ground above 900 metres. In mainland Portugal it has a restricted, declining population and was assessed as Endangered, with recurring fires identified as the main pressure.

summary: Flowering plant endemic to the Iberian Peninsula. It grows in wet meadows; in mainland Portugal it was assessed as endangered, with only three known locations and a severely fragmented population.

summary: A moss of unstated native origin, matted feather-moss occurs chiefly in temperate parts of the Northern Hemisphere and also in northern, central and southern Africa. It forms soft, often extensive green mats, with creeping, nearly feather-branched stems that cling firmly to rock, walls, concrete or tree bases.

A moss of unstated native origin, it forms dense, slightly glossy green, yellow-green or brownish mats with creeping stems and rising branches. It grows mainly in wet places along lime-free streams and rivers, especially on silicate rock, and occurs widely across the Northern Hemisphere and Oceania.

A tree native to southern and Southeast Asia, Australia and Polynesia, bishop wood was introduced to North America as an ornamental and is now considered invasive there. Its dense, dark red wood is used for furniture and bridges; its fruits make wine, its seeds are edible, and its leaves are eaten with chilli sauce in southern Laos.
edibilityNote: Fruits are made into wine, seeds are edible, and leaves are eaten with chilli sauce in southern Laos.

summary: An annual flowering plant native to mainland Portugal and also recorded across central and southern Europe, the Caucasus and Siberia. It grows in cultivated or disturbed ground, including annual grasslands, pastures and fallow fields, especially on sandy or ultrabasic soils. Flowering occurs from April to October.

summary: A tropical perennial native from tropical Africa and the Arabian Peninsula through parts of South and East Asia. This semi-succulent subshrub has large, serrated leaves and upright clusters of purple-blue flowers; its roots contain forskolin.
edibilityNote: Herbal teas are made from the plant, although the passage does not specify which parts are used.

summary: A tree native to northern Australia, New Guinea and the Maluku Islands of Indonesia, the weeping paperbark has thick white, pinkish or cream papery bark and drooping branches. Its cream to greenish-white flowers may appear at any time of year and were traditionally used by Aboriginal people to make a sweet drink.
edibilityNote: Aboriginal people traditionally used the flowers to make a sweet drink; bark was used to wrap food before underground-oven cooking.

summary: Herbaceous perennial legume native to parts of northern Africa, western Asia and Europe. It contains galegine, which contributed to the development of diabetes drugs, and the plant can be poisonous to mammals.

Flowering plant native to the Americas, from the southwestern United States through Central America to Argentina. Native peoples in Central America and Mexico have used wilted fresh leaves brewed and fermented in cool water for shamanic purposes.
A flowering plant of unspecified native origin, introduced in the Azores.

A herbaceous perennial native across parts of South, East and Southeast Asia, it has broad heart-shaped leaves and small greenish-yellow flowers framed by white bracts. Its fishy-tasting leaves are eaten fresh or cooked, while tender roots and rhizomes are used in regional Asian dishes; dried leaves may be brewed as tea.
edibilityNote: Leaves are eaten raw or cooked; tender roots and rhizomes are used in regional dishes, while dried leaves may be brewed as tea.

summary: A coastal plant whose native origin is unresolved, Carpobrotus aequilaterus is naturalised as a weed in several regions. Its edible fruit is said to taste like strawberry but has poor structure.
edibilityNote: The fruit is edible and reportedly tastes like strawberry, although it has poor structure.

summary: Tropical subshrub or shrub native to tropical Asia, New Guinea and Queensland, Australia. Its nutritious leaves are widely eaten as a vegetable, including in Philippine soups and salads, Indonesian bubur Manado and everyday cooking in Papua New Guinea.
edibilityNote: Leaves are eaten as a vegetable in Philippine and Indonesian dishes and are a widely consumed indigenous green in Papua New Guinea.

summary: A large shrub native to tropical America and Central and South Africa. It has broad leaves, yellow flowers and long simple stem hairs, and its prolific seed production makes it invasive in some regions.

Annual flowering plant native to the southeastern United States, with upright, freely branching, densely hairy stems. It has petal-free male and female flowers on the same plant and reddish-to-black seeds; it flowers from spring to fall through most of its range, but year-round in southern Florida.
A herbaceous perennial native to central and southwestern Asia. It has rough, hairy, fern-like foliage and large, uneven clusters of small, rigid, old-gold flowers in mid to late summer.

A wild, erect perennial herb whose native origin is not specified, devil's horsewhip is distributed throughout the tropical world and introduced as a common weed in many places. Its hairy stems and leaves carry long spikes of small green, spiny flowers, with flowering and fruiting reported from September to April.
Perennial climbing vine native to Japan, Korea, northern China and the Russian Far East. Its edible kiwiberries are small, smooth-skinned fruits that can be eaten whole without peeling.
edibilityNote: Fruit is eaten whole or processed; young leaves are eaten as a vegetable, and sap reportedly served as famine food in Korea.

summary: A small fern native across parts of Africa and Asia, Malesia, mainland Australia, New Zealand and Pacific islands, rough maidenhair fern grows in clumps from short, dark rhizomes. Young growth can be pinkish before maturing to dark green.
A fern native to South America, it has shiny, dark leafstalks resembling human hair. Its triangular fronds begin semi-upright and droop gracefully as they age.

An ornamental plant native to North Africa, Western Asia, the Mediterranean and Europe. Its flowers are often scarlet with dark basal spots, while its leaves and roots are poisonous to humans and livestock.
edibilityNote: The leaves and roots are poisonous to humans and livestock.

summary: Annual, or rarely biennial, herb native to Europe, western Asia and northwestern Africa. Its divided leaves smell unpleasant, and the fresh whole plant is poisonous, though drying destroys its toxins.
edibilityNote: The fresh whole plant is poisonous, but drying destroys its toxins; no human food use is documented.

summary: A perennial mint-family plant native to much of northern North America, especially the Great Plains and other prairies. It has anise-scented leaves used for seasoning, tea and salads, and bears abundant bright lavender flowers from June to September.
edibilityNote: The leaves are used as seasoning or tea and may be crumbled into salads.

summary: A rosette-forming agave endemic to central Arizona in the United States. It flowers once, producing golden-yellow blooms on a slender stalk that can reach eight metres, and only occasionally forms sparse offsets. It grows on rocky mountain slopes in granite and volcanic soils.

sources.title: Agave chrysantha Peebles
sources.attribution: Döring M (2022). German Wikipedia - Species Pages. Wikimedia Foundation. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/4wn9dt accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-15.

summary: A succulent perennial believed to have originated in northeastern Mexico, it forms suckers and has arching or backward-curving leaves beneath a very tall flowering stalk. It is cultivated for ornament, fibre and production of the alcoholic beverage pulque.
edibilityNote: It is cultivated to produce pulque; early Mexican specimens were also reported as cultivated for making this alcoholic beverage.

summary: A flowering shrub native to Texas, Cuba, and northeastern and east-central Mexico. Unlike many related species, it is evergreen.

Sprawling perennial herb native to western Mexico. Its often woody stems bear purple hairs and can root where they touch the ground. Coarsely serrated leaves and dense heads of white flowers help distinguish it.
edibilityNote: Near Sangau, India, dried leaves and flowers are prepared as herbal tea and taken to reduce blood pressure and blood sugar.

summary: A flowering plant native to the Philippines and northeastern Sulawesi. It has been introduced to numerous other tropical regions and is cultivated as an ornamental.

summary: A perennial grass native across most of Europe and temperate Asia. It spreads by above-ground runners rather than underground stems and is common in damp places, including ditches and lake margins. Its short green growth is popular for lawns.

A wild onion native to Turkey, Cyprus, Syria, Lebanon and the Palestine region, it unusually lacks the onion or garlic scent common to its group. Its dense flower clusters have white, star-like flowers with green midveins, while the ovaries vary in colour with age and location.

summary: A bulbous perennial wild onion from Eurasia, field garlic grows in dry places. Its pinkish-brown flower heads sometimes carry small bulblets, and the two-part papery covering has long points that often overtop the flowers.

A rhizomatous perennial grass native to Eurasia and northern Africa, creeping foxtail forms sod in damp or saline grasslands and along waterways. It is used for forage and erosion control, and flowers between April and July depending on location.
Perennial herb native to Brazil, Argentina and Paraguay, with underground tubers. Its clusters of three to eight flowers are red to reddish-purple, sometimes with brownish spots.

Flowering herb native to forests from northeastern Mexico through Central and South America to northeastern Argentina. Its young red, green or purple stems are finely hairy, while its leaves are often vividly reddish-purple. Small vanilla-coloured, pom-pom-like flowers grow in compact clusters.
edibilityNote: It is harvested from the wild for regional use as food, although the parts and preparation are not specified.

summary: A perennial herb native to central and southern Europe, the Mediterranean Basin, north Africa, Turkey and central Asia, excluding the Balearic Islands, Corsica, Crete and Cyprus. It has hairy, deeply divided lower leaves resembling hemp and usually bears pink or reddish-purple, heart-shaped flowers from July to September.
An annual flowering plant native to Mexico, northern Central America, the Caribbean, the Galápagos, and parts of the south-central and southeastern United States.

A small perennial semi-shrub native to North America. Its tiny purple flowers have yellow stamens, while dense hairs give its compound leaves a lead-grey appearance; its deep roots suit dry prairies, bluffs and open woodlands.
edibilityNote: Indigenous peoples used the leaves to make tea.

summary: A moss with no native origin specified in the supplied text. It forms yellow-green to brown-green cushions on persistently wet, shaded mountain rocks and, because it rarely produces spore capsules, usually spreads through detached leaves.
Moss native to North America and parts of Europe. It can form extensive black or brown cushions on wet, acidic, exposed rocks, and its leaves may curve to one side, especially when wet.

A moss found mainly around the Northern Hemisphere, black rock moss grows as dark, cushion-like tufts on exposed, usually acidic rock. Its mature spore cases lack a stalk and split along four vertical lines, opening when dry and closing again when moist.

A flowering plant native to Europe and central Asia, wild angelica is an annual or short-lived perennial. It has upright purplish stems and rounded clusters of tiny white or pale pink flowers in late summer.
edibilityNote: Eaten as a vegetable until the 20th century; stems were eaten fresh, while leaves were boiled for storage or cooked with milk.

summary: A leafy moss distributed across the Northern Hemisphere, chiefly in limestone areas, grows on shaded rocks and trees. It forms vigorous, non-glossy yellow-green or fresh-green carpets, with creeping stems producing sparsely branched ascending shoots.

A hornwort occurring across temperate Europe and North America, mainly in moist lowland fields and ditches. Its thin, dark-green body forms a rosette, while upright spore structures blacken as they mature and split open.
A hornwort with no native origin stated in the supplied sources. It is described as subcosmopolitan and has been reported from wet, shady places in England and Italy.

sources.attribution: GBIF Secretariat (2023). GBIF Backbone Taxonomy. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/39omei accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-15.

summary: A perennial herb native to northern North America, mainly from Alaska across Canada, with isolated populations farther south. Its small, nodding flowers combine blue-to-lavender outer parts with white or pale-yellow petals and appear from May into July or August.

A perennial flowering plant native to the Rocky Mountains of the United States and Canada, it grows in mountain meadows, open woods and alpine slopes. Its nodding flowers usually have yellow sepals, though these may be yellowish-pink or raspberry-pink, with white or cream petals and curved nectar spurs.

A perennial flowering herb native to mountainous parts of Europe, North and East Africa, Central and Eastern Asia and North America, it inhabits damp gravel and scree. Loose heads of white, four-petalled spring flowers rise above strongly toothed basal leaves and stalkless leaves that clasp the stem.

An evergreen perennial herb native to Crimea, Turkey, Iran, the Caucasus and the Mediterranean. It grows in limestone crevices, by streams and in alpine meadows, producing white flowers in early spring; cultivated forms may have pink or double flowers.

Deciduous small tree or shrub native to eastern Asia, from Russia and China through Taiwan, Korea and Japan. Its rough gray bark bears prickles, and large leaves accompany clusters of small white flowers followed by black fruit. In Japan and Korea, young spring shoots are eaten after cooking or pickling.
edibilityNote: Young spring shoots are eaten in Japan and Korea, commonly blanched, fried or pickled.

summary: A flowering evergreen shrub or tree native to Central America, Mexico and the southwestern United States, Texas madrone has smooth orange-brown bark that peels in thin sheets. Its white or pale pink bell-shaped flowers are followed by rough red berries that are reportedly edible, though related species have narcotic properties.
edibilityNote: The red berries are reportedly edible, although related species have narcotic properties.

summary: A palm endemic to Queensland, Australia, the Alexandra palm has a solitary trunk and a crown of feather-like fronds with silvery-grey undersides. Its fruit turns bright red when ripe, and the Kuku Yalanji people of Far North Queensland ate its palm heart.
edibilityNote: The Kuku Yalanji people of Far North Queensland ate the palm heart.

summary: A flowering plant native to sand dunes along the west coast of South Africa’s Cape Province, white arctotis is rare within its native range. It has also been introduced to New Zealand.
A compact flowering shrub native to East Asia, coralberry has thick, glossy dark-green leaves with tightly waved edges. Its clusters of glossy red berries can remain on the plant throughout the year.

A deciduous vine native to the Caribbean and Central America, it bears exceptionally large flowers smelling of rotting meat. The heart-shaped, purple-veined flowers have long tails and attract flies, while the plant contains carcinogenic aristolochic acid.

An annual herb native to Europe, Morocco and the Middle East. It grows as a weed in cornfields and fallow fields, favouring infertile, sandy, acidic soils. Its leaves form a basal rosette, while slender, largely leafless stems bear golden-yellow flower heads.
edibilityNote: Described as suitable only for animal consumption.

sources.title: Arnoseris minima (L.) Schweigg. & Körte
sources.attribution: GBIF Secretariat (2023). GBIF Backbone Taxonomy. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/39omei accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-15.

summary: A perennial aromatic herb native across much of Eurasia, from France to Japan. Its strongly scented, heavily branched stems are often purple-tinged, while young sea-green, silky-haired growth becomes yellowish and smooth at maturity. Young leaves are recorded as edible when cooked, although this use is minor and not widely documented.
edibilityNote: Young leaves are recorded as edible when cooked, but this use is minor and not widely documented.

summary: A sunflower-family plant native to parts of China, Japan, Korea, the Russian Far East and the Aleutian Islands. Its pale green to white leaves are thickly hairy on both sides, giving them a silvery appearance. Tall clusters of yellow flowers bloom from July to late August.

Sprawling perennial herb native to the tropical Americas. Its reddish stems and buds lead to pink or purple flowers with prominent stamens, and its leaves have tiny reddish, bristly teeth. The tender stems are edible and can be used as food.
edibilityNote: The tender stems are edible and used as food.

summary: A fern native across parts of Africa, western and central Asia, Europe, Macaronesia, the southwestern United States and Hawaii. Its thick triangular leaves are repeatedly divided, carried on reddish-green stalks, and bear chains of spore-producing patches beneath.
A perennial flowering herb native to most of Europe except Ireland, Iceland and the Greek islands, and also native to parts of western and central Asia, wild liquorice is sometimes used to make tea.
edibilityNote: The plant is sometimes used to make tea.

sources.attribution: Andre Carapeto % Ana Francisco, Paulo Pereira, Miguel Porto, felipe (2020). Lista Vermelha da Flora Vascular de Portugal Continental. Plazi.org taxonomic treatments database. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/ge693f accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-12.

summary: Spreading herb whose original range is unclear; subsp. gangetica was likely limited to Asia and subsp. micrantha to Africa. Its stems root readily at the joints, while its capsules dry from green to brown and explosively release their seeds. Some African communities eat the leaves as a vegetable.
edibilityNote: The leaves are eaten as a vegetable in some parts of Africa.

summary: An annual coastal plant native to Europe, North Africa, and western and eastern Asia. It has a shrubby appearance, narrow green or grey-green leaves, and small flower clusters, often forming dense stands on beaches, saltmarshes, and tidal riverbanks. Its leaves are edible when cooked.
edibilityNote: The leaves are edible when cooked.

summary: An annual plant native across parts of Middle and western Central Asia, Asia Minor, North Africa and Eastern Europe. It has a white branched taproot and produces two fruit types differing in size and colour. It commonly grows in salty soils and disturbed places such as roadsides, railways and dumps.

A tufted grass native to Europe, with seeds smaller than those of common oats. Its seeds are edible, and it was formerly cultivated as human food in Scotland, though it is now grown as livestock forage in South America.
edibilityNote: The edible seeds were formerly cultivated as human food in Scotland.

summary: A grass with no native origin stated, broadleaf carpetgrass forms low groundcover in moist, nutrient-poor soils and shaded places. It is used for permanent pasture and low-maintenance turf but is generally too short for harvested fodder.
Flowering bamboo native to China, Nepal, Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, Sri Lanka, Taiwan and northern Indochina. Its slender stems and dense foliage form clumps suitable for hedges and living fences.

A leafy liverwort recorded from Arctic Europe south to the Pyrenees and Bulgaria, and also across parts of Asia and North America. It forms yellow-green spongy mats, often mixed with other mosses, and has leaves divided into four broad, spine-tipped lobes.

A moss with no native origin specified, bird's-claw beard-moss is common across temperate regions but rare in the tropics. Its bright yellow-green, opaque leaves often twist around the stem when dry and spread outward when moist.

A perennial vine native to the Indian subcontinent, Southeast Asia and New Guinea. It grows quickly on soft stems and has thick, heart-shaped leaves with a mild flavour and slippery texture; the leaves and shoots are cooked in curries, soups and stir-fries.
edibilityNote: Leaves are eaten in numerous cooked dishes across Asia; cooked shoots are commonly used in Africa.

summary: A large annual herb native from Central Europe across Asia, it develops red autumn foliage and can detach and roll in the wind as a tumbleweed. In Japan, its dull black seeds are boiled, soaked and hulled to make tonburi, a garnish prized for its caviar-like texture.
edibilityNote: In Japan, boiled, soaked and hulled seeds are eaten as the garnish tonburi.

summary: An evergreen, sprawling shrub native to Angola, Mozambique, Zimbabwe, Eswatini and parts of South Africa. Its two rounded leaf lobes resemble a camel's foot, and wild plants generally bear brick-red flowers; cultivars may instead flower pink or orange-red.

Upright herbaceous perennial native to Argentina, Brazil, Paraguay and Uruguay. It has glossy, succulent leaves and red, pink or white flowers, which bloom in summer or throughout the year in warmer places; its fruits have three wings.

A flowering, shrub-like begonia native to Colombia and Venezuela, it has hanging succulent stems densely covered with glossy oval green leaves and clusters of small white flowers. The commonly cultivated variety, B. foliosa var. miniata, instead has pink or red flowers.
Flowering plant native to Jamaica, Venezuela, Colombia, Peru, Bolivia and southern Brazil. Its juice is applied to the skin to treat itching from insect bites.

A flowering herb from North America, widespread across much of Mexico and also found in Arizona and Guatemala. It produces numerous yellow or whitish flower heads and grows mainly in wet places such as marshes and streambanks.

A perennial bromeliad native to northern South America and parts of the Caribbean. It forms clumps of jar-shaped leaf rosettes that collect water and debris, and produces brush-shaped red or pink blooms, often nearly simultaneously in late summer or early autumn.

Grass native across much of Africa, the Middle East, southern and eastern Asia, Malesia and Australia. It is used as stored livestock feed and grazing for livestock and wild ruminants, and is sometimes planted to restore disturbed land.
An evergreen climbing shrub whose native origin is not supplied. It has thick thorny stems and drooping branches, with tiny white flowers surrounded by colourful papery bracts that resemble petals.
Moss native to much of the world outside South America and tropical regions, it can grow under artificial light in places without natural light, such as Crystal Cave in Wisconsin.

An orchid native to warmer parts of the Western Hemisphere, from southern Mexico and Florida through Central America and the Caribbean to northern South America. It is commonly called the tailed Brassia, spider orchid or cricket orchid.
A plant native to New Caledonia and Vanuatu in the western Pacific. Leafflower moths have been reared from its fruit there, and the fruit is presumed toxic and capable of causing liver injury.
edibilityNote: The fruit is presumed toxic and may cause liver injury.

summary: A perennial grass native and widespread in Britain and Europe except the extreme north. Fine stems carry distinctive green and purplish, hop-shaped flower clusters that droop from loose branches; in the UK it flowers from June to September.

A flowering grass native from the Mediterranean and Caucasus through the Middle East and Central Asia to Xinjiang, Afghanistan and Pakistan, large-headed brome thrives in disturbed habitats. It has been introduced at scattered sites in the Americas and central Europe.
A grass native from northern Italy to the Caucasus and China. Its basal leaf sheaths break into netlike fibres, while the leaf edges bear conspicuously uneven, irregularly spaced hairs.

sources.attribution: Info Flora, plazi (2021). Info Flora Schweiz - Poaceae. Plazi.org taxonomic treatments database. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/p2zqqq accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-15.

summary: An annual grass native from the Mediterranean through Crimea, the Middle East, the Caucasus and Central Asia to Xinjiang and the northwestern Indian subcontinent. It is somewhat weedy and typically grows in grasslands.

An annual plant native to the United States, it has creeping stems that root at their nodes and younger shoots that climb with tendrils. It grows beside rivers and lakes and along woodland edges and damp thickets.

Tender deciduous shrub native across much of South and Southeast Asia, southern China, the Himalayas and parts of the western Pacific. Its sweetly scented flowers are usually white, occasionally pale violet, and appear in late winter in slender clusters at the ends of long, loose branches. It can grow as woodland understorey scrub or a small tree.
An evergreen flowering shrub endemic to Madagascar, where it grows among mountain scrub. It has fragrant autumn and winter flowers ranging from deep yellow and orange to pink.

An annual flowering plant native to mainland Portugal and Mediterranean in global distribution. It has yellow flowers, deeply divided lower leaves and distinctive fruits with four toothed wings. In Portugal it inhabits floodplain grassland and riverside scrub margins, sometimes occurring in northern fields and fallow ground.

sources.attribution: GBIF Secretariat (2023). GBIF Backbone Taxonomy. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/39omei accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-15.

summary: A flowering plant native to the Mediterranean Basin and introduced elsewhere, including parts of North America. Its hairless, waxy stem passes through the fused bases of deep-green leaves, and it bears rounded clusters of yellow to yellow-green flowers.
Annual flowering plant native to the specified areas of mainland Portugal. It grows in wasteland, low-nitrogen meadows, damp shaded places and cultivated plots.
A moss with no stated native origin, it is widely distributed around the world. In one study, it showed intermediate sensitivity to the herbicide Asulam.

A robust perennial herb native to Mexico, the false bromeliad develops vigorous, bromeliad-like flowering shoots. Its leaves can turn burgundy-violet after prolonged sunlight, and its small fragrant white flowers appear from late winter to spring.

A succulent creeping perennial native from the southeastern United States through the West Indies to Argentina, creeping inchplant forms mats of delicate fleshy leaves that become smaller toward the shoot tips. Its rapid spread has made it invasive in Western Australia.

An annual or biennial flowering plant native to China and Korea. It bears a large solitary flower head, naturally reddish purple in the wild. Cultivated forms offer many colours and single or double flower heads, making it popular as an ornamental and cut flower.

sources.attribution: GBIF Secretariat (2023). GBIF Backbone Taxonomy. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/39omei accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-15.

summary: A plant of unspecified native origin, found in Canada and the eastern United States.

An annual or biennial flowering plant originating in southern Europe. Biennial plants form a leaf rosette in their first year and stems with long-lasting, bell-shaped violet-blue or rarely white flowers in their second; flowering runs from May to July in the Northern Hemisphere.

A biennial herb native to temperate Europe, it bears delicate upright, funnel-shaped flowers that are usually violet-blue but sometimes white. Their pointed petals spread outward, and surrounding vegetation may support the branches so the plant appears prostrate.

A herbaceous perennial native to European mountain ranges, including the Alps, it has narrow glossy foliage and cup-shaped lilac-blue or white flowers. It naturally grows in broad-leaved woods, woodland margins, meadows and rocky places.
Moss with a cosmopolitan distribution.

A fern native to the southeastern United States, Cuba, Costa Rica, Bolivia and Venezuela, long strap fern grows on other plants, generally in tree canopies. It has simple, hairless leaves and many fine rootlets covered with dark reddish-brown scales.

Aquatic perennial herb native to the wetlands of tropical America. Its narrow blue-green leaves are topped by large, delicate, pale-yellow flowers, and it grows at the margins of still or slow-moving water.

A fast-growing climbing plant native to eastern Argentina and Brazil. Its tough stem clings to supports, while its slightly fragrant creamy-white flowers develop into capsules that split into three parts and release hard, black, winged seeds.

A tuft-forming, spreading sedge native to parts of northern and western Europe. It has slender three-angled stems and narrow leaves that tend to droop at their tips, and grows in moist habitats including fen meadows and swamps.
A perennial sedge whose native origin is not stated, it commonly grows in dunes and other sandy habitats. It spreads through long runners beneath the soil surface.
A flowering plant native to mainland Portugal. Its listed varieties occur respectively across temperate parts of the Old World and in the Far East, Korea, and northern and central Japan.
Sedge native to Europe and North Africa. It grows in dense clumps and has widely separated flower spikes; in Europe it often inhabits wetlands, fens and coastal brackish marshes.
A sedge native to Europe, Asia and North Africa, it has become naturalized in Australia, New Zealand and scattered parts of North America.
A flowering sedge native to mainland Portugal, the Azores and Madeira. In Portugal it grows where maritime influence reaches cliff seepages, streams and wetlands.
A clump-forming sedge native to parts of Europe and North Africa. Its arching leaves are blue-green above and pale beneath, while its densely packed female flower spikes may stand upright or nod.
Sedge native across Europe. Its leaves and flowering spikes are characteristically hairy, though plants in wetter places may be less hairy.
A sedge found in Europe and western Asia as far as the Himalayas, and introduced elsewhere. It is poorly studied and treated as an unresolved species aggregate, with a history of taxonomic confusion.

An evergreen perennial sedge native to wetlands of Europe, western Asia, North Africa and eastern North America. It forms tussocks with bluish-green leaves and purplish-black flower spikes and seed heads in summer.
A sedge of unspecified native origin, it occurs in northern and western Europe and northeastern North America. Its leaves are pale blue on both sides, and its fruits are egg-shaped and spiked.

A sedge native to temperate Europe, spiked sedge grows in grassland, roadsides and waste ground, usually on heavy, slightly alkaline soils. Its stems are roughly triangular, while its roots, leaf sheaths and flower bracts contain distinctive purple pigment.

A biennial plant originating from the region between central Europe and Asia. It has delicately divided leaves and clusters of small white to pale-violet flowers. Its cooked roots, tender leaves and fruits are eaten, while the spicy, slightly sweet seeds flavour breads, cheeses, drinks and other foods.
edibilityNote: Cooked roots are eaten as a vegetable; tender leaves, fruits and seeds are used in salads, dishes, baked goods, cheeses and drinks.

summary: Clustering palm native to tropical Asia from India through Java to southern China. Its many leaflets resemble tail fins, while its ripe red or dark-purple fruits are harmful to people. Trunk pith can be processed into a flour resembling sago.
edibilityNote: Trunk pith can be made into sago-like flour, but the fruit contains irritating crystals and is harmful if eaten.

summary: A tree native to Australia and New Guinea, chiefly growing in stands along freshwater rivers and streams. It has fissured, scaly bark, often-drooping branchlets and leaves reduced to tiny scales arranged in whorls.
A flowering tree endemic to eastern Australia. It often produces root suckers, bears scale-like leaves on spreading or drooping branchlets, and grows near brackish rivers and estuaries.

A pod-bearing tree native to temperate provinces of China, Chinese catalpa bears bunches of creamy white flowers distinctly tinged with yellow. Its dark green leaves have three lobes, and its fruits are exceptionally narrow, long pods.

An annual flowering plant native to Europe, North Africa and the Middle East as far east as Iran. Its trailing stems bear finely divided leaves and small white or pink flower clusters, followed by oblong fruits covered in hooked spines.

Tall perennial flowering herb endemic to Macaronesia. It has three-part leaves and flower spikes coloured purple, lilac or pink, and grows in laurel forest and other shady places, generally above 500 metres.

A tropical African herb that may grow as a tender annual or perennial, with tiny flowers packed into vivid, plume-like heads. Its leaves and flowers are edible, especially in West Africa and Southeast Asia; one variety, Lagos spinach, is a major boiled green in West Africa.
edibilityNote: Leaves and flowers are edible; Lagos spinach is an important boiled green in West Africa.

summary: A flowering plant present in Portugal, with no whole-species native origin stated. There, subsp. exilis favours rocky, acidic ground around woodland, scrub, grassland and roadsides, while subsp. geresensis occupies similar acidic mountain habitats. Closely similar subspecies may require examination of seeds and flower heads for identification.

summary: Herbaceous perennial of unspecified native origin, widespread in the mountains of southern and central Europe. Its narrow, undivided leaves accompany flower heads with bright purple inner flowers and azure-blue or deep-mauve outer flowers.

An annual flowering plant native to southern tropical America, mainly growing in seasonally dry tropical areas. Another account describes it as a subshrub and reports that crushed leaves and flowers are used to wash fishing nets and attract fish.
