summary: Spring-blooming annual plant native to Mediterranean and temperate Europe, the Caucasus, Western Asia and northwestern Africa. It has been introduced and naturalised in North America, and the charity Plantlife lists it among 101 high conservation priorities in the UK.
An annual or biennial herb native to Central and western Europe. Its white petals are no longer than the sepals and are shallowly split, and it flowers from March to May.

A low annual herb native to Europe, northern Africa and southwestern Asia, it grows in patches on sandy ground and thin soils over rock. Its dull-green growth quickly yellows with age, and its small white petals are shorter than the papery-edged sepals.
Low, spreading perennial herb native to alpine central and southern Italy. Its densely hairy, silvery-grey foliage forms creeping carpets beneath star-shaped white flowers.

A shrub native to tropical parts of North and South America, orange cestrum bears orange or occasionally yellow flowers throughout the year. The flowers release a citrus-like scent at night, and the fruits are white berries.
An evergreen flowering shrub native to central Mexico. It has sometimes-purple, slightly hairy young twigs and dense clusters of hairy red flowers, followed by red berries with white interiors.
Thorny deciduous or semi-evergreen shrub native to eastern Asia. Its flowers are usually red but may be pink, white or green, and its fragrant, hard fruit resembles a quince.

A subtropical palm native to Belize, Guatemala, Honduras and southeastern Mexico, reed palm grows in moist woodlands and forests, often on limestone outcrops. Commonly kept as a houseplant, it has divided evergreen leaves, yellow flower clusters and small round black fruits.
A plant native to the Irano-Turanian region, it is an ancient introduced weed in Europe and now occurs in temperate crop-growing regions across most of the world.
An annual herb of unstated native origin, grey goosefoot is self-supporting, associated with freshwater habitats and has simple, broad leaves.
A flowering plant with no stated native origin, it is widely cultivated for the bitter-leaved vegetables known as endive and escarole. It is often confused with common chicory.
edibilityNote: Widely cultivated for its bitter leaves as the vegetables endive and escarole.

summary: Evergreen tree native to tropical Southeast Asia. Its aromatic bark is sold as cinnamon, while its leaves can season preserved foods and canned meat.
edibilityNote: The bark is sold as cinnamon, and the leaves are used as a spice for preserved food and canned meat.

summary: A herbaceous biennial, or often perennial, native to Europe. It begins as a dense rosette, then develops a tall, spiny stem topped with branching clusters of usually dark-purple flowers.

A tree native to southern Florida, the Caribbean, Guyana, Suriname and Venezuela, spiny fiddlewood bears small white flowers throughout the year in hanging clusters. Its rounded fruits ripen from red to black, and its leaf stalks are orange.

Flowering sedge native to temperate Europe and Asia, growing in mineral-rich boggy ground and beside lakes. Its hard, serrated leaves can cause deep cuts, though they were historically harvested for thatched roofs.

A deciduous woody climber that develops long, branched stems with sparse hairs. Its solitary, nodding violet bell-shaped flowers and dark brown hairy fruits appear from June to August. It favours acidic woodland habitats, especially pinewoods, scrub and thickets.

A climbing shrub native to Europe and western Asia. Its grooved stems, scented greenish-white flowers and clusters of fruit with long silky appendages create its characteristic old man's beard appearance; in Italy, the sprouts are harvested for omelettes.
edibilityNote: In Italy, the sprouts are harvested for omelettes.

summary: A deciduous shrub native to Taiwan, Vietnam and most of mainland China. It bears rounded clusters of fragrant rose, crimson or pink flowers in late summer, while its crushed leaves smell unpleasant. Its rapid suckering growth can form spreading colonies.
A tropical shrub native to Indonesia and Papuasia. It has square-shaped leaves and large, bright red, heart-shaped flowers and is grown as an ornamental.

Evergreen tropical and subtropical tree native from the Caribbean and Florida through southern Mexico and Central America to northern South America. It begins life on rocks or trees and can overtop and strangle host trees with aerial roots. Its leaves retain scratched writing, while its fleshy light-green fruit is toxic.
edibilityNote: The fleshy, light-green fruit is toxic.

summary: An herbaceous plant native across the Paleotropics, from tropical and southern Africa through southern and eastern Asia to Pacific islands. Usually annual but sometimes perennial in the tropics, it creeps along the ground and roots where its stems touch soil. According to one source, its young leaf tips are cooked and eaten in New Guinea.
edibilityNote: According to one published source, young leaf tips are cooked and eaten in New Guinea.

summary: Flowering plant whose native origin is not given in the supplied information. It is introduced in mainland Portugal.

Annual upright herb grown widely in tropical regions. Its bark provides jute fibre, while its leaves and young fruits are eaten as vegetables, dried leaves make tea or thicken soup, and the seeds are also edible.
edibilityNote: Leaves and young fruits are vegetables, dried leaves are used for tea and thickening soup, and seeds are edible.

summary: An evergreen shrub or small tree native from southern Texas to central Mexico, anacahuita bears white funnel-shaped flowers throughout the year and yellow-green, olive-like fruits. The fresh fruits are sweet but slightly toxic and can cause dizziness; jellies made from them are reportedly safe to eat.
edibilityNote: Fresh fruits are slightly toxic and may cause dizziness, but fruit jellies are reportedly safe to eat.

summary: A flowering plant native to Europe and Africa, strapwort grows along shingly European pool margins with fluctuating water levels and occupies varied habitats in Africa. It has been introduced to Australia and North America.

A grass native to Europe, the Middle East and North Africa, and widely naturalized in North America. It is rare in the United Kingdom and has narrow leaves with small flower clusters bearing shiny, lance-shaped bracts and hairy flower bases.

An evergreen tree endemic to New Zealand, karaka is mainly coastal, though it also grows inland in the North Island. It has thick, leathery green leaves and oval yellow-orange fruit. Māori ate the uncooked fruit flesh and the highly poisonous seeds only after lengthy detoxification.
edibilityNote: Māori ate the fruit flesh uncooked; the highly poisonous seeds required lengthy detoxification before consumption.

summary: An annual native to Latin America and the West Indies, king's salad bears purple, pink or white flower rays. Its soft, pungent leaves fold as night falls. In Indonesia and Malaysia, the leaves are eaten as a traditional raw salad called ulam.
edibilityNote: The leaves are eaten raw as ulam in Indonesian and Malaysian cuisine; in Brunei they were usually served with chilli paste.

summary: An annual flowering herb native to parts of the southwestern United States and most of Mexico, from Chihuahua to Oaxaca. Its deeply divided leaves have narrow segments, and its white, pink or violet flowers may show mixed colours within one population. Barbed fruits lodge in fur or clothing.

Fast-growing evergreen low shrub native to central and southern China. Its creeping branches root where they touch the ground; glossy leaves turn purple in autumn, and bright red berries persist well into winter.
Perennial herb native to Europe and Asia Minor. A single plant can bear numerous small flower heads, each packed with yellow ray flowers and lacking central disc flowers.

A European flowering herb widespread across much of Europe and Siberia, stinking hawksbeard may be annual, biennial or perennial. A plant can bear several flower heads packed with yellow ray florets and no central disc florets.

A medium-sized flowering tree native to the Americas, it bears simple leaves either alternately or in clusters on short shoots. Its large fruit is commonly dried and hollowed to make cups, bowls, water containers and musical instruments.

A herbaceous plant native to South Africa, Lesotho and Eswatini, it grows from large bulbs and thrives in wet places. Its spring and summer flowers are funnel-shaped and sickly-sweet scented, usually pink with a deep pink or red stripe but sometimes white or red.

An erect herb native to southern and central Europe, the Black Sea basin, and southwestern and Central Asia. It is covered with stiff hairs, usually bears four broad leaves at each node, and has tiny pale-yellow flowers.
A thin-stemmed herbaceous vine indigenous to Africa and naturalized widely in the New World. Its oval to oblong fruits have hairs, spines or wart-like bumps and are eaten raw, cooked or pickled.
edibilityNote: The fruit is eaten raw, cooked as a vegetable or pickled; it is also used in Brazilian stew.

summary: An upright herb native to South America, with rough, reddish glandular hairs on its sparsely branched stems. Its simple green leaves grow in opposite pairs and are paler underneath.
Small evergreen shrub native to Mexico, Guatemala and Honduras. It has fine, narrow, dark green leaves and purple, lavender or white flowers.
A hardy annual flowering plant native to Asia, Chinese forget-me-not has hairy leaves and sprays of sky-blue flowers in late summer. It is also grown as an ornamental.

Perennial herb native to North America, the Great Plains flatsedge grows in sunny, open places such as prairies, fields and roadsides. It spreads through underground stems and has triangular stalks topped by densely clustered, roughly spherical spikes.

A tender aquatic perennial native to Africa, papyrus forms tall, reed-like stands in shallow water, flooded swamps and lake margins. Its triangular green stems end in dense, feather-duster clusters of fine green rays, and it was historically used to make papyrus paper and boats. The pith of young shoots was eaten cooked or raw.
edibilityNote: The pith of young shoots was historically eaten both cooked and raw.

summary: A sedge native to eastern Africa, from Somalia to South Africa's Cape Provinces, and to Madagascar and Mauritius. It has been introduced to Florida, where it is considered invasive.

Flowering sedge native primarily to the Southeastern United States, extending from Martha’s Vineyard, Massachusetts, south to Tamaulipas, Mexico. This tufted perennial grows in dry sandy soils, open woodlands and thickets, and has a distinctive cylindrical flower cluster. Its fruits mature in summer.
Long-creeping sedge native to parts of Europe and Asia. It has tubers, a solitary triangular stem and a terminal flowering head with unequal radiating branches bearing many flattened spikelets.
A fern whose native origin is not supplied. Fortune's holly-fern has received the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit.

An upright, spineless shrub from the Mediterranean region, it has young branches tipped with white hairs and leaves divided into three leaflets. Its yellow flowers appear from late winter through spring and sometimes into summer, followed by pods covered in whitish hairs.
A perennial herbaceous plant from Central America, occurring in mountains around Mexico City. It has rhizomes, tuberous roots and upright stems topped with pink to deep-purple flower heads.
edibilityNote: According to one cited account, its roots or tubers were an important crop among pre-Columbian peoples of central Mexico, Yucatán and Guatemala.

summary: An annual grass native to eastern and southern Europe and western Asia, from the Balearic Islands to Turkmenistan. It is almost entirely immune to one form of wheat stem rust, while its Sr52 gene gives some resistance to the Ug99 strain.

Tuberous-rooted subshrub native to the southwestern United States and Central and South America. Soft greyish hairs cover its stems and leaves, while its white trumpet-shaped flowers become downward-inclined and its fruit is a spiny capsule. All parts are toxic and may be fatal if swallowed.
edibilityNote: All parts are toxic and may be fatal if eaten by people or animals.

summary: A herbaceous perennial native to temperate Asia and Europe, it has deeply divided leaves and upright spikes of blue or purple summer flowers. Ornamental cultivars also include pink, cream and white forms.

A deciduous flowering shrub native to Japan, Deutzia scabra grows naturally along forest edges and rocky openings. It bears clusters of white flowers from May to July, with upper leaves clasping the stem and lower leaves growing on stalks.

A herbaceous perennial native to northern China, Korea, Mongolia and southeastern Russia. Its slender green to grey-green leaves remain on the stems while the basal leaves usually wither during flowering. White, pink or red flowers appear alone or in small clusters from spring to midsummer, often with darker centres and serrated edges.
A moss with a cosmopolitan distribution.

A fast-growing creeping flowering plant distributed disjunctly from the southern United States through Mexico and parts of South America, with extinction reported in Arizona. It has dark green, kidney- or ear-shaped leaves, tiny whitish flowers and hairy capsules with dark seeds.

A perennial creeping herb native to Australia, New Zealand, Mauritius, Réunion and Rodrigues. It roots at the nodes and has soft, greyish-haired, kidney-shaped to round leaves with small, pale greenish-yellow, star-shaped flowers. It is cultivated as an ornamental groundcover or lawn substitute.

A moss found across Europe, parts of Asia, and from North America to northwestern South America. Its bright green to yellow-green mats are especially recognizable in late summer and autumn, when they are strewn with needle-like yellowish shoots; spore capsules are very rare.

Moss occurring in parts of Europe, Asia and North America, with its European range centred on mountainous Central Europe. It forms loose to moderately dense dark-green or yellow-brown carpets and has brittle, weakly sickle-shaped leaves; spore capsules are produced only very rarely.
A moss native to the Northern Hemisphere, including Japan.

A large perennial fern found throughout Asia and Oceania, it has an upright rhizome covered in short reddish-brown scales. Its long brownish leaf stalks have black, scaly bases. Young fronds are stir-fried or used in salads; they may contain mild fern toxins, though no major toxic effects are recorded.
edibilityNote: Young fronds are stir-fried or used in salads; they may contain mild fern toxins, but no major toxic effects are recorded.

summary: A liverwort native to Brazil, Dumortiera hirsuta is the sole species in its genus.

A flowering shrub native from Mexico and the Caribbean south to South America. It bears clusters of blue or lavender flowers followed by yellow or orange berries, while mature plants often develop thorns. Its leaves and unripe berries are toxic, although documented human cases are sparse.
edibilityNote: Leaves and unripe berries are toxic; human reports are sparse, including one historical presumed fatal berry poisoning.

summary: Flowering plant endemic to Brazil, also known as sawblade. It has a cultivar called ‘Yellow Glow’ and is a parent of several hybrid cultivars.

A herbaceous perennial native to southern Europe, northwestern Africa and southwestern Asia. It has rough, bristly leaves and hairy fruit resembling tiny cucumbers. When ripe, the fruit detaches and forcefully squirts seed-bearing liquid.
edibilityNote: The fruit-juice extract is poisonous when taken by mouth or nose; it was historically used medicinally as a powerful purgative.

summary: Perennial herb native to North America, especially the Great Plains of central Canada and the central United States. Its stems and leaves are hairy, and each long flower stalk ends in a head of pink or purple outer florets surrounding numerous orange florets.

Perennial cactus native to the Chihuahuan Desert and parts of northern Mexico and the southern United States. Young plants are spherical but become cylindrical, growing alone or in clusters with stems largely hidden by dense, variously coloured spines. Its pink or purple flowers each open for only one day, though staggered blooming can continue for a week.

A solitary cactus native to Chihuahua and Sonora in Mexico and Arizona and New Mexico in the United States, it rarely branches or forms offsets. Its new spines are reddish to magenta before fading to yellow or light pink, and its bright-pink flowers have white throats.

A branching perennial herb native to central and eastern Europe, from Germany and Italy east into Russia. It is described as the largest globe thistle and produces nearly spherical flower heads of white or pale blue florets.
A compact, bushy perennial thistle native to southern and eastern Europe and western and central Asia. It has broad prickly leaves and globes of steel-blue flowers in late summer.

An upright biennial found across the western Mediterranean; the supplied source does not explicitly describe this range as native. Its stems and leaves carry stiff bristles, while its funnel-shaped flowers may be reddish-purple, bluish-purple or change from pinkish-red to blue.

sources.title: Echium creticum L.
sources.attribution: Döring M (2022). German Wikipedia - Species Pages. Wikimedia Foundation. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/4wn9dt accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-15.

summary: Deciduous or semi-evergreen shrub or small tree native to China, Korea, Japan and Sakhalin in the Russian Far East. Its leaves are green above and silvery to orange-brown beneath. The juicy fruit is edible when ripe in mid- to late summer, with a sweet but astringent, rhubarb-like taste.
edibilityNote: Ripe fruit is eaten in mid- to late summer; it is juicy, sweet but astringent, and has fragile skin.

summary: A dense evergreen shrub native to Asia, including China and Japan, thorny olive has thorn-covered stems and leaves with silvery-white, brown-flecked undersides. Its sweet-scented yellowish or white flowers bloom in autumn, followed by reddish, silver-scaled fruit in spring.
A flowering plant native from the temperate and subtropical Old World to western Malesia, it is introduced in New England, where it occurs mainly around rivers.
A plant native from Europe through the Russian Far East and Nepal, and from subarctic America south to the northern United States.

Orchid with no explicitly stated native origin; it occurs from Florida and the Caribbean through Central America to northern Brazil and the Guyanas. Its flowers usually self-pollinate, sometimes before opening.

A flowering plant found across Britain, Ireland, most of Europe, and central and eastern Asia, while introduced elsewhere. It has mostly opposite, toothed leaves and pale mauve flowers, and commonly grows on disturbed or base-rich ground, in hedges and as a garden weed.
A flowering plant native to mainland Portugal, the Azores and Madeira. It grows in very wet places on siliceous ground, including stream margins, seepage slopes and rocks, and waterlogged meadows.

An evergreen horsetail whose native origin is not specified in the supplied information; its named varieties range across much of Europe, Asia and Africa, with one extending to Indonesia and Papua New Guinea. It can form colonies from underground roots and has untidy lower branches, sometimes with a blue-grey tinge.

A grass native to the Old World tropics, Eragrostis ciliaris has also been introduced across tropical and subtropical parts of the Americas and some Pacific islands. Its small, nutritious seeds are edible but difficult to harvest and handle, so they are usually regarded as famine food.
edibilityNote: The small, nutritious seeds are edible but difficult to harvest and handle, and are usually regarded as famine food.

summary: A strongly branched evergreen shrub native to the Himalayas, western China, India and Nepal. Its vivid gentian-blue flowers emerge from green-and-white veined bracts that remain after flowering, and its large dark-green leaves are hairy.

A warm-season lawn grass native to southern China, centipede grass forms thick sod and spreads by creeping stems. Its coarse, light-to-medium green growth tolerates some shade but has shallow roots and poor drought tolerance.
A perennial subshrub native to western Europe, cross-leaved heath has glandular leaves arranged in groups of four. Small pink, bell-shaped flowers droop in compact clusters during summer and autumn.
A flowering plant native to mainland Portugal.

Perennial herb native to the eastern Mediterranean. It forms clumps of spiny, leathery leaves and bears cylindrical summer flower clusters above silvery-blue bracts and branching light-blue to purple stems.

A hairless, spiny perennial with two natural varieties ranging across parts of Europe, North Africa and western Asia. It bears small greenish flower heads surrounded by large spine-like bracts. Its roots were formerly candied as sweets or boiled and roasted as a vegetable, while the plant has long featured in local dishes in Iran’s Mazandaran Province.
edibilityNote: Roots were formerly candied, boiled or roasted; the plant has been used in Mazandaran dishes for centuries.

summary: A coastal perennial flowering plant native to most of Europe and the Mediterranean, sea holly has bluish-grey, stiff, spiny leaves and compact flower heads resembling a thistle. Its roots were formerly candied as sweetmeat, while young shoots may be eaten like asparagus.
edibilityNote: Roots were formerly candied as sweetmeat, and young shoots may be eaten like asparagus.

summary: A herbaceous perennial native to central and southeastern Europe and Central Asia, blue eryngo has branched silvery-blue stems. Numerous small blue, cone-shaped flower heads surrounded by spiky bracts appear in summer.

Flowering tree native to Argentina, Uruguay, Bolivia, southern Brazil and Paraguay. It has irregular, spiny branches and bright red flowers, and grows wild along watercourses and in swamps and wetlands.

A bulbous perennial native to central and southern Europe, from Portugal to Ukraine. It has paired marbled leaves and solitary pink or lilac flowers, rarely white, whose petals bend backwards. The white bulb resembles a dog’s tooth.
edibilityNote: Leaves may be eaten raw in salads or boiled as a vegetable; starch from the bulb is used to make vermicelli.

summary: A spreading flowering shrub native to southern Chile and neighboring Argentina, redclaws has glossy, serrated evergreen leaves and bark that changes from red to gray as it ages. Its pink to crimson trumpet-shaped flowers bloom from July to October in the Northern Hemisphere.

A tree native to southeastern Australia, bangalay has rough bark on its trunk and branches and bears white flowers in summer and autumn. After bushfire, it can resprout from buds beneath its bark or from its swollen woody base.
A small to medium-sized tree native only to south-eastern Australia. It has rough, fibrous bark, often retains rounded blue-grey juvenile leaves, and produces white flowers in groups of three.

A tree, sometimes growing as a multi-stemmed mallee, endemic to southwestern Western Australia. It has rough fibrous trunk bark, elongated horn-tipped flower buds and exceptionally hard, strong timber.

A small to medium-sized tree endemic to eastern Australia, it has thick, deeply furrowed grey-black ironbark extending from its trunk to small branches. Its white flowers are rich in nectar, while its hard, dark-red timber is used in construction.

Large tree native to southwestern Western Australia, mainly along a narrow coastal corridor. It has rough, box-like bark, glossy leaves and white to cream flowers, with major flowering events every five to eight years.
edibilityNote: The flowers are used to produce honey, historically regarded as high quality but an unreliable source.

summary: A tree endemic to New South Wales, grey ironbark has dark, deeply furrowed bark on its trunk and branches. Its glossy curved leaves accompany clusters of mostly seven buds, white flowers and woody cup-shaped to conical fruit.
Tree native to eastern Australia. It grows in swampy or waterlogged ground and has thick, spongy reddish-brown bark, a dense canopy and white to cream flowers in autumn and winter.

A medium-sized to tall tree endemic to eastern Australia, the Sydney blue gum has rough, flaky bark near the trunk’s base and smooth bark above. Its white flowers grow from buds grouped in sevens, nines or elevens, followed by woody cylindrical, conical or cup-shaped fruit.

A moss of the sub-Mediterranean flora, lime-seep eucladium occurs mainly in southern and western Europe, with populations on several other continents. It forms dense olive, pale or bluish-green mats often crusted with lime and favors wet, lime-rich rocks and seepages.
A compact, clump-forming deciduous perennial native to Libya, Turkey, and eastern, middle and southeastern Europe. It bears acid-yellow flower heads at branch tips in spring and summer.

Herbaceous perennial native to central and southern Europe and much of temperate Asia. It has yellow-green flower bracts, explosively opening seed capsules and an extensive root system. All parts contain toxic white milky sap.

A flowering plant whose two named subspecies are native to mainland Portugal; subsp. exigua is also native to Madeira but introduced in the Azores. Both occur in annual grasslands, fallow ground, roadsides and wasteland, often on poor, somewhat disturbed soils. Subsp. exigua has tubercled seeds, while subsp. merinoi has transverse grooves and some tubercles.
A spurge native to most of Europe, northern Africa and Asia, it has two recognised subspecies. One is restricted to Cyprus and western Turkey, while the other occurs throughout the species’ range.
Spurge-family plant native to Mexico, Central America, the Caribbean, much of Andean South America, Suriname and French Guiana.

A woody succulent shrub native to Madagascar. It has densely spiny stems and fleshy leaves concentrated on new growth, though its form varies among cultivars. Small flowers framed by conspicuous red, pink or white bracts may appear throughout the year.
edibilityNote: Its moderately poisonous sap causes severe stomach pain, mouth and throat irritation, and vomiting if ingested.

summary: An annual herb whose native origin is not stated in the supplied information. It is self-supporting with simple broad leaves, and its flowers are visited by Plagiolepis pygmaea, Polistes and nomad bees.

A perennial herb native to Europe, serrated spurge has mostly long, narrow leaves, with more oval leaves near the stem tips. Its leaves are finely toothed, and its spherical fruits contain tiny grey seeds.

A shrub or small tree native to Africa, especially widespread in its northeastern, central and southern regions. Its smooth, succulent green branches resemble pencils, and its milky sap is toxic and corrosive, causing severe irritation and potentially temporary blindness.
edibilityNote: The milky latex is toxic; ingestion can burn the mouth, lips and tongue.

summary: A small evergreen shrub native to southern Africa, it is compact, densely branched and leafy. It grows in varied settings including forest edges, riverine bush, ravines, coastal scrub and grassland.

A deciduous shrub of unstated native origin, pearl bush is found mostly in China and Japan. It has a loose, upright form and clusters of round-petalled white flowers in late April to early May, followed by brown seed capsules.

A large evergreen fig tree native to southeastern Asia and many Pacific islands. It often begins life on another tree, sending roots to the ground and eventually overwhelming its host. Pollinated flowers develop inside orange-red, many-seeded figs.

A woody evergreen climber native to East Asia, including southern China, southern Japan, southern Korea and Vietnam. Its juvenile leaves are much smaller and thinner than its mature foliage, and it creeps over ground or climbs trees and walls.
edibilityNote: Fruit of var. awkeotsang is inverted and dried; seed-surface gel is extracted with water and set as aiyu or ice jelly.

summary: A North American moss also widespread through Northern Hemisphere forests, maidenhair pocketmoss forms robust dark green to brown-green mats. Its wavy, finely toothed leaves tend to curl downward at their tips when dry.

A moss of unstated native origin with a broad global distribution. It forms green mats chiefly on shaded, lime-rich rocks and soils, and has leaves with coarse teeth and a pale border of thick-walled cells.
A terrestrial moss with a cosmopolitan distribution. It has been recorded rarely at La Bouzaréah and Aït Idjer in Algeria.

sources.title: Fissidens exilis Hedw.
sources.attribution: GBIF Secretariat (2023). GBIF Backbone Taxonomy. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/39omei accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-15.

summary: A moss with no native origin stated in the supplied information. It is the largest member of its family and grows in turbulent water; its fronds were likened to phoenix feathers in China.

A moss with a nearly worldwide distribution, especially common in the Northern Hemisphere, though it is introduced in New Zealand. It forms dense green tufts with flattened leaves in two rows, resembling tiny fern fronds, and usually grows on soil or soil-covered rocks in wet, shaded places.

A deciduous flowering shrub native to China, golden-bell produces golden-yellow flowers in early spring. Its weeping form can grow along stream banks, and it also occurs naturally in thickets and grassy areas on slopes and in valleys.
Liverwort native to Europe and America.
A tree native to eastern and northeastern Mexico and the south-central United States, it produces male and female flowers on separate trees.
A liverwort with a cosmopolitan distribution. In Europe it occurs on rocks and tree trunks, especially beech, while Algerian records describe it as rare.

sources.title: Frullania tamarisci (L.) Dumort.
sources.attribution: GBIF Secretariat (2023). GBIF Backbone Taxonomy. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/39omei accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-15.

summary: A flowering sub-shrub native to the lower Southern Cone of South America. Its long arching stems bear many small, hanging tubular flowers over a long period, commonly in vivid red and purple. It is relatively cold-hardy, becoming deciduous in light frost and dying back above ground in harder frost.
A tall shrub or small tree native to Central America, it usually has smooth, upright branches. Its nearly round fruit is bluish-purple with a whitish waxy coating.

A flowering subshrub native to the Caribbean and northern South America, it is generally stemless and bears sword-shaped leaves ending in sharp tips. Its strongly scented, greenish to creamy-white flowers grow on a very tall stalk, after which the flowering section dies back and usually leaves young plants around its base.

An annual flowering herb native only to Texas in the south-central United States. It grows in sunny, sandy places and bears red or purple rays, rarely yellow, around yellow disc flowers with purple tips.

An annual herb native to much of Europe, white bedstraw has mostly upright, slightly ridged square stems and shiny, nearly hairless leaves. Its flowers are white or yellowish, and its fruits are hairless.
Plant native to Europe from Portugal to Ukraine. Known as waxy bedstraw, it is only sparingly naturalized in a few locations in Quebec, Ontario, Connecticut and New Jersey.

A herbaceous annual native to virtually all of Europe and parts of North Africa, Asia, Greenland and eastern North America. In Britain it grows on poorly drained neutral or acidic soils, while several northeastern US states classify it as a noxious weed.
An annual grass native to Europe, North Africa and southwestern Asia, nit grass bears a long, thin, smooth flower head of spikelets. It has become naturalized in scattered locations elsewhere.

Evergreen flowering shrub native to La Palma and Tenerife in the Canary Islands. Its narrow leaves have fine, silky silver hairs, and its strongly scented yellow flowers appear in late winter or early spring.

A deciduous shrub native to meadows and pastures in Europe and Turkey, dyer’s greenweed bears golden-yellow, pea-like flowers and shiny bean-shaped pods. Since ancient times it has been used to produce yellow dye, or green when combined with woad.
Herbaceous perennial of unstated native origin, it is found mainly in the eastern United States. Its clustered autumn flowers are white with distinctive purple stripes, and its seeds are wingless.
A herbaceous perennial native to Texas and Mexico, it behaves as an annual in temperate climates. It has a tuberous root and red, strawberry-like flower heads.

An erect shrub or slender tree endemic to Queensland, with divided leaves bearing narrow lobes. Its clustered flowers range from creamy white to bright scarlet or crimson, while its flowers and seed pods contain toxic hydrogen cyanide.
edibilityNote: Flowers and seed pods contain toxic hydrogen cyanide.

summary: A moss with no explicitly documented native origin. It forms loose yellow-green to dark-green mats that shimmer grey from their hair points. Its leaves lie loosely against the stem and twist when dry, but spread outward when wet; it fruits quite rarely.

An annual herb native to Ethiopia, Eritrea and Malawi, Niger has yellow flower heads and small black seeds resembling sunflower seeds. The seeds are eaten in southern India in chutney or curries, and their clear, nutty oil can be used directly for cooking.
edibilityNote: Seeds are eaten in southern India in chutney or curries; their oil is edible and may be used directly for cooking.

summary: A moss with a cosmopolitan distribution. It is recorded as common across numerous Algerian localities, including Tlemcen, Constantine, the Djurdjura region and El-Kala National Park.

sources.title: Gymnostomum calcareum Nees & Hornsch.
sources.attribution: Ros R M, Olaf S R, Eloy O W, Cerón E, plazi (2024). Revisiting the Bryophyte Checklist of Algeria: Exploring Diversity and Distribution. Cryptogamie, Bryologie. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/6xu7ry accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-15.

summary: An evergreen flowering perennial native to Southeast Asia, purple passion plant is widely grown as a houseplant. Its dark-green leaves, stems and flower bracts are covered in soft purple hairs, giving it a velvety appearance, while its yellow, orange or red flowers have a strong smell.

A mat-forming herbaceous perennial native to the mountains of central and southern Europe, where it grows on dry, chalky slopes. Through much of summer it bears masses of star-shaped white, lilac or light-purple flowers.

A flowering tree native to southern Mexico and introduced to the Caribbean, northern Central America and elsewhere. Its wood was extensively exported to Europe for fabric dyeing from the 17th through 19th centuries and remains a source of haematoxylin stain.
A bromeliad native to southern Texas, Mexico and Guatemala.

An evergreen climbing plant native to the Middle East, Persian ivy clings to trees, cliffs and walls with aerial rootlets. Its five-lobed juvenile leaves give way to unlobed adult leaves, and it has the largest leaves of any ivy.

An evergreen climber native to Europe’s Atlantic coast, it clings to trees, cliffs and walls with aerial rootlets or spreads as ground cover. The whole plant, including its blue-black berries, is slightly poisonous.
edibilityNote: The whole plant and its berries are slightly poisonous.

summary: A moss with a cosmopolitan distribution. It has been recorded rarely at several Algerian localities, including the Djurdjura region, Blida Atlas and Akfadou.

sources.title: Hedwigia ciliata (Hedw.) P. Beauv.
sources.attribution: Ros R M, Olaf S R, Eloy O W, Cerón E, plazi (2024). Revisiting the Bryophyte Checklist of Algeria: Exploring Diversity and Distribution. Cryptogamie, Bryologie. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/6xu7ry accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-15.

summary: An annual flowering plant native to mainland Portugal and distributed around the Mediterranean. It grows in dry grasslands on siliceous, limestone or sometimes sandy ground. Its upper leaves are lance-shaped, while its small petals may be no longer than the sepals or entirely absent.

sources.title: Helianthemum salicifolium (L.) Mill.
sources.attribution: GBIF Secretariat (2023). GBIF Backbone Taxonomy. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/39omei accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-15.

summary: An annual herb endemic to Texas, the Texas sunflower grows mainly in sandy coastal prairies along the Gulf Coast and in the Río Grande Valley. It usually carries one to three flower heads with yellow outer florets surrounding red or purple centres.
A flowering plant of unstated native origin, introduced in mainland Portugal and Madeira. In Portugal it occurs in gardens and has escaped onto coastal cliffs, dunes and woodland clearings.
An erect herb native to northern South America and the West Indies. Its upward-facing flowers collect rainwater for birds and insects, and bats and hummingbirds typically pollinate it.

An herbaceous perennial native to southern Mexico, Central America and northern South America, and naturalized in Florida and Jamaica. Its banana-like leaves accompany an upright flower cluster with red or orange bracts surrounding green, yellow or orange flowers.
An annual flowering plant native to mainland Portugal. It grows in dry watercourse beds on somewhat moist sandy soils, which may be slightly salty or nutrient-enriched.

sources.title: Heliotropium supinum L.
sources.attribution: GBIF Secretariat (2023). GBIF Backbone Taxonomy. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/39omei accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-15.

summary: A semi-evergreen flowering perennial native to central and western Europe, including southern England. It bears green flowers in spring. All parts are poisonous; eating any part can cause severe vomiting and seizures.
edibilityNote: All parts are poisonous; consumption can cause severe vomiting and seizures.

summary: A clump-forming daylily found in China, northeastern Italy and Slovenia, yellow daylily bears sweetly scented, lemon-yellow flowers. Its flowers are edible and are used in Chinese and Japanese cuisine.
edibilityNote: The flowers are edible and used in Chinese and Japanese cuisine.

summary: Roughly hairy perennial herb native to most of Europe, western Asia and northern Africa. Its sap may cause burns or rashes in sensitive people when contaminated skin meets sunlight. Pickled stems, leaves and flower clusters were historically used in an early form of borscht; young shoots are foraged and dried seeds used as a spice.
edibilityNote: Historically, pickled stems, leaves and flower clusters made an early borscht; young shoots are foraged, and dried seeds are used as a spice.

summary: A flowering plant whose recorded varieties glaberrima and setulosa are native to mainland Portugal. Both occur in sparse plant communities in paving cracks, along paths and in disturbed places, on clay-rich or stony soils.

A flowering plant with no stated native origin, it is found in North America. It is believed extinct in Connecticut and is listed as endangered in Illinois and Ohio. The Cherokee apply a hot root poultice to inflamed wounds and sores.
A semi-deciduous shrub or small tree native to southern China. Its single or double flowers open white or pink and deepen to red by evening, while its stems and leaf stalks are densely hairy.

A flowering plant native to most of Europe, common hawkweed has pale yellow flowers throughout summer. Its flower heads lack central florets, while the stalks below them bear scattered black hairs and contain a milky substance.

A hawkweed native to Europe, it has become naturalized in parts of North America and is considered a noxious weed in Washington state. It grows in fields, roadsides and forests, usually in well-drained soil.
A bulbous perennial native to tropical South America, though naturalized elsewhere. Its orange-red flowers appear before the bright green, strap-shaped leaves are fully developed.

An evergreen, sprawling shrub from the Himalayas through India and Nepal to Myanmar. Its red to orange-red flowers have broad, saucer-like calyces and long curved floral tubes; some varieties flower yellow or bronze.

A hardy deciduous tree found across Asia from eastern China and Korea to the Himalayas. It has glossy pointed leaves and clusters of small cream flowers. Its sweet, fragrant fleshy fruit stalk is edible raw or cooked and resembles raisins when dried.
edibilityNote: The fleshy fruit stalk is eaten raw or cooked; when dried, it looks and tastes like raisins.

summary: Aquatic plant native to South America, Central America, Puerto Rico, Trinidad and the Netherlands Antilles. Known as water poppy, it is grown in decorative ponds and has naturalized in several warmer regions worldwide.

Hairless creeping perennial native to parts of tropical Africa, the western Indian Ocean, the southeastern and south-central United States, Central America, the Caribbean and South America. It roots where its stems touch the ground and bears numerous white to creamy-yellow flowers.
A moss with a cosmopolitan distribution. It can grow under artificial light in places without natural light, including Niagara Cave.
An aquatic flowering plant native to Bangladesh, India, China and Malaysia. Popular in tropical aquariums, it grows and reproduces rapidly, and leaves near strong light may turn pink or orange.
A herbaceous perennial native to China and Korea. It has upright succulent stems, frosted-blue leaves, and flat clusters of star-shaped pink flowers from summer until the first frost.

A small, fragile perennial fern most frequent in western Europe’s oceanic regions, especially the British Isles. Its translucent leaves are only a single cell thick, and creeping underground stems produce dense colonies of overlapping leaves.

A plant native to Southern Europe, North Africa, West Asia and Macaronesia, white henbane is sticky and covered in woolly, glandular hairs. Its mostly yellowish-white flowers have green or purple throats, and the plant is described as slightly poisonous.

Black henbane is a poisonous plant native to temperate Europe and Siberia. Its foliage and seeds contain psychoactive chemicals, and ingestion can cause hallucinations, delirium, coma or death; historically, it was used to flavour beer before hops replaced it between the 11th and 16th centuries.
edibilityNote: Historically, henbane was used to flavour beer, but it fell from use when hops replaced it between the 11th and 16th centuries.

sources.title: Lista Vermelha da Flora Vascular de Portugal Continental — Hyoscyamus niger
sources.attribution: Andre Carapeto % Ana Francisco, Paulo Pereira, Miguel Porto, felipe (2020). Lista Vermelha da Flora Vascular de Portugal Continental. Plazi.org taxonomic treatments database. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/ge693f accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-12.

summary: An annual flowering plant native to mainland Portugal. Most current Portuguese records come from sparse grasslands on sandy river beaches or flood deposits of the Tagus and Douro, though it is also reported from field grasslands and roadsides, preferably on basic soils.

A flowering plant with no native origin stated, claspingleaf St. John’s wort occurs from Florida to New York and in Guatemala. It favors wet habitats and has yellow, five-petalled flowers, with upper leaves much larger than lower ones.

A low-growing perennial flowering plant found in Western Europe. Its thin trailing stems carry pale green leaves with tiny translucent glands and black-edged dots, while its yellow flowers often have a few black spots.

Perennial flowering herb native to Europe and Western Asia, where it grows in moist meadows. Its square stems bear opposite leaves with few or no translucent glands, while black dots may mark the leaves, petals and sepals. The flowers are yellow.

A widespread moss found on every continent except Antarctica, growing on trunks, logs, walls and rocks. Its creeping stems form dense mats of overlapping, curved leaves resembling miniature cypress branches.

Moss of unspecified native origin, widely distributed in Europe and the Aleutian Islands and also found elsewhere. It showed intermediate sensitivity to the herbicide Asulam in a study of moss growth.

An evergreen shrub native to South Africa, Madagascar and Southeast Asia, it forms compact growth with green leaves heavily spotted in pink or white, as if sprayed with paint. The spots may merge into larger colored areas, and cultivated forms range from white through pink to red.

A shrub native to Southern Europe, the Middle East and the region around the Caspian Sea. It has upright branches with dark-green leaves and fragrant summer flowers that may be pink, blue or, more rarely, white.
edibilityNote: According to Chaeremon, Egyptian priests ate hyssop with bread for ritual purification; its essential oil can cause seizures, even at low doses in children.

summary: An annual flowering plant native to Belgium, France, Germany, Great Britain, Italy, Spain and Switzerland. It has four prominently unequal petals; wild plants have white or pale violet flowers, while cultivated varieties may be deeper pink, violet or fuchsia.

A flowering evergreen subshrub native to southern Europe. It forms spreading mounds of glossy foliage and fragrant white flower clusters in spring and early summer, often cascading over rocks and walls.

Holly-family shrub native to coastal areas of the United States from Virginia to Texas. It grows mainly beneath pine forests and in moist or wet sandy habitats, resprouts from underground stems after controlled burning, and provides important nectar for beekeepers.

A slow-growing evergreen shrub native to eastern China and Korea. Its glossy rectangular leaves usually have four or five marginal spines, while dull white spring flowers are followed by large red berries ripening in early autumn.

Perennial grass native to tropical and subtropical Asia, Micronesia, Melanesia, Australia, Africa and southern Europe, cogon grass forms dense stands linked by extensive underground stems. Its sharp-pointed, finely toothed leaves have an off-centre pale main vein, and it is highly flammable even when apparently green.
edibilityNote: Young flower clusters and shoots may be eaten cooked; the roots contain starch and sugars.

summary: A flowering plant endemic to coastal Portugal from Nazaré to Sagres, violet cress mainly inhabits wet sand in clearings among junipers, pine forests and dry scrub.

A flowering bush of unspecified native origin, it has rich green, heart-shaped leaves. Its hollow stems were historically used in Brazil to make tobacco-pipe tubes, while its seeds and leaves are toxic when eaten.
edibilityNote: Seeds and leaves are toxic when eaten.

summary: A twining or trailing perennial climber probably originating in tropical Africa and now cultivated throughout the tropics. It has heart-based leaves and pale-yellow, funnel-shaped flowers with purple inside the base; its slender stems are hairy.

summary: A flowering perennial native to Japan, China, Korea and Russia, Japanese iris is widely grown as an ornamental. It has strap-shaped leaves and purple midsummer flowers with a flash of yellow.

A rhizomatous perennial native to Asia Minor, this iris forms large clumps and has white flowers marked with a prominent egg-yolk-yellow area. It is widely cultivated as an ornamental and has naturalized in several countries.
edibilityNote: Most parts, particularly the rhizomes and leaves, are poisonous if eaten and may cause stomach pain and vomiting.

summary: A hardy flowering perennial native to Croatia's Dalmatian coast, sweet iris grows from a rhizome and bears bluish-green sword-shaped leaves with pale purple to whitish flowers. Oil extracted from its rhizome, called orris root, is used to flavor foods, drinks and gin as well as perfumes.
edibilityNote: Orris oil extracted from the rhizome is used to flavor foods, drinks and gin.

summary: A rhizomatous flowering plant native to temperate eastern Asia, it has grey-green leaves, unbranched stems and early-summer flowers ranging from blue to red-violet, with rare white forms. Most parts, including the rhizome and leaves, are poisonous if eaten and may cause stomach pain and vomiting.
edibilityNote: Most parts, particularly the rhizome and leaves, are poisonous if eaten and can cause stomach pain and vomiting.

summary: A bulbous iris native to Spain and Portugal. It bears blue, violet, white or yellow flowers, typically but not always in May and June, while its grey-green leaves emerge in autumn and die after flowering. Florists value its striking colour combinations.

Evergreen flowering shrub native to Vietnam and southern China. It has fragrant yellow flowers from spring into summer, potentially year-round in warmer climates, and a scrambling habit that can be trained as a slender climber.
Shrub native to India, Nepal, Bhutan, Laos, Burma, Thailand and Vietnam. Unlike many jasmines, its attractive white flowers have no scent and are used in worship in Manipur.

A slender deciduous shrub native to China, winter jasmine has arching green shoots and a trailing, vine-like form. In the Northern Hemisphere, its bright yellow or white flowers appear from November to March, often on bare stems.
A deciduous flowering climber native to parts of Asia, though its exact country of origin is uncertain. It bears clusters of star-shaped white summer flowers with an intense fragrance.
edibilityNote: Jasmine is recognized as safe as a food ingredient by the US Food and Drug Administration.

summary: Flowering shrub or small tree native to Cuba and Hispaniola. It has a swollen trunk and three-lobed leaves whose middle lobe is much larger than the others. Male and female flowers occur separately.
A garden plant native to Mexico and the Caribbean, coralbush has been introduced across several tropical and subtropical regions. It is mildly toxic, and consumption causes gastrointestinal distress.
edibilityNote: Consumption is mildly toxic and causes gastrointestinal distress.

summary: Flowering rush native to temperate Eurasia. It has flat or slightly grooved leaves and brown seed capsules, and often grows in limestone-rich wetlands or disturbed places such as ditches, roadsides and canal banks.

Perennial flowering rush native to Europe, Asia and Africa. It forms tufts of stiff, blue-grey, wiry, ridged stems with shiny reddish-black basal sheaths, and bears loose clusters of tiny reddish-brown flowers from late spring to midsummer.
A coastal rush distributed across Europe, western Asia and the Maghreb; its native origin is not stated. Ancient Egyptians reportedly cut and chewed its fibres into chisel-shaped writing brushes.

A rush native from the Mediterranean region across temperate Europe, though not far into Scandinavia, it has been introduced to New Zealand and North America. It is particularly common on disturbed ridges in a human-created Western European fen-meadow habitat.

An evergreen succulent native to Madagascar, flaming Katy grows naturally in humus soil on the relatively cool Tsarantanana plateaus. It has glossy, scallop-edged leaves and produces red, pink, orange, gold or white flowers from late autumn into early winter; parts are poisonous if swallowed.
edibilityNote: Unspecified parts are poisonous if ingested.

summary: A succulent native to southwestern Madagascar, the alligator plant produces new plantlets along its leaf margins. Its fleshy leaves are green above and purple-blotched underneath, and all parts contain a very toxic steroid.
edibilityNote: All parts contain daigremontianin, described as a very toxic steroid.

summary: A succulent native to Madagascar, mother of millions produces numerous plantlets along the tips of its narrow, spotted leaves. It can become invasive and contains cardiac glycosides associated with fatal poisoning in grazing animals.

A frost-tender perennial succulent native to Madagascar. It has fleshy blue-green leaves with scalloped edges that may turn pink or red in strong sunlight or drought. Its lax stems often root where they touch the ground, producing new plants.

Succulent perennial native to parts of central and East Africa. Its fleshy leaves have irregular purple or brown blotches, creating a marbled appearance, while upright clusters of white, four-petalled, star-shaped flowers appear from late winter to spring.
edibilityNote: It may be toxic if ingested, but species-specific data are limited and cited adverse effects concern livestock and pets.

summary: Succulent native to Madagascar and naturalized across many tropical and subtropical regions. Miniature plantlets develop along its fleshy leaf margins, while its hanging flowers are red-orange.
edibilityNote: Contains cardiac glycosides that can cause cardiac poisoning, particularly in grazing animals.

summary: A deciduous tree whose two subspecies are endemic respectively to Fiji and Taiwan. It flowers in autumn with butter-yellow, red-based petals, followed by inflated capsules that change from red or green to brown before splitting open.

An annual herb native to northeastern Mexico and the southeastern and south-central United States, it generally produces one flower head per stalk. Each head has 12–35 yellow ray flowers and no central disc flowers.
A vigorous annual climber native to Africa and India, with large, softly hairy leaves and tendrils that help it climb. Its fruits are used to make bowls and other gourd vessels.

A fast-growing trailing flowering plant endemic to South Africa’s Western Cape, red brightfig has small fleshy leaves and glossy bright-red flowers that open only on sunny days. It blooms in spring, and only five small subpopulations are reported to remain.
A perennial woody shrub in the verbena family.

Perennial tropical shrub with no native origin identified in the source; it is common in Central and South America, the Caribbean and Hawaii, and also occurs in Africa and Madagascar. It usually bears three leaves at each node, with orange glands beneath, dense cylindrical flower spikes and juicy lilac-to-purple ripe fruit.

A perennial legume native to Europe and parts of Asia, growing in broad-leaved woods, clearings and woodland margins. Its leaves have paired leaflets but no tendrils, its red flowers turn bluer with age, and the foliage blackens as it withers.
edibilityNote: The source warns that its seeds are toxic and should not be confused with edible black peas of Pisum sativum.

summary: A cultivated legume with no undisputed native origin supplied, grass pea is grown for food and livestock feed in Asia and East Africa. It yields reliably in drought- and famine-prone areas. Its seeds contain a neurotoxin: immature seeds may be eaten like peas, but mature seeds need soaking and thorough cooking, and prolonged heavy reliance can cause lathyrism.
edibilityNote: Immature seeds are eaten like peas; mature seeds require soaking and thorough cooking. Leaves and stems are cooked in parts of Odisha.

summary: A perennial hawkbit native to Europe and introduced across North America. In a recent British study, it produced the most nectar among examined non-weed perennials, nearly twice that of the leading non-weed annual.
An annual herb with no supplied native origin, tall pepperwort is self-supporting, with simple, broad leaves. It can grow to 51 cm tall.

summary: A flowering plant in the mustard family native to temperate Asia and northern and eastern Europe. It has naturalized in southwestern Europe and North America.
Annual herb native to Egypt and western Asia. It grows quickly and has a mildly spicy, aromatic taste; mainly the leaves of young shoots are eaten in salads, soups, sautés and purées.
edibilityNote: Mainly young-shoot leaves are used in salads, soups, sautés and purées.

summary: Moss with a cosmopolitan distribution, reported absent only from Australia and the Pacific Islands. Its pointed oval leaves grow in two rows, and it can tolerate extremely acidic water and grow under artificial light where natural light is absent.

Moss native to Eurasia and North America, many-fruited leskea usually grows on tree trunks and branches near water, though it also occurs in drier areas. It has creeping stems with spreading branches and curved brown to yellowish spore capsules on red to brownish-orange stalks.

A moss native to and prolific in the eastern and midwestern United States, it also has a wide distribution across both hemispheres. It occurs less commonly in Ontario and is common through Europe into Asia.
Evergreen shrub native to the southeastern United States. It has glossy, laurel-like leaves and hanging clusters of urn-shaped flowers in spring.

A sand-loving grass native to the coasts of northern and western Europe, lyme grass has an extensive root network historically used to stabilize coastal sand. Its seeds were formerly eaten, including as a wild grain in Iceland from at least the 12th century.
edibilityNote: The seeds were historically eaten; Icelanders harvested the grass as a wild grain from at least the 12th century.

summary: A cool-season perennial grass native to Europe, western Asia and North Africa. Its emerging leaves are rolled rather than folded, a key identification feature, and it is widely cultivated for forage and turf. Some plants carry a seed-transmitted fungus whose alkaloids can harm grazing livestock.

An annual grass native to southern Europe, northern Africa, the Middle East and the Indian subcontinent. It grows in open tufts and is cultivated as forage, especially in Australia, where it is also a serious crop weed; infected flower spikes can become dangerously toxic to livestock.
edibilityNote: Ergot-infected plants can cause ergotism in humans, but no human food use is documented.

summary: Annual grass with a cosmopolitan distribution. It closely resembles wheat until the ear appears, but has more slender spikes and ripens black rather than brown. When infected by an endophytic fungus, eating it causes drunken nausea and can be fatal.
edibilityNote: Eating fungus-infected darnel causes drunken nausea and may be fatal.

summary: A shrub native to China, winter honeysuckle forms a tangled mass of slender, spreading branches. Its paired creamy-white flowers have a strong lemony fragrance, followed by red berries.

A liverwort of unstated native origin, it has pale-green translucent leaves that are two-lobed low on the stem but become notched or smooth higher up. It has a strong scent and grows mainly at tree bases, but also on fallen wood, soil, leaf litter and roots.
A climbing or sprawling perennial native to Mexico's Sierra Madre Oriental mountains. It climbs with twisting leaf stalks and bears pink-and-white tubular flowers in the wild.
An annual flowering plant native to mainland Portugal and Madeira, small-flower trefoil is introduced in the Azores. It grows in annual pastures, meadows and fallow ground on temporarily wet soils.

A herbaceous perennial growing throughout Europe in damp, open places. It has golden-yellow flower clusters on upright stems; the always-hollow stem and the turned-back sepals forming a green star on each bud distinguish it from related species.

A flowering rush whose native origin is unsettled. Its grasslike leaves have long white hairs, and its terminal flower spikes develop into round capsules from late spring; unlike most rushes, it favors upland woodland habitats.

A deciduous woody shrub whose native origin is not stated in the supplied information. It has highly branched, often curved or drooping stems with thorns and produces bright orange-red berries. The fruits may be infused with hot water to make goji tea.
edibilityNote: The fruits may be infused with hot water to make goji tea.

summary: A fern native to eastern Asia, from Pakistan and India to Japan, southeastern Asia and New Guinea. Its extremely long, vine-like leaves climb other vegetation, while fertile leaflets bear spores along their fringed edges.

A biennial flowering plant native to coastal eastern Asia and islands of the Indian and Pacific oceans. It grows along beaches and in maritime rock crevices, with fleshy spoon-shaped leaves and white flower clusters in late spring and early summer.

An annual flowering plant native to mainland Portugal, Lythrum thymifolia has narrow, lance-shaped leaves, mostly alternating but opposite at the base. Its solitary, four-petalled flowers grow from the leaf joints and have two stamens.

summary: A deciduous tree native to the southeastern United States, bigleaf magnolia has the largest simple leaves and single flowers of any native North American woody plant. Its heavy foliage often bends the branches, while mature orange-coated seeds hang from cone-like fruits on silky threads.

An annual garden plant native to Greece and Albania, and possibly naturalized elsewhere in Mediterranean Europe. It forms masses of fragrant, four-petalled flowers in pink, purple and white, with cultivated plants varying especially in height and flower colour.

An apple tree native to Russia, Mongolia, China, Korea, Bhutan, India and Nepal, it bears fragrant white spring flowers. Its small red-to-yellow fruits grow in dense clusters and are eaten fresh or dried.
edibilityNote: The fruits are edible and eaten fresh or dried.

summary: A crabapple tree native to the United States. Its common variety is concentrated in the upper Mississippi Valley prairies, while the Texas variety is confined to a small part of central Texas. It bears white or pink summer flowers and small, apple-like autumn fruit.
An annual or perennial herb or shrub native to North and South America, three-lobe false mallow has been introduced to Australia, Africa, and southern and eastern Asia.
A perennial shrub of unknown native origin, though Mexico has been suggested. It has hanging red tubular flowers with protruding stamens, pointed oval leaves and hairy stems.
edibilityNote: The plant is described as edible, but no part or preparation is specified.

summary: A succulent cactus native to Texas, northeastern Mexico, Cuba and Hispaniola. Its round or slightly elongated stems usually form dense clusters, and their appearance varies considerably among subspecies. Flowers commonly appear alongside edible fruit.
edibilityNote: The cylindrical fruit is edible, with juice confined to its outer walls.

summary: A fast-growing shrub or small tree native to southern Brazil, Uruguay, Paraguay and Argentina. It has striking hand-shaped leaves and pale green, bell-shaped flowers in summer.
A liverwort with no explicitly documented native origin, Marchantia paleacea is found in North America, Europe and eastern Asia. It is used as a model organism to study plant–fungus partnerships.

A moss found across circumboreal regions, with separate tropical mountain populations in Africa, Mexico and Colombia. It forms green, reddish-brown or blackish mats on wet, lime-free rocks in and beside streams, and its rounded leaves are distinctly notched.
A moss with no stated native origin, it occurs in Europe and North America. It forms dense black-green mats of branched stems, with spreading, boat-shaped leaves divided into two triangular lobes.
An annual herb native across the Mediterranean Basin, from Macaronesia to the Caucasus. It usually grows along the ground, sometimes with ascending stems, and is used as livestock forage.

An annual herb with no supplied native origin, star-fruited medick is self-supporting and has compound, broad leaves. It grows on dry, stony, usually alkaline soils in places such as pastures, field edges, banks and walls.

A small tree endemic to eastern Australia, it has white or creamy-white papery bark and a dense canopy. Its perfumed, creamy-white flowers briefly cover the tree between October and February, followed by woody capsules scattered along the stems.
A plant whose native origin is not supplied, tall melilot is a preferred food plant of three short-tongued bumblebee species found in the UK.

An annual flowering herb native to mainland Portugal and Madeira, elegant melilot grows upright and branched, becoming nearly hairless. It bears loose clusters of many fragrant flowers, followed by yellowish fruits with sharply marked crosswise folds and a prominent seam.
