summary: Annual legume with no explicitly stated native origin, distributed in southern Europe. It has grooved stem leaves, tiny flowers from June to August, and pods marked with curved veins.

A perennial grass native to parts of Africa, with fragrant foliage and long, slender stems that layer into thick mats. It can lean on other plants for support and has become invasive in places including Hawaii and parts of South America.

A liverwort, forked veilwort grows on many kinds of tree and shrub bark and occasionally on rocks. It forms slim, translucent yellow-green mats whose branches and central ribs characteristically fork at their tips; spore-bearing structures are rare.
A small annual grass native to western and southwestern Europe. It grows in open vegetation on moist sand, forming tufts of hair-thin stems with two or three leaves clustered at or near the base.

A perennial grass native to much of East and Southeast Asia. It forms dense clumps from underground stems, with purplish flowers held above the foliage, and is widely grown as an ornamental in temperate regions.

A moss native to Europe and eastern North America. It has upright stems, toothed leaves and pointed-lid capsules, and commonly grows in damp, acidic woodland on soil, logs, rocks, tree bases and stream banks.
A perennial grass native to Europe, western Asia and northern Africa. It forms dense tussocks of coarse, pointed leaves, with long, narrow purple flower spikes that are a key identifying feature.

A tree-like perennial shrub native to Central America and southern Mexico. Its young leaves are deeply divided but become palmately lobed, while abundant white-and-yellow daisy-like flowers appear from late autumn to winter. It can form dense invasive stands where introduced.

A flowering plant broadly distributed across the western Mediterranean, Moricandia arvensis ranges from the Canary Islands and northern Africa to southern Europe, but was introduced to France, Corsica and Sardinia. Its photosynthesis uses an intermediate carbon-fixation system.

Fast-growing, drought-resistant tree native to northern India. It has feathery foliage and hanging three-sided pods, and its young pods and leaves are widely cultivated as vegetables, although Australia prohibits their retail food use because safety evidence was insufficient.
edibilityNote: Leaves, immature pods, seeds, flowers, roots and seed oil are used as food; excess root compounds may harm, and Australia prohibits retail food use.

summary: A large climbing vine native to tropical Central and South America and the West Indies, it climbs into the forest canopy. Its ridged pods bear orange-brown stinging hairs that cause intense itching, while its seeds have been used as famine food.
edibilityNote: The seeds have been used as famine food.

summary: Perennial warm-season grass native to eastern North America. It forms clumps topped by feathery purple-pink flowers with a cloudlike appearance, while its green leaves turn copper in autumn.
A fast-growing tree originating in the Americas, especially Mexico and Peru. It bears small, round, very sweet edible fruits, while its weak wood breaks easily in strong winds and storms.
edibilityNote: The small, very sweet fruit is edible and nutritious.

summary: A perennial bulb native to the Mediterranean region and naturalized elsewhere. A tassel of bright blue to violet sterile flowers rises above brownish-green fertile flowers. In Italy and Greece, its bulbs are eaten as a delicacy, traditionally boiled repeatedly or served pickled in olive oil.
edibilityNote: Bulbs are a delicacy in Italy and Greece; historically seasoned, and today often boiled repeatedly, pickled and kept in olive oil.

summary: A highly variable tree or shrub native to the Hawaiian Islands and ʻEua in Tonga, naio ranges from a dwarf shrub at the tree line to a large tree. Its fragrant white or pink flowers occur year-round, followed by juicy, bitter, waxy-white fruit that often dries while still attached.

A perennial herb endemic to the western Azores, it was reported only from Flores and Corvo, with the last wild populations on Flores described as recently extinct. Its deep blue-purple flowers have yellow centres and grow on spirally curved stems. It inhabits waterfalls, wet rocks and high wet meadows.

Aquatic plant native to Europe and Asia, inhabiting ponds, streams and other waters. Its whorled leaves occur both underwater and above the surface, with the exposed leaves smaller than the submerged ones. The flowers emerge above the water and are reported to bloom in August.

An annual submerged aquatic herb native to Europe, Asia and North Africa, it grows in dense clusters in calm water. Its highly branched stems break easily, while its strap-shaped leaves have clearly visible serrations.

A leafy liverwort with no native origin specified, distributed across Europe, Macaronesia, Japan and North America. It forms dense green-to-brown carpets, sometimes reddish in sunny places, and produces dark-brown oval spore capsules that mature in spring.
A flowering grass native to mainland Portugal and the Azores. It is the predominant herbaceous cover in the Serra da Estrela, where it is commonly called servum.

A grass native to Argentina, Chilean needle grass has strong colonising potential and is considered a serious threat to native species and habitats. Its release, possession, transport and trade are prohibited in the Canary Islands.

A grass native to the southwestern United States, northern Mexico and Argentina, Mexican feathergrass is cultivated ornamentally but readily escapes. In Australia it is considered a major potential threat to native grasslands, eucalypt woodlands and agricultural production.

A herbaceous perennial native to the Caucasus, Turkey and northern Iran, it has aromatic leaves and violet or lilac-blue summer flowers. Like other catmints, it can produce a euphoric effect in some domestic cats.

A tropical fern native to Florida, Mexico, the West Indies, Central and South America, Africa and Southeast Asia, this is the largest sword fern and can develop exceptionally long fronds. In the Democratic Republic of the Congo, its young leaves are cooked and eaten as a condiment or leafy vegetable.
edibilityNote: In the Democratic Republic of the Congo, young leaves are cooked and eaten as a condiment or leafy vegetable.

summary: An ornamental plant with a broad, possibly cultivation-influenced distribution around the Pacific, it is notable for its bright orange berries. Of 21 children reported to have ingested the plant, five developed mild poisoning symptoms including tiredness, stomach pain and vomiting.
edibilityNote: Of 21 children reported to have ingested the plant, five developed mild poisoning symptoms including tiredness, stomach pain and vomiting.

summary: An ornamental tobacco plant whose commonly grown varieties open their flowers in the late afternoon or evening and release a floral scent through the night. Flower colours include white, pink, yellow and lime green.

A rainforest plant native to South America, Aztec tobacco is exceptionally potent, with leaves containing up to nine times more nicotine than common tobacco. Its nicotine-rich leaves are used to produce pesticides and in varied cultural preparations.
edibilityNote: In Peru it is drunk as juice for entheogenic purposes; no human food use is documented.

summary: A flowering plant with no supplied native origin, red monk's-wort occurs around the western Mediterranean, including North Africa, the Iberian Peninsula and Sicily. It favors arable meadows, pasture, fields and roadsides, usually on alkaline soil but sometimes acidic soil, with some preference for disturbed, nitrogen-rich ground.

A small liverwort found on rotting forest logs across northern temperate and subarctic regions. Its leaves grow in two rows and each forms a tiny water-holding pocket; plants often turn reddish-purple in autumn and winter.

An aquatic plant native to Louisiana, Florida, Texas, Mexico and the Bahamas. Its leaves are green above and purple beneath, while its fragrant flowers function as female on their first day and male during the following two days.
edibilityNote: The plant is used for food, but the source does not specify parts, preparation or historical context.

summary: A small shrub indigenous to South Africa, it has fragrant yellow spring flowers followed by bright-red sepals and fruitlets that turn black when ripe. Cultivated as an ornamental, it is invasive in Australia and New Zealand.

A basil species native to Africa, including Madagascar, and southern Asia, African basil has leaves used in Nigeria to prepare pepper soup, rice, beans, plantains and other dishes. Its seeds seem to need strong sunlight to germinate, although they have germinated during an average UK summer.
edibilityNote: In Nigeria, the leaves are used in pepper soup, rice, beans, plantains and other dishes.

summary: Wildflower native to Europe and Asia. It bears pinkish-red flowers from June to September and is partly parasitic on grass roots, commonly growing in low-fertility soils.
A flowering plant native from central and southern Mexico through Honduras to Panama. It grows mainly in humid tropical environments.

A liverwort found in temperate, ocean-influenced parts of Europe and North America, as well as northern Mexico. It grows horizontally in dense mats, ranging from pale yellow-green to reddish-brown, particularly in bogs and other moist settings.

An aquatic flowering herb native from Ireland to central Siberia and from southern Scandinavia to the Mediterranean, it favours reedbeds and pools with fluctuating water levels. Its finely divided lower leaves are threadlike underwater but have flat, oval segments when emerging above water.
edibilityNote: Not widely used because of poisoning danger; its fruits are reputed to cause vertigo, drunkenness and narcotic symptoms.

summary: Flowering plant native to Mexico and the southeastern United States. Beach evening-primrose grows on coastal dunes and other disturbed sandy areas and has been introduced to many places worldwide.

Perennial herb widespread across the temperate Northern Hemisphere, throughout North America and Eurasia. Its pointed leaves are smooth above and woolly beneath, while its pale brown flower heads have green-centred bracts with papery brown edges.
A cactus that may have been endemic to Mexico but has been widely introduced. Unlike most Opuntia species, it is pollinated by hummingbirds.

A succulent, thorny shrub native to Argentina, Brazil, Paraguay and Uruguay, it develops a broad, almost tree-like crown. It has shiny green flattened shoots, dark yellow flowers and spineless, pear-shaped red fruit.

A tree-like cactus native to San Luis Potosí and Hidalgo in Mexico and to Nicaragua. Its flattened green stem segments are finely velvety and bear irritating short bristles, while its fleshy, seed-filled ripe fruits are edible.
edibilityNote: The fleshy ripe fruits are edible but full of seeds and protected by irritating bristles.

summary: A flowering plant whose young flower shoots are eaten as a vegetable, similarly to asparagus. It was once abundant near Bath in England.
edibilityNote: Young flower shoots are eaten as an asparagus-like vegetable.

summary: A moss widespread across the Northern Hemisphere, with separate occurrences in southern South America. Often growing on tree bark and stone near settlements, it is distinguished by transparent, glass-like leaf tips and capsules almost buried among the leaves.

A perennial grass of obscure native origin, with sources proposing widely different regions. Its thick, pointed, branching underground stems spread repeatedly and can form dense colonies or floating mats. Introduced across many tropical and subtropical areas, it is often a serious invasive weed.

A deciduous woody vine native to Korea, Japan and northern and eastern China. It climbs using branched tendrils tipped with sticky disks, and its usually three-lobed leaves turn orange-yellow to intense scarlet in autumn.
edibilityNote: Traditionally used as a culinary sweetener in Japan, although its dark blue fruit is inedible.

summary: A tropical to subtropical perennial grass native to Mexico and South America, bahiagrass is remembered for its prominent V-shaped flower head. Its creeping stems root along the ground and form dense turf.

Evergreen climbing shrub native to Central and northwestern South America, sweet granadilla climbs surrounding vegetation using coiling tendrils. Its aromatic, sweet-musky flowers last only one day. Ripe yellowish-orange fruits contain hard black seeds surrounded by translucent, sweet, edible pulp.
edibilityNote: The translucent pulp surrounding the hard black seeds is the edible part of the ripe fruit and tastes sweet.

summary: A fast-growing flowering vine native to Mexico, Guatemala and parts of South America. Its white-and-purple flowers are followed by blue or purple fruit containing edible orange pulp, though the pulp is not especially flavourful and the plant is not cultivated for fruit.
edibilityNote: The orange fruit pulp is edible but not particularly flavourful; the vine is not cultivated for its fruit.

summary: A vining passionflower with three-lobed leaves and ornate flowers followed by yellow-green fruits. It is grown as an ornamental and can be a minor pest in some areas.

A densely branching shrub native to South Africa, oak-leaved geranium has sticky, aromatic leaves divided into stiff, coarsely toothed, oak-like lobes. Its flowers are pink with darker pink markings, and its stems become woody with age.

A thallose liverwort occurring in North America, Europe, North Africa and parts of Asia, common pellia forms patches in damp, sheltered places. Its irregularly branched green body may have a red or purple tinge, and it produces spherical greenish-black capsules on pale green stalks.

A bristly perennial native to southwestern Europe, particularly northwest Iberia and France. It can retain green leaves through winter, and its pink buds open into vivid blue flowers with white centres. Its leaves and stems can irritate skin.
edibilityNote: Blue flowers garnish salads or drinks; roots remain liver-toxic after cooking, and leaves are toxic in large quantities.

summary: An evergreen flowering perennial native to tropical America. It has cupped, leathery leaves and shiny, winding spikes of white flowers, while cultivated plants may have variegated foliage. It is often confused with Peperomia magnoliifolia, although living plants differ in their waxy rather than fleshy leaves.

A scrambling cactus shrub native to South America, it has spiny, non-succulent stems and large leaves. Its leaves and fruits are edible, and the leaves are a popular vegetable in parts of Minas Gerais, Brazil.
edibilityNote: Leaves and fruits are edible; the leaves are traditionally eaten as a vegetable in parts of Minas Gerais, Brazil.

summary: A cactus native to eastern and southern Brazil, the rose cactus grows as a shrub or small tree. Unlike most cacti, it keeps its leaves and bears showy, rose-like flowers ranging from pale pink to purplish pink.
edibilityNote: The leaves can be eaten as a salad or used in stews.
